name: Serratia bacterial leaf spot
summary: A pathogenicity-confirmed Cannabis bacterial disease producing small vein-limited angular lesions that can coalesce across leaves, stems and flower parts. Red bacterial ooze is useful supporting evidence, but neither lesion shape nor red material is species-confirmatory; plant-linked isolation and molecular identification are required.
affectedParts: whole aerial plant in severe greenhouse observations
stages: field or other production context not established
indicators: Small dark-brown 1–3 mm lesions are angular or vein-limited on hemp leaves
Early lesions are localized around veins rather than uniformly circular
Lesions coalesce into larger irregular necrotic regions as disease advances
Compatible injury can extend from leaves to stems and flower parts
Red bacterial ooze or streaming can emerge from affected tissue, including after a lesion is punctured
Dark-pink raised colonies and Gram-negative bacilli were part of the original isolate description
16S rRNA plus rpoB sequence evidence supports Serratia marcescens rather than a visual bacterial-leaf-spot label
Reproduction of compatible lesions after inoculation, symptomless controls, and reisolation provide pathogenicity support
exclusions: Angular or vein-limited lesions are present without plant-linked bacterial isolation or molecular evidence
Red, pink, or sap-like material is present without microscopy, culture, and plant linkage
Round dark-margined lesions with gray-brown centers and pepper-like fungal sporulation support Exserohilum
Pycnidia or another fungal fruiting structure support Septoria or another fungal leaf spot
Xanthomonas or another bacterial pathogen is identified from the same lesions
Lesions remain confined to an exposure edge or spray/contact pattern and no organism is recovered
Mite or thrips organisms and feeding signs explain stippling, silvering, bronzing, or scarring
Only detached, stock, vendor, forum, generated, or low-resolution imagery is available without collection and laboratory metadata

progression.description: Small 1–3 mm dark-brown lesions develop along or between veins; a still image may resemble several bacterial, fungal, or contact-injury classes.
Angular lesion margins become more evident as necrosis is bounded by venation and multiple lesions accumulate.
Adjacent lesions merge into larger irregular necrotic regions; capture the same marked leaf over time rather than inferring progression from unrelated plants.
Compatible lesions may occur on stems and flower parts as well as leaves; document each affected part and retain plant linkage.
Large tissue areas and whole plants were lost in the original greenhouse observations, but that report does not establish a universal severity timeline or field outcome.

lookAlikes: Other bacterial leaf spot or blight
Contact spray, droplet, or mechanical injury
confirmation: Capture the intact plant, canopy distribution, affected organs, both leaf surfaces, lesion scale, vein relationship, and a close-up of any ooze before sampling.
Sample several fresh, active lesion margins with intact plant identifiers; retain matched asymptomatic tissue and environmental/exposure history as controls.
Use aseptic bacterial isolation and record colony morphology, but do not identify Serratia from pink or red pigment alone.
Use Gram reaction/microscopy plus validated molecular identification; the original report used 16S rRNA and rpoB sequence evidence.
When causal ground truth is required, link the same plant and lesion sample to pathogenicity evidence or an equivalent qualified plant-diagnostic conclusion, not merely an environmental isolate.
Investigate fungal fruiting structures/spores and other recovered organisms because hemp leaf diseases overlap and mixed infections can occur.

Keep symptom-only, angular-lesion-only, red-ooze-only, detached-leaf, mixed-pathogen, unlinked-laboratory, low-resolution, stock, forum, vendor, or generated captures out of the confirmed Serratia class and route them to human review.
immediateActions: Separate strongly affected propagation material and avoid moving wet symptomatic tissue through clean areas.
Preserve fresh, plant-linked lesion samples before sanitation or treatment and photograph sampling locations.
Avoid manipulating or puncturing suspect lesions outside an appropriate diagnostic workflow.
correctivePlan: Use laboratory-confirmed bacterial-disease sanitation and management appropriate to the production system; visual appearance alone does not justify a Serratia-specific intervention.
Correct documented splash, sanitation, or leaf-wetness risks without treating those conditions as proof of pathogen identity.
prevention: Sanitize tools and contact surfaces between plant groups and minimize splash movement from symptomatic plants.
Use clean propagation material and retain lot/plant identifiers through diagnostic sampling.
Scout leaves, stems, and flower parts together so multi-organ progression is documented rather than reconstructed from isolated close-ups.
warnings: Serratia includes strains of human-health relevance; use appropriate hygiene and qualified diagnostic-laboratory handling.
Angular necrotic lesions, red ooze, and pink-red colonies are supporting observations, not species-specific ground truth.
The original report was greenhouse-bound and included cultivar Carmagnola; do not generalize its timing, severity, distribution, or cultivar response.

The NC State hemp image is a generic bacterial leaf spot/blight differential with no explicit species-level caption, item-level creator credit, reusable license, or linked laboratory record; it must remain hidden from display and training.

sources.title: First Report of Serratia marcescens Causing a Leaf Spot Disease on Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa)
supportedClaims: Greenhouse-grown hemp developed small dark-brown 1–3 mm vein-limited angular lesions on leaves, stems, and flower parts; lesions coalesced into larger necrotic regions and red bacterial ooze was observed.
Serratia marcescens was supported by colony/microscopic traits and 16S rRNA plus rpoB sequence evidence.
Inoculated hemp developed similar lesions, controls remained symptomless, and the organism was reisolated, providing pathogenicity evidence rather than visual association alone.

The original observation and pathogenicity work were greenhouse-bound and included Cannabis sativa cultivar Carmagnola, so they do not establish universal field, cultivar, age, severity, or timing labels.

sources.title: Surveying for Potential Diseases and Abiotic Disorders of Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa) Production
supportedClaims: A North Carolina 2017–2018 hemp diagnostic survey identified 16 diseases caused by fungi, bacteria, oomycetes, and nematodes; the study used clinic diagnostics, morphology, sequence data for representative organisms, and pathogenicity testing for its confirmed disease set.

Fusarium foliar and flower blight was common in submitted samples and involved F. equiseti and F. graminearum; flowers developed surface hyphae and light-brown necrotic tips while leaves developed circular light-brown lesions about 1 cm wide with dark margins and gray-brown aging centers.
Exserohilum rostratum leaf spot occurred on leaves and stems as round brown-to-black lesions with darkened margins and abundant conidia, with ITS1/RPB2 evidence supporting the identification.

Rhizoctonia solani was found on roots and crowns with plant wilting and necrotic lesions just above the soil line; pigmented septate hyphae showed characteristic right-angle branching and sequence evidence supported R. solani.

Southern blight caused whole-plant wilt in reproductive hemp during hot midseason conditions, with abundant hyphae and russet-brown sclerotia on roots/lower stems and sequence/phylogenetic evidence supporting Athelia rolfsii/Sclerotium rolfsii.
Meloidogyne incognita was identified from galled hemp roots with females and egg masses; affected plants had some associated stunting.

The survey documented Serratia-associated, vein-limited angular hemp lesions and red bacterial ooze emerging from punctured lesions, while emphasizing that hemp leaf diseases overlap visually and require diagnostic separation.

sources.title: Exserohilum Leaf Spot Causing Problems in NC Hemp
supportedClaims: NC State Extension identifies Exserohilum rostratum leaf spot on multiple industrial-hemp strains in North Carolina and warns that other hemp leaf spots can look similar, so accurate diagnosis is important.
The institutional hemp description states that Exserohilum can affect leaves, stems, and flowers; leaf lesions are most distinct as small round spots with dark-brown margins and gray-brown centers.
As lesions age, spores may appear in gray-brown centers like fine ground pepper and lesions may coalesce into larger irregular necrotic areas; these are progression cues, not species confirmation.
The page names bacterial, Fusarium, and Septoria leaf spots as similar hemp diseases and characterizes bacterial leaf spot/blight as angular, supporting explicit differential checks.

NC State Extension states that hemp leaf spots can look similar and accurate diagnosis is important; its industrial-hemp bacterial leaf spot/blight reference is characterized only as angular lesions and is not presented as species-confirmed Serratia ground truth.

The same institutional differential describes Exserohilum lesions as small, round spots with dark-brown margins and gray-brown centers that may develop pepper-like spores as they age, helping separate a fungal leaf-spot pattern from vein-limited bacterial-compatible injury.
The page identifies bacterial, Fusarium, and Septoria leaf spots as visual alternatives to Exserohilum, supporting a multi-pathogen differential rather than an image-only bacterial species label.

sources.title: Pathogen Safety Data Sheets: Infectious Substances – Serratia spp.
authors: Pathogen Regulation Directorate, Public Health Agency of Canada
supportedClaims: The Public Health Agency of Canada identifies Serratia species as Gram-negative rods and notes that many, but not all, species or strains produce a red-to-pink pigment; pigment therefore cannot be required for or used alone as species confirmation.

The agency describes Serratia species as opportunistic pathogens, classifies the genus as Risk Group 2 while noting that the classification may not apply to every species, and specifies Containment Level 2 practices for potentially infectious material or cultures.

For work with infected material or cultures, the sheet calls for protective clothing, gloves where direct contact is unavoidable, eye protection where splashes are possible, and controls for aerosol-producing procedures.

media.alt: Detached industrial-hemp leaf with angular necrotic lesions, presented by NC State Extension as bacterial leaf spot and blight.
media.caption: NC State Extension Figure 2 generic bacterial leaf spot/blight differential. The page characterizes angular lesions but does not provide a species-level caption, plant-linked laboratory result, individual creator credit, or reusable license.
media.creator: NC State Extension Plant Pathology; individual image creator not stated
media.license: Copyright/reuse and automated-training terms not stated on the NC State Extension landing page
media.requiredAttribution: NC State Extension Plant Pathology, Figure 2 in “Exserohilum Leaf Spot Causing Problems in NC Hemp” by Lindsey D. Thiessen, published August 16, 2019. Obtain documented rights-holder permission and species-level provenance before display, copying, modification, or automated training.
media.diagnosticLabel: serratia-marcescens-leaf-spot — generic industrial-hemp bacterial leaf spot/blight differential, not Serratia ground truth
useLimitations: Reference-link metadata only; no media file is copied into the repository.
Do not display, copy, modify, or use for automated training until reusable rights are documented.
The landing page labels the figure only as bacterial leaf spot and blight with angular lesions; do not convert the asset filename into a Serratia species label.
Detached-leaf close-up lacks whole-plant distribution, matched opposite surface, progression, scale, collection metadata, and plant-linked culture or molecular confirmation.
Angular lesions overlap Xanthomonas and other bacterial diseases, downy mildew, fungal leaf spots, and contact injury.
media.stage: detached industrial-hemp leaf; production stage not stated
media.severity: moderate lesion coverage; causal severity not established

name: Xanthomonas bacterial leaf spot
summary: A documented bacterial leaf spot of hemp in which small water-soaked lesions progress to approximately 1–2 mm necrotic centers surrounded by comparatively broad yellow halos; images can support triage but cannot distinguish the bacterium from fungal or abiotic look-alikes.
stages: growth stage not established in cannabis-specific primary evidence
indicators: Small water-soaked leaf spots before necrosis develops
Necrotic centers approximately 1–2 mm in diameter
Yellow halos approximately 2–3 mm wide
Discrete lesions with a halo wider than the necrotic center
Focal spotting rather than a whole-leaf nutrient-mobility gradient
exclusions: White surface colonies, fungal fruiting structures, or diagnostic spores support a fungal cause
Fine stippling, webbing, or organisms on the leaf underside support arthropod feeding
Damage follows spray droplets, contact points, or a documented chemical application and does not progress after exposure ends
Symptoms follow a measured older-leaf or younger-leaf nutrient pattern without discrete water-soaked lesions
A plant diagnostic laboratory identifies another pathogen or abiotic cause from a representative active lesion

progression.description: A small water-soaked spot develops in leaf tissue; record both leaf surfaces because general bacterial leaf spots can first be more apparent from below.
The center becomes necrotic at roughly 1–2 mm across while a yellow halo roughly 2–3 mm wide surrounds it, producing a small dark center with a proportionally broad chlorotic border.

Cannabis-specific primary evidence used here does not establish a dependable late-stage coalescence, defoliation, stem, or flower pattern. Do not infer those labels from general-host bacterial leaf-spot images.

lookAlikes: Septoria or other fungal leaf spot
Edema or water-soaking from physiological stress
confirmation: Photograph the whole plant and both sides of several leaves, then capture a scale-referenced close-up showing the necrotic-center and halo dimensions and the distribution of lesions across the canopy.

Submit fresh, recently expanding lesions that include the transition between healthy and affected tissue to a plant diagnostic laboratory; keep samples separate, cool, and dry according to that laboratory’s instructions.

Ask the laboratory to distinguish bacterial from fungal leaf spot and, if a Xanthomonas isolate is recovered, identify it with validated physiological and molecular or sequence-based methods rather than morphology alone.
Microscopic bacterial streaming may support a bacterial differential, but absence of streaming does not exclude bacteria and streaming does not confirm Xanthomonas cannabis to species.
Map reports using the current accepted name Xanthomonas cannabis while retaining Xanthomonas campestris pv. cannabis as a historical synonym for literature and laboratory searches.
immediateActions: Flag the plant and pause movement of cuttings or symptomatic foliage until laboratory triage.
Handle suspect foliage only when dry, avoid splash between plants, and clean hands and tools before moving to unaffected plants.
Keep unconfirmed lesion photographs out of bacterial ground-truth and training sets.
correctivePlan: Base removal, sanitation, and any crop treatment on the confirmed diagnosis and local legal label; a visual bacterial-leaf-spot suspicion is not a treatment prescription.
Inspect nearby plants for comparable small haloed lesions and document whether new lesions appear after splash or handling events without treating that association as proof.
If laboratory results do not recover or identify the bacterium, reopen fungal, arthropod, chemical, and physiological differentials.
prevention: Use documented healthy propagation material and retain lot or mother-plant traceability.
Minimize leaf wetness and splash during routine handling where compatible with the production system.
Disinfect tools and segregate symptomatic material under a written sanitation protocol.
warnings: A photograph or video cannot confirm Xanthomonas cannabis; lesion size and halo geometry are triage features only.
The key symptom measurements come from a historical Japanese hemp report and do not establish current local prevalence, cultivar susceptibility, or production-system risk.
General greenhouse bacterial-leaf-spot guidance is used only for differential diagnosis and handling precautions, not as cannabis-specific epidemiological proof.
No cannabis-specific image or video with verified reuse and automated-training permission was found for this batch; no media was copied or admitted.

sources.title: Bacterial leaf spot of hemp caused by Xanthomonas campestris pv. cannabis in Japan
sources.publisher: Springer Nature on behalf of the Phytopathological Society of Japan
supportedClaims: The cannabis-specific Japanese report described leaf lesions with necrotic centers approximately 1–2 mm in diameter and yellow halos approximately 2–3 mm wide.
Pathological, physiological, and genetic characterization linked the Japanese causal bacterium to the organism historically named Xanthomonas campestris pv. cannabis in Romania.

sources.title: Comparative genomics of a cannabis pathogen reveals insight into the evolution of pathogenicity in Xanthomonas
supportedClaims: Cannabis bacterial leaf spot was described as water-soaked lesions followed by necrosis with a yellow halo.
The study sequenced two geographically distinct strains previously isolated from symptomatic cannabis tissue in Japan and Romania and proposed the species name Xanthomonas cannabis.

sources.title: Species: Xanthomonas cannabis
sources.organization: List of Prokaryotic names with Standing in Nomenclature (LPSN)
supportedClaims: Xanthomonas cannabis (ex Severin 1978) McKnight et al. 2026 is the validly published correct species name.
The historical names Xanthomonas campestris pv. cannabis and the 2015 proposed name “Xanthomonas cannabis” are homotypic synonyms; type strain identifiers include ICMP 6570, LMG 9042, and NCPPB 2877.

sources.title: Bacterial Leaf Spot on Greenhouse Ornamentals
supportedClaims: Across greenhouse ornamental hosts, bacterial and fungal leaf spots can be visually confounded; bacterial streaming can support suspicion but may be absent, and diagnosis by a plant disease clinic is recommended.

As general bacterial-leaf-spot precautions rather than cannabis-specific epidemiology, splashing water and handling wet plants can spread bacteria, so suspect plants should be handled dry and separately.

name: High-temperature or high-light exposure
summary: Measured high temperature or unusually intense light can alter Cannabis physiology, yield, and flowering development, but published Cannabis experiments do not validate cupping, bleaching, or a single PPFD or temperature value as a universal visible injury diagnosis.
affectedParts: canopy nearest a local heat or light source
indicators: Air temperature, leaf temperature, PPFD, photoperiod, and humidity are recorded at the affected canopy position across time
Abnormal new inflorescence clusters develop on top of older inflorescences during sustained high-temperature flowering exposure
Flower maturation or production differs from a matched cultivar under a cooler measured regime
Gas-exchange or chlorophyll-fluorescence measurements change even when a specific foliar lesion is absent
A spatial gradient repeats with measured temperature or irradiance rather than merely with leaf age
exclusions: No time-stamped canopy-level temperature, leaf-temperature, PPFD, photoperiod, or humidity record supports an exposure event
Only upward leaf curl, pale tissue, dry margins, or canopy posture is visible
Mites, thrips, webbing, cast skins, eggs, frass, or feeding scars are present
Root-zone water content, irrigation history, pH, EC, or root disease explains the distribution better
The change follows nutrient, pesticide, growth-regulator, or other chemical application
Only late-flower senescence or cultivar-typical inflorescence architecture is visible
High PPFD alone is treated as injury even though the plant is acclimated and temperature and water status are within its measured response range

progression.description: Record canopy and leaf temperature, PPFD, photoperiod, humidity or vapor-pressure deficit, carbon dioxide, irrigation status, cultivar, and exact duration before assigning an environmental-exposure label.

Photosynthesis, respiration, transpiration, stomatal conductance, and water-use efficiency can change with temperature; controlled Cannabis results show that the direction and optimum are variety dependent and may precede a specific visible lesion.

At 31/27 degrees Celsius day/night versus 25/21 degrees Celsius in one controlled study, abnormal new clusters developed atop older inflorescences and normal maturation was disrupted; dry-matter response differed between the two genotypes.

Compare new leaves and inflorescences after the measured exposure is corrected; persistent or spreading changes without a matching environmental gradient require renewed pest, pathogen, root-zone, nutrition, and genetic evaluation.

lookAlikes: Water shortage or excessive vapor demand
High root-zone EC or pH-related nutrient unavailability
confirmation: Map PPFD and air temperature at multiple canopy positions and times; measure leaf temperature with a calibrated contact or infrared method and record humidity or vapor-pressure deficit, photoperiod, carbon dioxide, and lamp distance.
Compare affected and unaffected plants of the same cultivar, developmental stage, irrigation treatment, and root-zone condition; include a cooler or lower-exposure reference when available.
Inspect leaf undersides and protected new growth with magnification for mites and thrips, and document the root system, substrate water content, pH, and EC.
Use serial whole-plant, canopy, and close-up images with an exposure log; do not convert a single photograph or uncalibrated camera color shift into heat- or light-stress ground truth.

For abnormal flowering, inspect multiple inflorescences over time and compare with cultivar records to separate heat-associated reversion or foxtailing from normal architecture, late-flower growth, or genetic traits.
immediateActions: Preserve the pre-correction environmental log and matched photographs, then remove an acute unsafe heat load or equipment fault gradually.
Verify irrigation delivery and root-zone moisture before changing light, humidity, or irrigation together.
Quarantine or isolate only when pest or infectious disease evidence warrants it; environmental exposure alone is not contagious.
correctivePlan: Correct the measured source, such as a canopy hot spot, failed cooling or air mixing, excessive lamp proximity, or an abrupt unacclimated light increase, while changing one controllable factor at a time.
Re-map the canopy after correction and score only new tissue and subsequent inflorescence development against a matched control.
Escalate persistent abnormalities to pest microscopy, root-zone testing, tissue analysis, or a plant diagnostic laboratory rather than repeatedly reducing light without evidence.
prevention: Log canopy-level PPFD, photoperiod, air and leaf temperature, humidity or vapor-pressure deficit, carbon dioxide, and irrigation status by zone.
Map hot spots and irradiance gradients after fixture, HVAC, canopy-height, or density changes.
Retain cultivar- and stage-matched healthy reference sequences because published temperature optima and production responses vary among Cannabis genotypes.
warnings: Upward curl, tacoing, bleaching, pale tops, dry margins, and leaf angle are nonspecific and are not validated Cannabis heat- or light-stress ground truth without measured exposure and exclusion checks.

A controlled Stillwater trial produced linearly increasing inflorescence yield through 1,800 micromoles per square metre per second; therefore PPFD magnitude alone does not prove injury or define a universal damaging threshold.
Temperature optima for photosynthesis differed among tested drug- and fiber-type varieties, so 25, 30, 35, or 40 degrees Celsius must not be generalized into one cultivar-independent diagnosis.
The abnormal inflorescence-cluster observation came from defined 31/27 degrees Celsius flowering treatments in two genotypes and should be labeled treatment-associated, not universally heat-specific.
No reusable Cannabis symptom photograph with exposure measurements and adequate causal confirmation was admitted in this record; media remain empty rather than promoting anecdotal or vendor imagery.

sources.title: High air temperature reduces plant specialized metabolite yield in medical cannabis, and has genotype-specific effects on inflorescence dry matter production
sources.organization: Environmental and Experimental Botany (Holweg et al.)
supportedClaims: In controlled short-day production, plants of two medical Cannabis genotypes were compared at 25/21 and 31/27 degrees Celsius day/night temperatures and at PPFDs of 600, 900, and 1,200 micromoles per square metre per second.

The higher-temperature treatment reduced total cannabinoid concentration in both genotypes but reduced inflorescence dry matter only in Harmony CBD, demonstrating a genotype-specific production response.

High temperature produced abnormal new inflorescence clusters on top of older inflorescences and disrupted normal maturation; this flowering morphology is treatment-associated but is not a universal image-only heat threshold.

sources.title: Temperature response of photosynthesis in different drug and fiber varieties of Cannabis sativa L.
sources.organization: Physiology and Molecular Biology of Plants (Chandra et al.)
sources.publisher: Springer Nature on behalf of the Prof. H. S. Srivastava Foundation for Science and Society
supportedClaims: Across three drug-type and four fiber-type Cannabis varieties measured from 20 to 40 degrees Celsius, photosynthetic optima varied by variety from about 25 to 35 degrees Celsius.

Dark respiration approximately doubled from 20 to 40 degrees Celsius in all tested varieties, while photosynthesis, transpiration, stomatal conductance, and water-use efficiency showed variety-dependent responses.
The experiment measured gas exchange rather than a validated visible heat-injury syndrome, so its temperature values must not be used as universal image-label thresholds.

sources.title: Cannabis Yield, Potency, and Leaf Photosynthesis Respond Differently to Increasing Light Levels in an Indoor Environment
sources.organization: Frontiers in Plant Science (Rodriguez-Morrison et al.)
supportedClaims: Indoor-grown Cannabis sativa Stillwater was exposed during flowering to average canopy PPFDs from 120 to 1,800 micromoles per square metre per second.
Dry inflorescence yield increased linearly through the highest tested PPFD even though leaf-level photosynthesis saturated below 1,800 micromoles per square metre per second.

The high-light experiment did not establish a universal PPFD injury threshold or validate cupping, bleaching, or edge necrosis as light-specific visual symptoms; light exposure must be interpreted with cultivar, acclimation, canopy position, temperature, carbon dioxide, and water status.

In Stillwater during the 12-hour flowering phase, chlorophyll-content index was higher in week 1 than weeks 5 and 9 and was consistently higher in upper- than lower-canopy fan leaves; the authors described evidence of early senescence but stated that the contributions of leaf age and plant ontogeny to diminished week-9 photosynthesis were unresolved.
The study measured chlorophyll index and physiology rather than validating a yellow-leaf appearance, harvest date, or universal late-flower-fade sequence.

name: Herbicide injury — clomazone-type bleaching
summary: An exposure-confirmed hemp differential for Group 13 clomazone injury. Compatible new-growth bleaching is highly nonspecific: a clomazone label requires a temporally and spatially plausible soil-carryover, pre-emergence, or vapor-drift pathway, ideally strengthened by records or residue analysis.
affectedParts: older foliage later in sustained injury
indicators: The youngest expanding leaves or shoot tips become pale green, pale yellow, or nearly white while older pre-exposure foliage may initially retain more green pigment

Pigment loss can be interveinal, marginal, patchy, or nearly complete rather than following a single Cannabis-specific shape; occasional pink-to-purple margins may occur in sensitive non-Cannabis plants
Affected tissue may remain bleached and growth-reduced, advance to necrosis under severe exposure, or be followed by normally green new growth after a limited exposure
Several Cannabis plants share a boundary, downwind, previous-crop, treated-soil, bed, container-lot, equipment, or irrigation-source pattern rather than a random single-leaf pattern
Susceptible weeds or other plant species near the same field edge may show compatible pigment loss, strengthening a vapor-drift hypothesis without proving the active ingredient
A documented commercial hemp field case linked clomazone soil carryover to bleaching of newly formed tissue and nonrecovery
A controlled pre-emergence greenhouse screen found severe stand, height, and biomass reductions in Felina 32 hemp at the tested clomazone rate, establishing hemp sensitivity under those conditions
exclusions: No plausible clomazone or related pigment-inhibitor source, timing, route, field history, neighboring application, equipment pathway, or residue evidence can be established
Iron, sulfur, manganese, root-zone pH, EC, water status, or tissue results explain the leaf-age and canopy pattern better
Bleaching is restricted to the most light-exposed canopy surface or lamp footprint and measured irradiance or heat history supports photooxidative injury
Stable sectoral or clone-recurrent variegation persists without an exposure gradient, growth suppression, or injury progression
Magnification finds broad mites, hemp russet mites, thrips, feeding scars, eggs, cast skins, or webbing linked to the affected tissue
Discrete lesions, surface growth, ooze, vascular discoloration, root/crown disease, or validated pathogen testing supports an infectious cause
Rapid droplet-shaped scorch, bronzing, or near-immediate necrosis fits a contact or PPO-inhibitor exposure better than carotenoid-inhibitor bleaching
Color loss disappears under neutral calibrated lighting or is attributable to clipping, white balance, overexposure, compression, or infrared imaging

progression.description: A soil, pre-emergence, carryover, contaminated-equipment, irrigation, or off-target vapor pathway precedes symptoms; preserve records before altering the site.
New shoot tips and expanding leaves lose pigment first, ranging from pale green or yellow to nearly white while older foliage may remain greener.
Limited exposure may be followed by green new growth above older bleached leaves; sustained or severe injury can suppress growth and extend pigment loss.
Severely bleached tissue can become necrotic, and young plants exposed through soil may be more severely affected than established plants receiving limited drift.
The North Carolina carryover case did not recover, but institutional sources describe recovery after lighter exposure; outcome cannot be inferred from one frame.

lookAlikes: Broad mite or hemp russet mite injury
confirmation: Capture neutral-color whole-area video plus matched upper, middle, and lower canopy stills, close-ups of both leaf surfaces, and unaffected comparison plants before any correction.

Map affected and unaffected Cannabis plants against field edges, wind direction, previous-crop rows, treated soil, bed or container lots, irrigation zones, traffic routes, and application or transplant dates.
Photograph susceptible weeds and other plant species along affected and unaffected edges; shared bleaching supports an exposure plume but does not identify clomazone.

Reconstruct product, active ingredient, rate, formulation, application, weather, soil, prior-crop restriction, equipment-cleanout, substrate, and water-treatment records with a qualified crop professional.

Preserve plant, soil, water, and product samples under an accredited laboratory chain of custody when residue analysis is appropriate; interpret nondetection with sampling time, analyte, matrix, and method limits.
Measure root-zone pH, EC, moisture, and temperature and obtain plant tissue analysis where appropriate to test nutrient and root-zone alternatives.
Inspect growing tips with magnification and submit plant-linked tissue for pathogen testing when pest or infectious differentials remain plausible.
Keep symptom-only, detached-leaf-only, non-Cannabis, generated, vendor, anecdotal, unverified, and exposure-unlinked samples out of the confirmed clomazone class and automated training.
immediateActions: Stop further suspected exposure without disturbing evidence; preserve labels, spray and field records, weather data, equipment-cleanout history, and representative samples.
Segregate suspect plant lots and prevent contaminated soil, substrate, water, tools, or equipment from moving into unaffected production areas.
Do not apply speculative nutrients, pesticides, or flushing treatments before documenting the pre-correction pattern and root-zone measurements.
correctivePlan: Base any response on the confirmed exposure route, residue context, plant stage, local pesticide law, and qualified agronomic guidance; this diagnostic record does not recommend herbicide use or a universal remediation.
Track the same plants and fixed viewpoints through later growth, recording whether green tissue resumes, bleaching progresses, necrosis develops, or plants fail to recover.
Investigate nutrient, light, pest, and pathogen alternatives concurrently when exposure evidence is incomplete or mixed.
prevention: Maintain complete pesticide, crop-rotation, field, substrate, water, and equipment-cleanout records and review legally applicable plant-back restrictions before hemp establishment.
Use drift-reduction, buffer, application-timing, and equipment-segregation practices required by the product label and local regulations.
Record baseline imagery and unaffected comparison areas so a later boundary or plume pattern can be evaluated.
warnings: Bleached Cannabis tissue cannot identify clomazone, dose, formulation, route, or legal source from appearance alone; photo/video confidence is capped at 0.20.
The controlled clomazone experiment tested one hemp cultivar, one greenhouse soil system, and one pre-emergence rate; its quantitative injury is not a universal Cannabis threshold.
The field nonrecovery case and institutional lighter-exposure recovery guidance describe different exposure contexts and should not be collapsed into a deterministic prognosis.
The two licensed NC State images show grape and pokeweed, not Cannabis; they are transfer references for color and field-edge context only and are excluded from Cannabis training and evaluation.
No licensed, plant-linked Cannabis clomazone progression image or verified diagnostic video was located for this batch.
This profile is an injury-identification differential, not a pesticide recommendation or substitute for label, regulatory, laboratory, or professional advice.

sources.title: Surveying for Potential Diseases and Abiotic Disorders of Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa) Production
supportedClaims: North Carolina hemp diagnostic submissions included root binding, excess water, nutrient disorders, and herbicide injury as important abiotic differentials.

Root-bound transplants were commonly reported and affected plants did not reliably overcome the bound root system after field transplanting; secondary Fusarium and Pythium infections were also observed.
Clomazone carryover caused bleaching of newly formed hemp tissue in a documented commercial field case and the plants did not recover.

Field and diagnostic observations also documented manganese toxicity as interveinal yellowing followed by interveinal necrosis, supporting it as a real hemp differential but not a camera-only diagnosis.

sources.title: Evaluating herbicide tolerance of industrial hemp (Cannabis sativa L.)
sources.publisher: Wiley on behalf of the Crop Science Society of America
supportedClaims: In a randomized greenhouse pre-emergence screen using Cannabis sativa cultivar Felina 32, clomazone at 1.4 kg active ingredient per hectare produced only two surviving plants per pot, 8 cm mean plant height, and 0.6 g mean biomass at eight weeks, versus seven plants, 49 cm, and 13.5 g in the untreated check.

Across the greenhouse screen, clomazone was among treatments that reduced stand count 43–71%, height 47–84%, and biomass 73–96% relative to the untreated check; the paper groups clomazone and norflurazon as highly injurious pigment inhibitors.

Clomazone was screened pre-emergence in the greenhouse but was not advanced into the field study, so the experiment supports severe hemp sensitivity under its tested rate and conditions rather than a universal field threshold or a visual diagnosis.
The authors reported that hemp responses varied across environments, years, and cultivars for tested herbicides and called for corroboration before commercial recommendations.

sources.title: Herbicide Damage Symptoms on Hemp
sources.organization: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources, UC Weed Science
sources.publisher: Regents of the University of California
supportedClaims: The institutional hemp demonstration exposed plants to herbicides used near hemp production to document injury expected from specific active ingredients or related modes of action.

Its clomazone example identifies carotenoid-biosynthesis inhibition: bleaching ranges from yellow to almost pure white, begins in newly formed tissue, may progress to older tissue as existing carotenoids turn over, and can advance to necrosis.

The guide distinguishes potentially dramatic but rarely lethal established-plant drift injury from more damaging soil-carryover injury to seedlings or young transplants; these are contextual patterns, not dose-independent outcome guarantees.

The source PDF contains mixed herbicide-treatment photographs without a verified reusable asset license or panel-level training labels, so those figures are citation evidence only and are not indexed as reusable media.

sources.title: Carotenoid Pigments
supportedClaims: Carotenoid-pigment-inhibitor injury can produce white, pale-yellow, or pale-green new shoot tips and leaves, occasional pink-to-purple margins, reduced growth, and later necrosis; resumed green growth can appear above older bleached foliage in less-sensitive plants.

The guide identifies clomazone as a soil-absorbed Group 13 pigment inhibitor with high vapor-drift potential and recommends inspecting susceptible weeds and other plants along field edges for a shared exposure pattern.

Severe iron deficiency, bleaching infections, contact-herbicide injury, PPO-inhibitor bronzing, air pollution, and insect-growth-regulator exposure can overlap visually and require contextual exclusion.
The grape and pokeweed photographs are explicitly credited to J. Neal under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, but they are non-Cannabis transfer references and do not establish clomazone injury in hemp.

name: Alternaria leaf spot
summary: A Cannabis brown-blight and leaf-spot differential supported by pathogenicity studies. Small dark or yellow spots, brown-to-gray lesions, halos, concentric rings, perforated centers, and black sporulation are compatible with Alternaria, but none is species-specific. Confirmed labels require plant-linked culture or validated molecular evidence; photo or video alone is capped at moderate-low confidence.
affectedParts: seed and propagation material as possible pathogen reservoirs
indicators: Small dark or yellow spots develop on Cannabis leaves and enlarge into brown-to-gray lesions; the Chinese pathogenicity report described irregular brown lesions with light-yellow halos.
Compatible lesions may be circular or irregular, may have dark black-to-purple borders or yellow halos, and may show concentric rings, but any one of these patterns can be absent.
Lesion centers can become fragile or perforated as disease advances, creating a shot-hole appearance that is not unique to Alternaria.
Sooty black spore masses can develop in lesion centers, and affected leaf or bud surfaces can darken from brown toward brown-black as sporulation develops.
OSU field observations found some hemp spots about 0.1 inch or smaller, while more humid conditions can be associated with larger spots; size is contextual rather than a diagnostic threshold.

Alternaria-associated disease can involve leaves, petioles, stems, buds, inflorescences, or propagation material, so a whole-plant and organ-level sequence is more informative than a detached-leaf crop.
Repeated lesions associated with wet foliage, affected residue, or a wind/water spread pattern support a foliar pathogen pathway but do not identify Alternaria by themselves.
exclusions: Dark pycnidia embedded in lesions and laboratory evidence support Septoria rather than Alternaria.
Gray-brown sooty growth concentrated on corresponding lower-leaf lesions and Pseudocercospora morphology or sequence evidence support Pseudocercospora.
Round pale-centered lesions with melanized conidiophores and laboratory evidence support Cercospora.
Bipolaris, Colletotrichum, Exserohilum, Fusarium, Stemphylium, a bacterial pathogen, or another organism is recovered and linked to the sampled lesion.
Spots follow a spray boundary, droplet pattern, abrasion, heat/light exposure, or mechanical contact and do not continue to develop like an infectious lesion.
Chlorosis or necrosis follows a symmetric canopy/leaf-age pattern and measured pH, EC, moisture, or tissue data support an abiotic cause.
Punctures, stippling, frass, webbing, larvae, mites, or thrips account for the visible damage.
The only evidence is an unlinked detached leaf, stock image, generated image, vendor chart, or symptom description without a traceable sampled plant.

progression.description: Conidia associated with infected crop or weed residue can move by wind or water; no visible lesion is required immediately after exposure.
Small dark or yellow spots appear on leaf tissue; the first-report material began with small upper-surface spots.
Spots enlarge into brown-to-gray circular or irregular lesions, sometimes with dark borders, yellow halos, or concentric rings.
Compatible lesion centers or affected outer surfaces may darken and develop sooty black spore masses under conducive conditions.
Lesions can merge, centers may break or perforate, and disease may involve petioles, stems, buds, or other Cannabis tissues; the sequence is not universal across tissue types.

lookAlikes: Pseudocercospora olive or sooty leaf spot
Nutrient, pH, salinity, or water-stress necrosis
confirmation: Capture a traceable series from the same plant: whole canopy, upper/middle/lower canopy, both leaf surfaces, lesion-center macro with a scale, and any petiole, stem, bud, or inflorescence involvement.

Record plant ID, cultivar, stage, production setting, symptom-onset date, leaf or node age, recent wetness or irrigation events, nearby residue, environmental conditions, and any spray or mechanical exposure.
Before treatment, submit fresh representative lesion margins and, when relevant, affected petiole, stem, bud, or inflorescence tissue to a qualified plant diagnostic laboratory.

Use culture and fungal morphology plus validated molecular identification from the sampled plant for an Alternaria organism label; preserve isolate and locus details when species-level resolution matters.
When multiple fungi or bacteria are recovered, require lesion linkage or pathogenicity evidence and keep the sample multi-label or unresolved rather than choosing the visually closest name.

Compare lesion progression with matched healthy plants from the same cultivar, stage, source group, and environment; absence of symptoms in appropriate controls strengthens but does not replace organism evidence.
Keep symptom-only, detached-leaf-only, unlinked culture, mixed-organism, low-resolution, and stock/vendor/generated captures out of the confirmed Alternaria class and route them to human review.
immediateActions: Preserve representative untreated tissue and traceable photographs before removing heavily affected material.
Separate symptomatic propagation material from clean stock and reduce avoidable prolonged leaf wetness while diagnosis is pending.
Map affected plants against irrigation zones, airflow, cultivar blocks, incoming plant lots, and residue sources.
correctivePlan: Use a disease-management plan appropriate to the organism confirmed by the diagnostic laboratory and the production setting.
Remove or contain confirmed diseased material and residue as locally appropriate, then monitor tagged plants for new lesions.
Evaluate response with new-growth and lesion-count records; old necrotic tissue will not become healthy after correction.
prevention: Use clean propagation material and do not move symptomatic plants, tools, or debris into clean areas.
Improve air circulation, limit avoidable leaf wetness, and manage infected crop or weed residue where feasible.
Scout both leaf surfaces and multiple canopy levels with consistent plant IDs so early spots can be followed over time.
warnings: Brown lesions, yellow halos, concentric rings, shot holes, and black sporulation are not individually specific to Alternaria.
Alternaria alternata and potentially other Alternaria species can affect Cannabis; a generic image cannot resolve species.
The two primary studies are regional and used specific isolates, tissues, and production contexts; prevalence, severity, and timing are not universal.
Alternaria can be recovered from seed or inflorescence material, but recovery alone does not prove it caused every visible lesion.
No image or video was added in this batch because no stable, item-level, panel-resolved Cannabis Alternaria asset with sufficiently clear reuse and training rights was verified.
All symptom-only, mixed-organism, detached, unlinked-laboratory, and low-resolution samples require human review.

sources.title: First Report of Leaf Spot on Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa) Caused by Alternaria alternata in China
supportedClaims: Industrial hemp leaf spots began as small spots and developed into brown irregular lesions with light yellow halos; lesion centers could perforate as disease advanced.
The isolate was identified as Alternaria alternata by morphology and multilocus molecular evidence, and inoculated healthy hemp developed similar lesions while controls remained asymptomatic.
Re-isolation from inoculated plants fulfilled Koch postulates, so the record supports an organism-confirmed Cannabis leaf-spot diagnosis rather than visual similarity alone.

sources.title: Pathogenicity of seedborne Alternaria and Stemphylium species and stem-infecting Neofusicoccum and Lasiodiplodia species to cannabis (Cannabis sativa L., marijuana) plants
supportedClaims: Alternaria alternata was recovered from Cannabis inflorescences and surface-sterilized hemp seed in Canadian production material, extending the diagnostic context beyond leaf lesions alone.
The study confirmed pathogenicity of recovered fungi by inoculating Cannabis leaves, stems, buds, rooted cuttings, and mature plants; disease ratings varied with tissue type and pathogen.
Alternaria, Stemphylium, Neofusicoccum, and Lasiodiplodia were evaluated in the same work, so a lesion or blight photograph cannot assign Alternaria without plant-linked organism evidence.
The article is licensed CC BY-NC-ND 4.0; no figure was admitted as media because a stable item-level original asset URL and panel-resolved Cannabis Alternaria label were not verified in this review.

sources.title: Hemp (Cannabis sativa)-Brown Blight (Alternaria Diseases)
sources.organization: Pacific Northwest Plant Disease Management Handbook
sources.publisher: Oregon State University, Washington State University, and University of Idaho
supportedClaims: Alternaria alternata and potentially other Alternaria species can infect Cannabis leaves, petioles, stems, and flower parts; infected crop and weed residue can produce conidia that move by wind and water.

Compatible Cannabis symptoms include small dark or yellow leaf spots that enlarge into brown-to-gray circular lesions, sometimes with concentric rings, dark borders, yellow halos, or sooty black spore masses in lesion centers.
Cannabis leaves and buds can begin brown and darken toward brown-black as sporulation develops; these organ and temporal observations are compatible signs, not species confirmation.
OSU surveys in 2021 observed hemp leaf spots about 0.1 inch or smaller, while higher relative humidity can be associated with larger spots; lesion size is therefore context-dependent.
The institutional guidance emphasizes improving air circulation, minimizing leaf wetness, and removing infected leaves; these are risk-reduction measures and do not substitute for diagnosis.
The page is institutionally copyrighted and exposes no explicit reusable license for disease media; no page graphic was copied or indexed as training ground truth.

name: Anthracnose leaf spot
summary: A laboratory-confirmed Cannabis leaf-spot disease caused by Colletotrichum fioriniae. A Kentucky first report established a light-green-speck to tan-centered, dark-margined lesion sequence and fulfilled pathogenicity testing, while a later university survey only corroborated separate field occurrences. Photographs cannot distinguish it from other leaf-spot pathogens or physical injury.
affectedParts: adjacent leaf tissue when lesions coalesce
both leaf surfaces for paired documentation
stages: field-grown reproductive hemp in the first report
indicators: The reported sequence began with scattered light-green specks rather than an immediately open hole.
Developing lesions became round or angular and approximately 3 to 4 mm across.
Compatible lesions had tan centers, darker brown margins, and yellow halos, but this color combination is not unique to anthracnose.
Lesion centers could crack and later drop out, creating a shot-hole or frog-eye appearance only after surrounding lesion development.
Multiple lesions could coalesce into larger necrotic regions rather than remaining isolated dots.
Lesions reaching a margin could be associated with marginal scorching, puckering, or twisting.
A useful image set pairs the full leaf and plant context with calibrated close views of intact early, developing, and center-loss lesions.
Compatible C. fioriniae culture morphology plus multilocus sequence evidence from the same lesion substantially strengthens the label; visual morphology alone does not.
exclusions: Physical holes, chewing, hail tears, handling damage, or training injury occur without a preceding discolored lesion, halo, or lesion-linked fungus.
Dark embedded pycnidia and a compatible laboratory result support Septoria leaf spot.
Gray-brown sooty or velvety lower-surface conidial patches support Pseudocercospora.
Tan-to-white centers with conspicuous melanized conidiophores and a compatible result support Cercospora leaf spot.
Concentric target-like rings or dark central sporulation with a compatible isolate support Alternaria as a differential.
Angular water-soaked lesions, bacterial streaming or ooze, and a plant-linked bacterial identification support bacterial leaf spot.
A sharp spray, lamp, aisle, contact, or weather boundary without lesion-linked Colletotrichum evidence supports abiotic injury.
Culture, microscopy, multilocus sequencing, or repeated representative sampling identifies another organism or fails to link C. fioriniae to the lesions.

progression.description: Capture symptom-free leaves and plant position before or beside the affected cohort whenever matched controls are available.
Scattered light-green specks appear while tissue remains intact; record leaf age, canopy position, both surfaces, and field distribution.
Specks develop into approximately 3 to 4 mm round or angular lesions with tan centers, darker margins, and yellow halos.
Necrotic centers crack and may drop out; follow the same tagged lesion so an insect or mechanical hole is not mistaken for progression.
Lesions merge into larger necrotic areas, and marginal involvement may accompany scorching, puckering, or twisting.

lookAlikes: Four-lined plant bug or other puncture injury
Caterpillar, beetle, slug, or snail feeding
Hail, wind, handling, or training tear
Edema or localized water-related tissue collapse
confirmation: Photograph the entire plant and canopy neighborhood, then both surfaces of several affected and unaffected leaves with a scale and stable plant identifiers.
Track the same intact early lesions through center cracking or loss; a single frame of an existing hole cannot establish the reported progression.
Collect multiple fresh lesions spanning intact early margins to developing centers before saprophytes obscure the lesion edge, following the receiving laboratory's packaging instructions.
Use lesion-edge culture and trained morphological examination to recover a dominant compatible Colletotrichum isolate, while recording other organisms recovered from the same tissue.

For C. fioriniae-level confirmation, require plant-linked multilocus sequence evidence comparable to the four-gene approach in the first report; do not assign the species from color, ITS alone, or a generic Colletotrichum image.
Where causality is uncertain or the isolate represents a new host or presentation, use pathogenicity evidence with symptom reproduction, reisolation, and symptomless controls.

Keep symptom-only, shot-hole-only, detached-leaf-only, mixed-pathogen, culture-unlinked, single-locus-only, generated, vendor, anecdotal, forum, unverified, and low-resolution samples out of confirmed training labels and route them to human review.
immediateActions: Tag and photograph representative plants before removing tissue, preserving the spatial pattern and lesion sequence.
Separate symptomatic propagation material from clean stock and retain traceable fresh samples for a plant diagnostic laboratory.
Map affected plants against cultivar blocks, irrigation or splash zones, airflow, recent foliar applications, handling paths, and weather injury.
correctivePlan: Base disease management on the organism confirmed by the diagnostic laboratory and the production setting rather than on the anthracnose name or a photograph alone.
Contain or remove confirmed diseased material as locally appropriate and follow new lesion incidence on tagged plants; old necrotic tissue will not recover.
Reassess the diagnosis if new lesions do not follow the documented sequence or if repeated plant-linked tests do not support C. fioriniae.
prevention: Use clean propagation material and avoid moving symptomatic leaves, debris, tools, or splash water into clean production areas.
Reduce avoidable prolonged leaf wetness and retain adequate spacing and airflow where feasible.
Scout with stable plant IDs and matched full-plant, full-leaf, and macro views so early specks can be distinguished from later center loss.
warnings: Shot-hole, frog-eye, tan-center, dark-margin, yellow-halo, puckering, and coalescence features are not individually or jointly species-specific in a photograph.

The first report is a narrow Kentucky report; it does not establish national prevalence, cultivar susceptibility, universal canopy or leaf-age preference, infection timing, yield loss, or action thresholds.
The 2021 Kentucky survey only reports separate field occurrences and explicitly characterizes its findings as preliminary; it does not validate a camera-only label.
A Colletotrichum culture without plant and lesion linkage can represent incidental or secondary recovery and is not sufficient ground truth.
No image or video was indexed because no stable, item-level Cannabis anthracnose asset with clear reuse rights, plant linkage, and species-resolved confirmation was verified.
All symptom-only, hole-only, detached, mixed-organism, unlinked-laboratory, single-locus-only, low-resolution, and rights-unclear samples require human review.

sources.title: First Report of Anthracnose Leaf Spot Caused by Colletotrichum fioriniae on Hemp (Cannabis sativa)
supportedClaims: Hemp anthracnose lesions began as light-green specks and developed into 3 to 4 mm round or angular spots with tan centers, darker brown margins, and yellow halos; centers could crack or drop out and lesions could coalesce.
Colletotrichum fioriniae was identified by morphology and four gene sequences, and inoculation reproduced characteristic leaf spots while controls remained symptomless.
Shot-hole or frog-eye appearance is not species-specific and must be differentiated from other fungal and bacterial leaf spots.

sources.title: Observations of Insect and Disease Pests on Field Grown Hemp in Kentucky
sources.organization: Science of Hemp: Production and Pest Management Conference Proceedings
sources.publisher: Auburn University College of Agriculture and Alabama Agricultural Experiment Station
supportedClaims: A 2021 University of Kentucky survey at the Spindletop Farm and Robinson Center observed separate cases of anthracnose identified as Colletotrichum fioriniae in field-grown hemp research plantings.

The survey covered hemp grown for cannabinoid, grain, and fiber purposes and documented multiple fungal diseases in the same season, so field context does not make a photographed lesion specific to anthracnose.

The conference report explicitly described its results as preliminary and called for additional research; it does not establish prevalence, cultivar susceptibility, symptom timing, yield impact, or a visual decision threshold for anthracnose.

name: Bipolaris leaf spot
summary: A laboratory-confirmed hemp leaf-spot and blight disease associated with Bipolaris gigantea. Kentucky field studies add useful temporal and canopy context, but lesion appearance overlaps other fungal, bacterial, insect, and abiotic injuries and cannot resolve species, genotype, ploidy, or transmission source.
affectedParts: middle and upper canopy leaves for paired comparison
nearby symptomatic weeds as unproven epidemiological context
indicators: Compatible disease begins as localized necrotic leaf spots and can progress to extensive leaf blight, but no single lesion shape or color is diagnostic.

In two Kentucky experiments Bipolaris was first observed seven to eight weeks after planting and increased through the end of the season; capture planting date and repeated observations rather than treating this timing as universal.
Those experiments found greater disease in the middle canopy than the upper canopy, so a useful capture pairs both levels; cultivar, site, and season can alter the pattern.
Photograph the full plant and intact leaf before macro views so lesion burden, canopy level, leaf age, margins, centers, coalescence, and any defoliation remain linked.
Record both leaf surfaces and include a scale and neutral color reference because surface growth, reproductive structures, and color can separate important differentials.
Compatible Bipolaris conidia or culture from the photographed lesion strengthens the label, but recovery alone does not establish causation when other organisms are present.

Lesion-linked ITS and partial 28S evidence supported the original Kentucky report; broader multilocus work documented multiple B. gigantea genotypes and ploidy states that photographs cannot distinguish.
Nearby symptomatic weeds can provide sampling context, but their presence does not prove the infection source or direction of movement.
exclusions: Dark pycnidia embedded in lesions and a Septoria-confirmed isolate support Septoria leaf spot rather than Bipolaris.
Pale-centered round lesions with melanized conidiophores and a Cercospora-confirmed isolate support Cercospora.
Sooty or olivaceous reproductive growth concentrated on the lower surface and appropriate laboratory evidence support Pseudocercospora.
Concentric zonation or central dark sporulation plus a lesion-linked Alternaria identification support Alternaria, although rings alone are nonspecific.
Center cracking or loss must be followed from an intact lesion; physical holes, chewing, hail tears, handling damage, or training injury exclude a symptom-only Bipolaris label.
Angular water-soaked lesions, bacterial streaming or ooze, and a lesion-linked bacterial isolate support bacterial leaf spot.
A sharp spray, row, field-edge, lighting, irrigation, or contact boundary with no compatible organism supports abiotic or chemical injury.
A different dominant lesion-linked pathogen, mixed recovery without causal resolution, or symptomless inoculated controls excludes a confirmed B. gigantea label.

progression.description: Record matched symptom-free plants, cultivar, planting date, canopy levels, field position, recent weather, irrigation, and exposure history.
Tag intact localized spots and photograph the whole plant, whole leaf, both surfaces, and calibrated lesion macro views before tissue removal.
Reimage tagged leaves and map new lesions to determine whether necrotic area and lesion number increase rather than relying on unrelated single frames.
Document coalescing necrosis, canopy loss, and defoliation while preserving representative advancing margins for laboratory work.
Link each culture, morphology result, molecular result, and any pathogenicity test back to the photographed plant and lesion.

lookAlikes: Caterpillar, beetle, slug, or snail feeding
Hail, wind, handling, or training tear
Nutrient, salinity, drought, or root-zone stress
confirmation: Capture the same intact lesions through progression and preserve plant ID, cultivar, planting date, canopy level, both leaf surfaces, field map, exposure history, and collection time.
Examine advancing lesion margins and both surfaces with magnification for pycnidia, conidiophores, conidia, bacterial signs, arthropods, or physical tearing before selecting a label.
Submit tissue spanning healthy and advancing lesion margins; recover and document a dominant compatible fungus while retaining mixed-organism results rather than selecting the closest visual class.
Use lesion-linked fungal morphology and validated molecular evidence for a Bipolaris organism label; preserve loci, sequence quality, database/version, and isolate identifiers.
Require validated multilocus evidence when exact B. gigantea placement or genotype-level interpretation matters; ITS-only, single-locus, morphology-only, and image-only evidence remain provisional.

When causality matters, require symptom reproduction, recovery of the same organism, and symptomless appropriate controls; nearby weed isolates alone do not establish source or transmission direction.

Keep symptom-only, detached-leaf-only, mixed-pathogen, culture-unlinked, ITS-only, single-locus-only, low-resolution, generated, vendor, anecdotal, forum, and unverified samples out of the confirmed class and route them to human review.
immediateActions: Preserve representative untreated tissue and traceable photographs before removing heavily affected material.
Separate symptomatic propagation material from clean stock and reduce avoidable prolonged leaf wetness while diagnosis is pending.
Map affected plants against cultivar blocks, canopy levels, irrigation, airflow, field edges, residue, weeds, and possible exposure boundaries.
correctivePlan: Use a disease-management plan appropriate to the organism confirmed by the diagnostic laboratory and the production setting.
Remove or contain confirmed diseased material and residue as locally appropriate, then monitor tagged plants for new lesions.
Evaluate response using new lesion incidence and severity records; old necrotic tissue will not become healthy after correction.
prevention: Use clean propagation material and avoid moving symptomatic plants, tools, or debris into clean areas.
Improve air circulation, limit avoidable leaf wetness, and manage infected crop or weed residue where feasible.
Scout consistent plant IDs across canopy levels and over time so early spots, disease increase, and confounders can be separated.
warnings: Necrotic spots, expanding blight, canopy loss, and weed co-occurrence are not individually specific to Bipolaris.

The seven-to-eight-week onset, middle-canopy predominance, cultivar differences, and combined-disease yield results are study-specific observations, not universal Bipolaris timing, distribution, susceptibility, yield, or action thresholds.
The original report used ITS and partial 28S placement, while later multilocus work found multiple genotypes and ploidy states; photographs cannot resolve this diversity.
Recovery from a lesion or nearby weed does not by itself prove causation, infection source, or transmission direction.
No image or video was indexed because no stable, item-level, plant-linked B. gigantea asset with sufficiently clear reuse and training rights was verified.
All symptom-only, detached, mixed-pathogen, culture-unlinked, single-locus-only, low-resolution, and rights-unclear samples require human review.

sources.title: First Report of Hemp Leaf Spot Caused by a Bipolaris Species on Hemp (Cannabis sativa) in Kentucky
supportedClaims: Outdoor hemp in Kentucky developed severe necrotic leaf spot and blight associated with a lineage identified morphologically as Drechslera gigantea and placed within Bipolaris by ITS and partial 28S sequence analysis.
Inoculated hemp leaves developed symptoms while noninoculated controls remained symptomless, supporting pathogenicity rather than visual association alone.
The fungus was also associated with symptomatic dicot and monocot weeds in affected fields, but co-occurrence does not establish the direction or source of transmission.

This regional first report supports a Cannabis-specific Bipolaris disease; it does not establish universal lesion morphology, canopy preference, timing, prevalence, cultivar susceptibility, yield loss, or action thresholds.

sources.title: Leaf Spot Disease Development and Its Effect on Yield of Essential Oil-Producing Hemp Cultivars in Kentucky
supportedClaims: Two Kentucky field experiments in 2020 and 2021 evaluated Bipolaris, Cercospora, and Septoria leaf spots across four essential-oil hemp cultivar groups.
In those experiments Bipolaris was first observed seven to eight weeks after planting and increased through the end of the season; this is a study observation, not a universal onset rule.
All three evaluated leaf spots were more severe in the middle canopy than the upper canopy, and susceptibility differed among cultivar groups; neither pattern is a universal diagnostic threshold.
Reported yield associations concerned the combined leaf-spot disease complex under the tested cultivars, sites, and seasons and must not be attributed to Bipolaris alone.
Overlapping leaf-spot syndromes mean paired canopy observations, temporal follow-up, fungal morphology, culture, and molecular diagnostics are more reliable than one lesion photograph.

sources.title: Seeing double on Cannabis: Haploids and heteroploids of Bipolaris gigantea on hemp and other dicots
sources.publisher: Taylor & Francis on behalf of the Mycological Society of America
supportedClaims: The study examined Bipolaris gigantea isolates from hemp leaf-spot lesions and nearby weeds collected across 11 Kentucky counties.
Twenty-three isolates were analyzed by multilocus phylogenetics and seven were also whole-genome sequenced, revealing multiple genotypes and both haploid and apparently heteroploid isolates.
Haploid and heteroploid isolates caused similar disease on hemp, so lesion appearance cannot resolve ploidy, genotype, or the source host.

Species- and genotype-level labels therefore require lesion-linked laboratory evidence; a symptom photograph or single recovered isolate cannot establish population structure or transmission direction.

name: Botrytis gray mold and bud rot
summary: A destructive Cannabis flower, stem, leaf, seedling, and postharvest disease associated with brown water-soaked or necrotic decay and, when conditions permit, gray to gray-brown sporulation. Internal flower decay can be poorly represented by an exterior view, and brown bud rot is not species-specific without laboratory confirmation.
affectedParts: fan leaves under severe disease pressure
indicators: One or more bracts or sugar leaves within a flower turn water-soaked, tan, or brown and collapse
Brown necrosis and mycelium occur inside a flower when it is carefully opened
Gray to gray-brown fuzzy growth or dusty spore masses develop on dead flower or stem tissue under humid conditions
Localized flower decay expands until much or all of an inflorescence is brown, dry-rotted, or collapsed
Stem lesions become pale or brown cankers and may split, girdle, or break; black sclerotia can occur
Under severe late-harvest pressure, small circular leaf spots can enlarge, merge, and become vein-delimited necrotic areas, sometimes with yellow margins
Multiple affected flowers cluster in dense, humid, poorly drying canopy zones and increase on serial inspection
exclusions: White superficial colonies occur without brown internal decay and microscopy supports powdery mildew
Only pistils or evenly aging leaves have browned while bracts, stems, and internal flower tissue remain firm and free of advancing lesions
Fusarium, Penicillium, or another mold is recovered from the active lesion instead of Botrytis
White cottony mycelium and the laboratory result support Sclerotinia rather than Botrytis
Damage stops after a documented heat, light, spray, or mechanical event and no mycelium, spores, or advancing rot develop
Caterpillars, frass, chewing, or webbing explain the localized flower collapse
A single postharvest discoloration image is available without intact-tissue context, environmental history, microscopy, culture, or molecular testing

progression.description: A small water-soaked or brown area develops on bracts, adjacent leaves, or a stem; exterior images can understate internal flower involvement.
Necrosis spreads through nearby bracts and flower tissue, with internal brown decay or mycelium becoming apparent when the affected flower is examined safely.
Gray to gray-brown fuzzy growth and spore masses develop on necrotic tissue; their absence in a dry image does not exclude an earlier or inactive infection.
A large portion or the whole inflorescence can be destroyed, stems can canker or break, and internal decay can persist into harvested material.

lookAlikes: Fusarium flower mold or bud rot
Normal pistil browning and late-flower senescence
Caterpillar or other boring-insect injury with frass
Heat, light, spray, or mechanical injury
confirmation: Capture the affected flower exterior, a safely exposed interior cross-section, a close-up of the active lesion margin, surrounding flowers, and a whole-plant distribution view with scale; do not infer a clean interior from an exterior photograph.

Record serial change plus flowering or harvest stage, canopy location, temperature, relative humidity, condensation or wetness duration, irrigation or rain exposure, air movement, and drying conditions; these variables describe risk but do not confirm the organism.
With appropriate containment and protective procedures, sample the interface between advancing diseased and apparently healthy tissue rather than only dry dead tissue.

Submit representative flower or stem tissue to a plant diagnostic laboratory for microscopy and isolation plus a validated molecular or sequence-based assay when a Botrytis species label matters; request testing that considers Fusarium, Penicillium, Sclerotinia, and other flower molds.

Keep the image label at suspected gray mold or bud rot unless organism evidence is linked to the photographed plant and lesion; morphology or an environmental match alone is not laboratory confirmation.
immediateActions: Isolate or clearly mark suspect plants and stop moving affected flowers, tools, clothing, or debris through clean areas.
Avoid shaking or uncontained opening of visibly sporulating flowers; collect diagnostic images and samples with procedures that limit spore dispersal.
Separate visibly moldy harvested material from apparently clean material and do not consume or distribute it.
correctivePlan: Base crop removal, sanitation, environmental correction, and any treatment on the confirmed diagnosis, current local law, the production system, growth stage, and the current product label.
Reduce persistent tissue wetness and correct airflow or humidity problems documented in the affected zone without treating an environmental adjustment as proof that Botrytis caused the lesion.
Reinspect fixed flowers and neighboring plants over time; document new lesions and laboratory results, because old necrotic tissue will not recover.
prevention: Scout both exterior and protected interior flower zones during flowering and before harvest, especially where tissue dries slowly.
Sanitize tools between plants, remove crop debris without dispersing it, and prevent infected propagation or harvested material from entering clean zones.
Maintain traceable records linking plant, room or field position, media, environmental logs, sample identifier, and laboratory result.
warnings: Brown flower decay, gray fuzz, humidity, or a damaged sugar leaf alone is not species-level ground truth; multiple fungi and noninfectious injuries overlap visually.
Opening diseased flowers can expose hidden decay but can also release spores; use containment and appropriate protective procedures.
Temperature and humidity ranges reported by institutions are conducive-condition context, not universal diagnostic thresholds.

The CC BY composite figure is reference-only pending panel-level annotation and dataset-split review; the three university photographs have no explicit reuse license and remain hidden metadata references.
Do not use or distribute visibly mold-contaminated flower.

sources.title: Pathogens and Molds Affecting Production and Quality of Cannabis sativa L.
sources.organization: Frontiers in Plant Science (Punja et al.)
supportedClaims: Across sampled indoor, greenhouse, and field Cannabis crops, flower buds with brown discoloration, blighted bracts and leaves, tissue decay, and grayish-brown mycelium yielded cultures identified as Botrytis cinerea by morphology and ITS-rDNA sequencing.

The study documented a visual sequence from browning and decay of leaves and bracts in developing inflorescences to destruction of the entire inflorescence, as well as internal mycelium and decay in harvested flowers.

Under severe late-harvest disease pressure, Cannabis leaves developed small circular spots that enlarged and coalesced into necrotic, often vein-delimited areas, sometimes with yellow margins; this leaf presentation was contextual rather than a standalone diagnostic rule.

Botrytis cinerea, Fusarium oxysporum, and Penicillium olsonii recovered from harvested buds each produced browning and decay after inoculation under high humidity, demonstrating that brown bud rot is not species-specific in an image.

Figure 4 is a multi-panel Cannabis reference containing early and advanced inflorescence disease, internal harvested-bud decay, culture and microscopy views, and leaf lesions; the article and figure are licensed CC BY 4.0.

sources.title: Hemp (Cannabis sativa)-Gray Mold (Botrytis Bud Blight and Stem Canker)
sources.publisher: Oregon State University, Washington State University, and University of Idaho
supportedClaims: Gray mold can affect Cannabis seedlings, stems, foliage, and flowers; brown water-soaked bud spots can progress to dead inflorescences covered by brown to gray-brown spores.
Stem infection can produce cankers, splitting or breakage, and black sclerotia, while heavily affected plants can decline quickly under conducive conditions.
Cool, humid or wet conditions and prolonged tissue wetness favor disease, but environmental conditions are risk context rather than proof of cause.

The page photographs show a close exterior bud-rot view, a close sporulating-flower view, and a whole-plant distribution view; each is credited to Cynthia M. Ocamb in 2020, and the page states copyright without an explicit media-reuse license.

sources.title: Gray Mold of Industrial Hemp
supportedClaims: Brown water-soaked lesions on hemp stems, leaves, or flowers can become necrotic and develop gray spores; stem lesions can girdle stems, cause breakage, and form black irregular sclerotia.
Seedlings and cuttings can damp off under cool, wet conditions, with necrotic or water-soaked roots, while moist and humid production conditions favor disease development.

Fusarium flower mold can resemble gray mold but lacks the characteristic gray spore masses, Fusarium cankers lack gray spores and sclerotia, and Sclerotinia produces white mycelial mats; these features guide triage but laboratory confirmation remains appropriate.
