name: Septoria leaf spot complex
summary: A lower- and inner-canopy hemp leaf-spot syndrome caused by Septoria species. Dark pycnidia within expanding brown-gray lesions are useful evidence, but modern work shows more than one Septoria species can infect Cannabis.
indicators: Disease often begins on lower or inner-canopy leaves
Small irregular brown-to-gray spots expand to several millimeters
Dark round pycnidia can be visible within lesions
Older leaves may defoliate as disease advances
exclusions: Sooty conidial masses on the underside support Pseudocercospora
White-centered round lesions with a pronounced dark border support Cercospora as a differential
Shot-hole lesions and Colletotrichum evidence support anthracnose
No fungal structures or lab evidence are present and an abiotic exposure fits the distribution better

progression.description: Small discolored spots appear on older or inner leaves.
Brown-to-gray lesions enlarge and reproductive structures may become visible.
Lesions multiply and older foliage can yellow and drop.

confirmation: Examine lesions for pycnidia and submit representative tissue for fungal identification when species matters.
Use morphology and molecular sequence data for species-level Septoria classification because S. cannabis and S. cannabicola cannot be separated by a generic spot photo.
immediateActions: Document lower-versus-upper canopy distribution and both leaf surfaces.
Limit movement of symptomatic foliage into clean production areas.
correctivePlan: Use confirmed-disease sanitation and environmental management appropriate to the system.
Track new lesion development after intervention.
prevention: Scout lower and inner canopy foliage early.
Reduce prolonged leaf wetness and carryover of infected debris where practical.
warnings: Septoria species taxonomy on Cannabis is not reducible to visual symptoms.
Do not train a species classifier from mixed Septoria figures without organism-confirmed labels.

sources.title: Reemergence of Septoria Leaf Spot Caused by Septoria cannabis on Hemp in Kentucky
supportedClaims: Septoria leaf spot was documented on hemp primarily on lower leaves and inner canopy, with small irregular brown-to-gray lesions expanding to roughly 5 to 7.5 mm and dark pycnidia in lesions.
Eight isolates were tested for pathogenicity on greenhouse-grown hemp and diagnostic loci were sequenced; morphology and sequence evidence supported Septoria cannabis in the Kentucky material.
Visual lesion appearance alone cannot separate Septoria from other hemp leaf-spot pathogens.

sources.title: Septoria cannabicola, a new species on Cannabis sativa from Japan
supportedClaims: Molecular phylogeny and morphology demonstrated that Cannabis leaf spot historically attributed to Septoria cannabis can involve a distinct species, Septoria cannabicola.
Natural symptoms began as indistinct yellow spots on lower leaves and progressed to brown irregular lesions and premature defoliation of older leaves.
Species-level Septoria naming therefore requires laboratory evidence rather than lesion appearance alone.

sources.title: Leaf Spot Disease Development and Its Effect on Yield of Essential Oil-Producing Hemp Cultivars in Kentucky
supportedClaims: Two Kentucky field experiments in 2020 and 2021 evaluated Bipolaris, Cercospora, and Septoria leaf spots across four essential-oil hemp cultivar groups.
In those experiments Bipolaris was first observed seven to eight weeks after planting and increased through the end of the season; this is a study observation, not a universal onset rule.
All three evaluated leaf spots were more severe in the middle canopy than the upper canopy, and susceptibility differed among cultivar groups; neither pattern is a universal diagnostic threshold.
Reported yield associations concerned the combined leaf-spot disease complex under the tested cultivars, sites, and seasons and must not be attributed to Bipolaris alone.
Overlapping leaf-spot syndromes mean paired canopy observations, temporal follow-up, fungal morphology, culture, and molecular diagnostics are more reliable than one lesion photograph.

name: Southern blight
summary: A pathogenicity-confirmed Cannabis soil-line and crown disease caused by Athelia rolfsii. A plant-linked basal lesion with cottony white mycelium and numerous round tan-to-brown sclerotia is strongly compatible, but wilt, yellowing, brown crown tissue, white growth, or sclerotia in isolation cannot establish the label.
affectedParts: lower stem at and immediately above the soil line
stem tissue in controlled hydroponic infection
stages: six-leaf vegetative plants in controlled inoculation
indicators: A dark-brown-to-tan lesion or discoloration is centered at the soil line or crown and remains anatomically linked to the declining shoot.
Compatible crown decay may extend into the taproot in field disease, but a controlled five-day hydroponic infection caused stem recovery and canopy wilt without visible root browning or root rot.
Leaves yellow, droop, or wilt and the plant may collapse above the same basal lesion; canopy symptoms alone remain nonspecific.
Extensive cottony white mycelium develops on diseased crown or lower-stem tissue and can extend onto the immediately adjacent soil or substrate.
Multiple spherical sclerotia develop within the plant-linked mycelium, beginning pale and maturing light tan, russet, or dark brown.
Sclerotia in the Greek field isolate were reported at 0.5–2.0 mm, but size is isolate- and study-specific and is supporting morphology rather than a universal threshold.
Lesion-derived cultures produce compatible white mycelium, septate hyaline hyphae with occasional clamp connections, and brown sclerotia; morphology supports but does not replace molecular evidence.
A confirmed label links the same plant and active basal lesion to qualified isolation, validated molecular identification, and preferably symptom reproduction plus reisolation.
exclusions: No basal lesion, crown decay, plant-linked mycelium, or sclerotia are found and measured water deficit explains the wilt.
Roots are soft, water-soaked, or cortex-sloughed and plant-linked oomycete testing supports Pythium or another water mold.
Dry brown root rot or a reddish-brown sore-shin lesion is linked to Rhizoctonia morphology or molecular evidence without Athelia-compatible sclerotia.
Vascular discoloration and lesion-linked Fusarium isolation or molecular evidence support Fusarium wilt or crown/root rot.
White growth with black external or internal sclerotia and laboratory evidence supports Sclerotinia white mold or crown rot.
Blackened roots or crowns with microsclerotia and organism evidence support charcoal rot rather than southern blight.
Firm integrated root galls plus nematode recovery support root-knot nematodes.
Measured hypoxia, high EC, extreme pH, root restriction, or stem injury explains decline and no active pathogen-linked basal lesion is present.
White material wipes or dissolves as mineral, spray, fiber, algae, or other residue and the underlying tissue lacks an active lesion and sclerotia.
Only a canopy, detached lesion, culture plate, sclerotium, mixed-treatment composite, low-resolution image, or unlinked laboratory result is available.

progression.description: An active lesion begins at the soil line or crown; the exact incubation period cannot be inferred from an unknown field image.
Dark tan-to-brown tissue expands around the lower stem or crown and may extend toward the taproot in field presentations.
Leaves yellow, droop, or wilt above the affected crown while the lower-stem lesion remains the key anatomical anchor.
Cottony white mycelium spreads across diseased basal tissue or nearby substrate and round sclerotia develop from pale to tan or dark brown.
The plant may collapse or die while sclerotia remain with the crown, soil, or debris; timing and incidence vary across setting, cultivar, isolate, and moisture-temperature context.

lookAlikes: Nonliving white residue, fibers, algae, or substrate growth
confirmation: Capture the same intact plant at whole-canopy, soil-line, crown, and root scales with a ruler or other scale; preserve the shoot-to-lesion-to-root connection.
Photograph the active lesion margin, cottony growth, and sclerotia in place before handling, then record whether the structures are embedded in plant-linked mycelium or merely loose on substrate.
Mark the plant and repeat images to document basal lesion expansion, canopy decline, mycelial spread, and sclerotial color development rather than assembling progression from unrelated plants.
Record cultivar, plant age and stage, field or protected/hydroponic setting, location, date, irrigation, drainage, substrate, soil-line temperature and moisture context, and nearby affected plants.
Submit fresh active crown/lower-stem tissue, representative sclerotia, and when involved taproot tissue under the same plant identifier; retain paired apparently healthy material when feasible.
Use lesion-derived culture and microscopy to document compatible hyphae, clamp connections, and sclerotia, but do not assign Athelia rolfsii from morphology alone.
Use validated molecular identification linked to the lesion-derived isolate; an ITS-only result requires appropriate sequence quality, reference comparison, and expert interpretation.

For causal ground truth, prefer pathogenicity evidence with compatible symptom reproduction, appropriate controls, and reisolation; do not universalize the 16-day, 80%, or five-day hydroponic outcomes.

Route symptom-only, detached, culture-only, inadequately resolved ITS-only, mixed-pathogen, mixed-treatment, unlinked, low-resolution, stock, vendor, forum, generated, or rights-unclear samples to human review.
immediateActions: Photograph and preserve the plant-linked crown lesion, mycelium, and sclerotia before sanitation, treatment, or disposal removes diagnostic evidence.
Separate suspect root-zone material where operationally appropriate and prevent movement of wet soil, substrate, pots, tools, footwear, or debris from the affected area to clean areas.
Record the distribution of affected plants and measured moisture/drainage conditions while preserving samples for a qualified plant diagnostic laboratory.
correctivePlan: Base pathogen-specific action on a plant-linked qualified laboratory result and measures legal for the crop, jurisdiction, and production system.
Remove confirmed infected plant material and associated sclerotia with sanitary handling appropriate to the site; clean tools, containers, footwear, and contact surfaces before reuse.
Correct documented excess moisture, drainage, or contaminated-debris risks without treating environmental response as retrospective proof of A. rolfsii.
prevention: Exclude or contain contaminated soil, substrate, transplants, containers, and plant debris and maintain lot and location identifiers through scouting and diagnostic sampling.
Scout the soil line and crown during warm, wet risk periods instead of relying on canopy wilt, and retain repeat plant-linked photographs when a lesion is found.
Maintain sanitation and production-history records so recurrent affected zones, equipment routes, prior hosts, irrigation patterns, and confirmed outbreaks can be investigated.
warnings: Photo/video-only confidence is capped at 0.30; a compatible image remains a differential unless the same plant, basal lesion, fungal signs, and organism evidence are linked.
Wilt, yellowing, collapse, crown browning, cottony growth, and brown spherical structures each overlap other pathogens, abiotic root failure, injury, residue, or mixed disease.
The 19.1% incidence in Greece, 80% response at 16 days in one Kompolti inoculation, and five-day Ferimon hydroponic response are study-specific, not universal Cannabis rates or timelines.
The hydroponic study recovered the pathogen from stems without visible root browning or root rot, so taproot rot must not be required in every early presentation.
The 0.2% chitosan condition inhibited root growth and did not prevent visible disease; the experiment does not establish chitosan as a universal treatment or an untreated visual baseline.
Hot or wet conditions increase plausibility but do not identify the pathogen; exact temperature, moisture, sclerotial size, and management responses from one study are not universal thresholds.
White or brown sclerotia-like structures do not visually separate Athelia from every Sclerotinia, Rhizoctonia, substrate, or debris differential without plant-linked expert examination.

The CC BY 4.0 controlled-study figure combines four treatments, four timepoints, hydroponic culture, chitosan-confounded roots, and not-to-scale insets; it is displayable reference context but prohibited from automated training.
No licensed panel-resolved field progression or verified diagnostic video was located; symptom-only and evidence-unlinked observations remain subject to human review.

sources.title: Surveying for Potential Diseases and Abiotic Disorders of Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa) Production
supportedClaims: A North Carolina 2017–2018 hemp diagnostic survey identified 16 diseases caused by fungi, bacteria, oomycetes, and nematodes; the study used clinic diagnostics, morphology, sequence data for representative organisms, and pathogenicity testing for its confirmed disease set.

Fusarium foliar and flower blight was common in submitted samples and involved F. equiseti and F. graminearum; flowers developed surface hyphae and light-brown necrotic tips while leaves developed circular light-brown lesions about 1 cm wide with dark margins and gray-brown aging centers.
Exserohilum rostratum leaf spot occurred on leaves and stems as round brown-to-black lesions with darkened margins and abundant conidia, with ITS1/RPB2 evidence supporting the identification.

Rhizoctonia solani was found on roots and crowns with plant wilting and necrotic lesions just above the soil line; pigmented septate hyphae showed characteristic right-angle branching and sequence evidence supported R. solani.

Southern blight caused whole-plant wilt in reproductive hemp during hot midseason conditions, with abundant hyphae and russet-brown sclerotia on roots/lower stems and sequence/phylogenetic evidence supporting Athelia rolfsii/Sclerotium rolfsii.
Meloidogyne incognita was identified from galled hemp roots with females and egg masses; affected plants had some associated stunting.

The survey documented Serratia-associated, vein-limited angular hemp lesions and red bacterial ooze emerging from punctured lesions, while emphasizing that hemp leaf diseases overlap visually and require diagnostic separation.

sources.title: First Report of Southern Blight Caused by Sclerotium rolfsii on Hemp (Cannabis sativa) in Sicily and Southern Italy
supportedClaims: Infected hemp developed dark brown-to-tan discoloration at the soil line, crown and taproot rot, foliar yellowing, whole-plant collapse, white cottony mycelium, and tan-to-dark-brown spherical sclerotia.
Pathogenicity was reproduced on hemp and Sclerotium rolfsii was reisolated while noninoculated controls remained symptomless.
High summer temperatures and high soil moisture were associated with the reported outbreak but are risk context, not diagnostic proof.

sources.title: First report of southern blight caused by Athelia rolfsii on hemp in Greece
supportedClaims: A flowering Kompolti hemp field in Crete showed wilt, chlorosis, yellowing and collapse linked to dark-brown soil-line discoloration, crown/taproot rot, cottony white mycelium, and light-to-dark-brown spherical sclerotia; the reported 19.1% incidence is specific to that August 2021 field.
Morphology, an ITS sequence deposited as GenBank OL348356, 100% identity to cited accessions, and phylogenetic analysis supported Athelia rolfsii isolate SRC1 rather than a symptom-only label.

Crown inoculation of six-leaf Kompolti plants reproduced wilt, yellowing, collapse, mycelium, and sclerotia in 80% of plants after 16 days, followed by reisolation; that rate and timing are bounded to the reported isolate, cultivar, inoculation method, and 29 ± 2°C experiment.
Cottony mycelium, round sclerotia, and crown-centered disease are discriminating evidence only when they remain linked to the same plant and organism-confirmation workflow.

sources.title: Hormonal and proteomic analyses of southern blight disease caused by Athelia rolfsii and root chitosan priming on Cannabis sativa in an in vitro hydroponic system
supportedClaims: In a controlled Root-TRAPR hydroponic experiment with Cannabis sativa cultivar Ferimon, an ITS-confirmed Athelia rolfsii isolate was placed at the crown and caused yellowing, drooping, and wilt within five days in both unprimed and chitosan-primed plants.

The experiment recovered A. rolfsii from inoculated stem tissue but not root tissue; visible root browning or root rot was not observed during the five-day infection window, showing that root rot is possible in field reports but is not required in every early controlled presentation.

The study used four treatment groups and four timepoints; 0.2% chitosan inhibited root development and did not prevent visible disease, so chitosan-treated morphology cannot serve as an untreated southern-blight progression series.

ITS evidence, controlled inoculation, compatible disease, recovery of the fungus from inoculated plants, and absence from controls provide causal support that is stronger than canopy appearance alone.

The five-day hydroponic Ferimon response, chitosan results, hormone changes, enzyme responses, and root-growth measurements are experiment-specific and are not universal diagnostic thresholds or treatment recommendations.

media.alt: Composite of Cannabis sativa plants in a transparent hydroponic system across four timepoints and four control, chitosan, Athelia rolfsii, or combined treatment groups.
media.caption: CC BY 4.0 controlled-study Figure 2 showing Cannabis morphology across days 0, 6, 8, and 13. It combines four treatment groups and not-to-scale insets; chitosan changes root growth, so the composite is reference context rather than panel-level southern-blight training ground truth.
media.creator: Pipob Suwanchaikasem, Shuai Nie, Jamie Selby-Pham, Robert Walker, Berin A. Boughton, and Alexander Idnurm
media.requiredAttribution: Suwanchaikasem et al. (2023), Plant Direct, Figure 2, https://doi.org/10.1002/pld3.528, licensed CC BY 4.0.
media.diagnosticLabel: southern-blight-athelia-rolfsii — laboratory-confirmed four-treatment, four-timepoint Cannabis composite reference only
useLimitations: The source figure is a 4-by-4 multi-treatment, multi-timepoint composite rather than a single positive diagnostic image.
Control, chitosan-only, Athelia rolfsii, and chitosan-plus-pathogen groups must not be collapsed into one class.
Chitosan independently inhibited root development, and right-side shoot and root insets are explicitly not to scale.
The hydroponic Ferimon experiment ended five days after crown inoculation and did not show visible root browning or root rot; it does not represent field progression or every cultivar.
Display with the full caption and attribution; do not crop, relabel, or use for automated training until panel identities, timepoints, treatment confounding, and sample linkage are resolved.

name: Stable chlorotic sectoring / suspected genetic variegation
summary: Sharply bounded chlorotic or chlorophyll-deficient sectors can be consistent with somatic mutation or mosaicism in Cannabis, but no published Cannabis image morphology proves genetic cause; treat this as an exclusion-based phenotype until serial lineage evidence and appropriate laboratory work support the attribution.
affectedParts: successive leaves from one shoot or meristem
whole plant only when a documented cultivar trait is established
stages: flowering; stage specificity is not established
indicators: Abrupt yellow, cream, pale-green, or near-white tissue adjoining normally green tissue within the same leaf
Sector-shaped or longitudinal pigment loss rather than uniform whole-leaf yellowing
The same shoot position or clonal lineage is mapped across successive leaves and time rather than inferred from one detached leaf
Affected tissue retains its boundary while new observations document whether the pattern remains localized, expands, disappears, or is joined by distortion and stunting
Matched images preserve upper and lower leaf surfaces, whole-plant distribution, branch identity, scale, cultivar, developmental stage, and camera-lighting conditions
exclusions: Validated testing detects a virus or viroid consistent with the sampled tissue and syndrome
Mosaic, mottling, line patterns, curling, brittle growth, shortened internodes, stunting, or reduced inflorescence performance progress beyond the original sector
Chlorosis follows leaf age, interveinal or marginal patterns, or a measured tissue-nutrient, substrate-pH, or root-zone-EC abnormality better than a branch lineage
Microscopy or organism sampling confirms thrips, mites, leafminers, or another pest associated with the marks
The distribution maps to a lamp, spray, pesticide, plant-growth regulator, abrasion, heat event, or other documented exposure
Camera white balance, glare, shadow, senescence, or cultivar pigmentation explains the apparent color boundary

progression.description: Capture calibrated whole-plant, branch, upper-surface, and lower-surface views; assign a symptom-only chlorotic-sector label, not a genetic ground-truth label.

Mark the shoot and record successive leaves and any cuttings over time. A stable lineage association increases suspicion of a developmental or genetic origin but does not exclude latent or localized infection.
Compare matched healthy tissue and evaluate pests, root-zone pH and EC, nutrient status, exposure history, and a region- and facility-appropriate virus/viroid panel before narrowing the cause.

Use genetic or meristem-lineage analysis when a genetic claim matters. Cannabis somatic mosaicism has been sequenced within one mother plant, but published evidence does not establish a universal visible phenotype or inheritance rule.

lookAlikes: Mosaic, mottling, or line-pattern syndrome of unresolved cause
Lettuce chlorosis virus or other regional virus
Iron, manganese, magnesium, or nitrogen disorder
Camera color, glare, or shadow artifact
confirmation: Do not confirm genetic variegation, chimerism, mutation, virus freedom, or training ground truth from a photograph or video.
Record the exact leaf, node, branch, plant, cultivar, propagation source, date, stage, lighting, and serial change; include healthy plants of the same cultivar and environment.
Inspect both leaf surfaces and protected growth with magnification, and document pest organisms or their absence separately from the color phenotype.

Measure root-zone pH and EC and review irrigation, tissue or solution analysis, nutrient history, spray records, lamp position, temperature, and mechanical injury before assigning a developmental explanation.

Submit symptomatic and matched asymptomatic tissue to a plant diagnostic laboratory for a locally appropriate validated virus/viroid differential; a negative targeted assay excludes only the agents and sample covered by that assay.
When a genetic attribution is operationally important, compare mapped sectors and clones and use qualified genetic or meristem-lineage analysis; persistence alone is supportive context, not proof.
immediateActions: Keep the visual label at “chlorotic sectoring—cause unresolved” and flag it for human review.
Pause distribution of suspect cuttings and separate them from verified genetic-trait references until infectious causes are reasonably excluded.
Preserve serial imagery and matched tissue before pruning or discarding the affected shoot.
correctivePlan: Correct only measured root-zone, nutrient, pest, or exposure problems and document whether new growth changes.
If validated pathogen testing is positive, move the sample to the confirmed pathogen class and follow the facility’s sanitation and plant-health protocol.
If differential testing is negative and the pattern tracks a shoot or clone, retain a “suspected genetic/developmental” label unless genetic evidence supports a stronger claim.
prevention: Maintain cultivar, mother-plant, cutting-position, and clone-lineage records.
Use tested propagation stock and tool-sanitation practices so a stable-looking pattern is not assumed noninfectious.
Capture healthy reference plants under repeatable lighting and camera settings for color comparison.
warnings: “Genetic mosaicism” describes within-organism genetic variation; a visible “mosaic symptom” is not evidence of that mechanism.
The Cannabis mosaicism sequencing study sampled one mother plant and did not link its variants to visible leaf sectors.
The VIGS bleaching experiment was an intentionally virus-vector-induced gene-silencing phenotype and must not be treated as proof that natural bleaching is inherited or noninfectious.

The composite reference image mixes four unresolved mosaic-like presentations with panel e, which the authors characterize as somatic-mutation-associated chlorotic sectors; preserve panel labels and never train the entire composite as one genetic class.
Negative molecular, microscopy, or indicator-host findings are bounded by sample quality, agent coverage, assay performance, and observation time.
This reviewed record validates an uncertainty-bounded workflow, not image-only genetic ground truth; all symptom-only samples remain human-review items.

sources.title: Accumulation of somatic mutations leads to genetic mosaicism in cannabis
sources.publisher: Wiley on behalf of the Crop Science Society of America
supportedClaims: Deep whole-genome sequencing of top, middle, and bottom samples from one 1.5-year-old Cannabis mother plant detected many variants unique to individual canopy samples, demonstrating within-plant genetic mosaicism in that plant.
The study examined a single mother plant and did not validate a visible leaf-sector pattern as a diagnostic marker of somatic mutation, heritability, or clonal stability.

sources.title: Virus-induced gene silencing (VIGS) in Cannabis sativa L.
supportedClaims: Experimental silencing of Cannabis phytoene desaturase and magnesium-chelatase-subunit-I genes produced spotted leaf bleaching, 70–73% lower target-transcript expression, and corresponding carotenoid or chlorophyll-a reductions.

This deliberately induced, virus-vector phenotype shows that perturbing pigment-related gene expression can create visible bleaching; it does not establish that naturally occurring sectors are genetic or safe from infectious differentials.

sources.title: Challenges to Cannabis sativa Production from Pathogens and Microbes—The Role of Molecular Diagnostics and Bioinformatics
sources.organization: International Journal of Molecular Sciences (Punja et al.)
supportedClaims: The authors documented Cannabis leaves with mosaic, mottling, and line patterns that superficially resembled viral symptoms, and separately illustrated sharply chlorotic, chlorophyll-deficient sectors attributed to somatic mutation in Figure 4e.

Defined broad-spectrum and specific RT-PCR assays did not detect the targeted viruses in tested OG Kush and Headband tissues; positive controls worked, no virus-like particles were seen in the examined Cannabis samples by transmission electron microscopy, and inoculated indicator hosts remained symptomless for three weeks.

Those negative results apply only to the sampled tissues, agents, assays, and observation period and therefore do not establish genetic causality or exclude every virus, viroid, pest, nutrient, root-zone, or chemical cause.

media.alt: Composite figure of Cannabis leaves with unresolved mosaic-like patterns in panels a through d and chlorotic sectors attributed by the authors to somatic mutation in panel e
media.caption: Rights-cleared reference composite from the author preprint corresponding to the peer-reviewed Punja et al. paper. Only panel e is presented by the authors as somatic-mutation-associated chlorotic sectoring; panels a–d are visually overlapping, unresolved mosaic-like differentials. It is not genetic ground truth.
media.creator: Zamir K. Punja, Dieter Kahl, Ron Reade, Yu Xiang, Jack Munz, and Punya Nachappa
media.requiredAttribution: Punja ZK, Kahl D, Reade R, Xiang Y, Munz J, Nachappa P. Figure 4 in the 2023 Preprints.org version of “Challenges to Cannabis sativa Production from Pathogens and Microbes—the Role of Molecular Diagnostics and Bioinformatics,” CC BY 4.0; link the source and license and indicate any modification.
useLimitations: Reference URL only; the asset is not copied into the repository.
Panel e is the suspected somatic-mutation comparison; panels a–d are unresolved mosaic-like differentials and must not inherit the genetic label.
No panel is sequence-confirmed as the cause shown; retain panel labels, caption context, and human review.
CC BY permits automated use with attribution, but this composite is excluded from training eligibility because its panels contain different and incompletely resolved labels.
media.severity: mixed chlorotic and mosaic-like foliar patterns

name: Armyworm caterpillar feeding complex
summary: A multi-species noctuid caterpillar differential for hemp. Plant-linked larvae can accompany grouped early skeletonization, later irregular chewing or defoliation, and occasional bud entry, but body color, holes, silk, frass, or floral injury cannot distinguish armyworms from corn earworm, tobacco budworm, cutworms, or loopers. Species labels require diagnostic larval morphology or expert confirmation.
affectedParts: maturing buds and flowers at high populations
soil or surface beneath plants for mature wandering larvae
indicators: A plant-linked noctuid caterpillar with three pairs of true thoracic legs and five rear proleg pairs is documented beside fresh hemp chewing injury, separating the non-looper body plan from three-proleg-pair loopers
Young larvae and an associated egg mass occur on a leaf underside, with grouped surface feeding or skeletonization near the hatch site
Older larvae occur singly with fresh irregular holes, shredded edges, expanding defoliation, or tissue stripped toward major veins
Fresh frass, feeding margins, larval position, and same-plant time sequence link the organism to new injury rather than merely co-locating it with old holes

Beet-armyworm-compatible larvae show lengthwise green-yellow striping and a small dark lateral spot on the second segment behind the head, with the full morphology visible rather than inferred from color alone
Yellowstriped-armyworm-compatible larvae show paired yellow-to-orange dorsal stripes, a lateral dark spot on the fourth segment behind the head, and black triangular dorsal-side markings
Bertha-armyworm-compatible larvae are green to black with a pale lateral stripe, but this variable appearance supports only a differential until expert identification

At high plant-linked populations, larvae may move into maturing buds with visible feeding, silk, and frass; the larva must be recovered because floral tunneling more strongly raises corn earworm or tobacco budworm differentials
exclusions: No active larvae, egg masses, fresh frass, or advancing feeding margins are found after repeated day and sheltered-canopy inspection, and the damage is old
A green caterpillar with three rear proleg pairs and a looping gait supports cabbage, alfalfa, or soybean looper rather than this five-proleg-pair armyworm differential
A larva embedded in hemp flower material with bud tunneling and associated rot is corn-earworm- or tobacco-budworm-compatible until morphology establishes otherwise
Adult Japanese beetles or spotted cucumber beetles are actively linked to the skeletonization or holes and no caterpillars are present
Slug or snail mucus, nocturnal rasping, or mollusk recovery explains the chewing pattern without caterpillar evidence
Grasshopper or katydid mandible feeding and organism evidence explain the missing tissue
Hail, wind, handling, training, equipment, or contact injury explains tears aligned with exposure or manipulation rather than active feeding fronts
Body color, a purported inverted-Y head mark, one lateral spot, silk, frass, or holes alone cannot establish species because several noctuid larvae vary and overlap

progression.description: Pale ribbed eggs may occur in a mass on a leaf underside, sometimes partly covered with moth hairs; eggs alone require rearing or expert review.
Young larvae feed together near the hatch site and may scrape or skeletonize leaf tissue while leaving a localized clustered distribution.
Older larvae separate and feed singly, producing larger irregular holes, shredded margins, or expanding leaf-area loss.
High local populations can defoliate foliage and may move toward maturing buds, where larvae, fresh frass, silk, and exact feeding location must be documented.
Mature larvae may move inward, downward, or toward soil to pupate, leaving old damage without a visible feeder; regional timing and generation counts must not be used as a universal Cannabis clock.

lookAlikes: Hail, wind, handling, equipment, or training tear
Leaf-spot center loss or shot hole
confirmation: Capture the same uninterrupted plant-linked sequence: whole plant and canopy position, both surfaces of the damaged leaf, fresh feeding margin, frass or silk, larva beside injury, and scaled dorsal, lateral, head, and ventral views.

Count the three true thoracic leg pairs and rear proleg pairs and record gait; five rear proleg pairs support the non-looper noctuid group while three rear pairs plus looping motion supports the cited loopers.
Record egg-mass structure and covering, larval number, size range, grouping versus solitary behavior, exact leaf or bud location, plant stage, and repeat observations of newly consumed tissue.

Use multiple high-resolution markings together rather than body color alone: photograph the head, second and fourth segments behind the head, lateral stripes or spots, dorsal stripes, and dorsal-side triangles where present.

Dissect or gently open damaged floral material on camera and preserve the recovered larva; do not assign armyworm from silk, frass, tunneling, or bud rot without excluding corn earworm and tobacco budworm.
Preserve representative larvae for rearing or qualified entomological identification and use validated molecular identification when a species-level Spodoptera or Mamestra label is required.

Keep damage-only, frass-only, silk-only, egg-only, moth-only, body-color-only, incomplete-marking, detached-leaf, non-Cannabis, organism/injury-unlinked, low-resolution, stock, Shutterstock, BugGuide, vendor, generated, anecdotal, forum, and unverified samples out of the confirmed class and route them to human review.
immediateActions: Mark affected plants and preserve plant-linked larvae, egg masses, frass, and pre-intervention images before disturbing feeding sites.
Inspect leaf undersides, fresh feeding fronts, inner canopy, maturing buds, and the surface beneath plants, recording larvae by size and location.
Separate suspected floral feeding from bud-rot diagnosis and preserve both entomology and plant-pathology samples when decay is present.
correctivePlan: Use an integrated response based on confirmed caterpillar identity, larval size, density, crop stage, fresh injury, regional guidance, and options currently legal for hemp in the jurisdiction.
Track new injury and live larvae at fixed marked plants; old holes and stripped tissue do not recover and cannot measure treatment response.
Protect beneficial arthropods and flower quality, and reopen the differential if feeding advances without recovery of a compatible larva.
prevention: Scout leaf undersides for egg masses and grouped young larvae before injury disperses, while recording regional season rather than assuming a universal late-season window.
Maintain plant- and location-specific counts across field edges and interiors so clustered egg laying is not converted into a whole-field severity label.
Conserve documented natural enemies where appropriate and remove alternate-host or crop-residue risks only within a locally supported IPM plan.
warnings: This record is an armyworm complex, not a species classifier; Spodoptera, Mamestra, corn earworms, budworms, cutworms, and loopers overlap in color and chewing injury.
Photo or video alone is capped at 0.30 because even detailed larval images may lack ventral prolegs, complete segment markings, plant linkage, or species-confirming characters.

Utah hemp guidance reports few armyworms and little foliar injury locally, while Missouri describes potentially severe feeding; neither regional observation establishes universal prevalence, severity, yield loss, or an economic threshold.

The Pacific Northwest hemp guide identifies corn earworm as the most damaging regional caterpillar and says other mature-hemp caterpillar injury is usually minor; bud injury must not be defaulted to armyworm.
The Florida synthesis distinguishes established, intercepted, and reported species and warns that presence does not prove reproduction or damage; regional lists are not image ground truth.

The Florida field-guide armyworm images are Shutterstock or BugGuide references without verified item-level automated-training permission. No media was copied or indexed, and no training-eligible asset is included.

sources.title: Insect Pests of Industrial Hemp in Missouri
supportedClaims: Spotted cucumber beetle adults feed on hemp foliage and floral tissue, producing holes and ragged edges, while larvae can feed on root hairs and root tips.

The Missouri Extension guide lists chlorotic spots, curling, terminal stunting, distorted buds, and bud abortion as possible tarnished plant bug injury on hemp; these institutional symptom claims conflict with earlier hemp literature that had not documented foliar symptoms and therefore require organism-linked human review.
Dectes texanus larvae can bore inside hemp stems and pith, producing internal galleries, wilting, dieback, swollen or split stems, and increased breakage risk.
Cabbage looper larvae feed on hemp leaves, often from lower-leaf undersides upward, producing large irregular holes and potentially damaging floral buds.
Japanese beetle adults feed on hemp foliage and can skeletonize leaves between veins; adults are metallic green with bronze wing covers and often aggregate.
Armyworm larvae can create irregular holes and skeletonization and may enter hemp buds or flowers, where silk and frass can accompany feeding injury.
Hemp insect pressure varies by region, growth stage, and variety, so damage morphology without organism evidence should not be treated as species confirmation.

sources.title: Armyworms
sources.organization: Utah State University Extension Integrated Pest Management
supportedClaims: Utah hemp guidance covers beet armyworm (Spodoptera exigua), bertha armyworm (Mamestra configurata), and yellowstriped armyworm (Spodoptera ornithogalli), so armyworm is a multi-species complex rather than one visual label.

The guide describes beet armyworm larvae as generally light green with lengthwise green-yellow stripes and a small black spot on each side of the second body segment, yellowstriped armyworms as green to black with yellow-orange dorsal stripes, a fourth-segment lateral spot, and black dorsal-side triangles, and bertha armyworms as green to black with a pale lateral stripe.

Eggs are pale, ribbed, usually occur in masses on leaf undersides, and may be partly covered with moth hairs; young larvae feed in groups while older larvae feed singly and may curl into a C-shape when disturbed.
On hemp, young larvae may skeletonize foliage while older larvae produce irregular holes, shredded leaves, or defoliation; silk may occur and high populations may move into maturing buds.

Utah observations found few caterpillars and little foliar damage in field hemp and assigned a low-to-medium threat level; regional timing, generation count, severity, and treatment guidance are not universal Cannabis thresholds.

sources.title: Hemp-Caterpillars
sources.publisher: Oregon State University, Washington State University, and University of Idaho Extension
supportedClaims: Pacific Northwest hemp guidance groups multiple noctuid caterpillars, including bertha armyworm and spotted cutworm, as hemp pests and states that all have three pairs of true legs behind the head.

Corn earworm, tobacco budworm, bertha armyworm, and spotted cutworm have five pairs of rear prolegs, while the cited loopers have three pairs and move with a looping gait; proleg and gait evidence is more discriminating than damage pattern or body color.

Corn earworm is identified as the most damaging caterpillar in the regional hemp context because it feeds and tunnels in flower buds and can contribute wounds associated with bud rot; floral injury must not automatically be assigned to armyworm.

The guide describes damage to mature hemp from caterpillars other than corn earworm as usually minor in the Pacific Northwest, which conflicts with treating every armyworm-like larva or damaged bud as a high-severity event.
Regional host, timing, damage, and management statements are bounded to Pacific Northwest hemp and do not provide a universal species-level image rule or armyworm treatment threshold.

sources.title: Arthropod and mollusk pests of hemp, Cannabis sativa (Rosales: Cannabaceae), in Florida
sources.publisher: Oxford University Press on behalf of the Entomological Society of America
supportedClaims: The Florida synthesis reports beet armyworm (Spodoptera exigua) and yellowstriped armyworm (Spodoptera ornithogalli) among noctuids established in Florida and associated with hemp, while bertha armyworm and Spodoptera litura are marked as intercepted rather than established records.
The authors distinguish reported presence from pest impact: not every one of the 105 listed arthropod and mollusk species can reproduce, complete its life cycle, or damage hemp.

The paper emphasizes identification across life stages and warns that immature organisms can be confused; occurrence in a regional list or an organism-only image is not plant-linked proof of injury, prevalence, or severity.

Armyworm images in the article field guide are credited to Shutterstock or BugGuide rather than presented with clear item-level automated-training rights; they are not added as reusable dataset media.

name: Cabbage looper feeding injury
summary: A chewing-caterpillar diagnosis that requires a Trichoplusia ni larva linked to fresh Cannabis injury. Irregular holes, windowpane feeding, frass, flowers with missing tissue, an adult moth, or a green looping caterpillar alone are not species-level ground truth.
affectedParts: lower foliage reported in Missouri hemp
floral buds and flower tissue reported in Missouri hemp
stages: outdoor crop when larvae are present; calendar timing is regional
indicators: A pale-green, relatively smooth larva is physically linked to fresh chewing on the same Cannabis leaf or flower
The larva arches its body into a characteristic loop while crawling; behavior should be captured on video rather than inferred from one curved pose
A ventral macro view shows two pairs of abdominal prolegs on abdominal segments five and six, with the terminal anal pair recorded separately
Thin white longitudinal stripes occur along the back and sides, and the body narrows toward the anterior and broadens toward the posterior
Fresh lower-surface feeding or translucent windowpanes can precede through-leaf, irregular holes; this early-instar sequence is cross-crop transfer context unless recorded longitudinally on Cannabis
Sticky frass occurs beside a fresh feeding site and is linked to the photographed larva rather than treated as species-specific by itself

Missouri hemp guidance reports feeding beginning from lower-leaf undersides and moving upward, with severe injury capable of stripping foliage or damaging floral buds; other regions and cultivars may not follow this distribution
Detached Cannabis leaves support Trichoplusia ni feeding, but consumption and larval growth varied between the limited cannabinoid-free and CBD-dominant F2 genotypes tested
exclusions: No larva, specimen, fresh feeding front, or linked frass is found after repeat underside, canopy, and flower scouting; retain only a generic historical chewing-injury label
The larva has four pairs of abdominal prolegs or another complete proleg pattern inconsistent with cabbage looper
Dark thoracic legs or microscopic body microspines support soybean looper; unresolved plusiine larvae remain genus-, subfamily-, or caterpillar-level observations
A green caterpillar appears in a still image without a usable ventral proleg view, scale, looping-gait sequence, or expert specimen determination
Skeletonization is associated with aggregating metallic-green, copper-winged Japanese beetle adults rather than a caterpillar
Shot holes or ragged margins are linked to flea beetles or spotted cucumber beetles, or rasping holes and slime are linked to slugs or snails
Torn tissue aligns with hail, handling, fan abrasion, training damage, or spray injury and no chewing organism or fresh frass is linked to the lesion
An adult moth, egg, pupa, cocoon, frass deposit, or non-Cannabis larva is documented without a larva-linked Cannabis feeding event

progression.description: Small ridged eggs or a visiting adult may be present on foliage, but neither establishes larval feeding or a Cannabis infestation; preserve and rear or obtain expert identification when relevant.

Cross-crop guidance describes young larvae feeding on leaf undersides and sometimes leaving the opposite epidermis intact. On Cannabis, record the larva, both leaf surfaces, and the same marked site over time before assigning this sequence.
Larger larvae can expand translucent windows into irregular through-holes with nearby frass. Record new leaf area removed and organism counts rather than inferring severity from one old hole.

Missouri hemp guidance reports upward movement, foliage stripping, and possible floral-bud damage. Treat plant position, rate, and flower involvement as observed field metadata, not universal species behavior.

Chewed tissue persists after larvae leave and a thin cocoon may occur under foliage or in debris. Without new feeding or a linked organism, the residual frame is historical injury rather than active cabbage looper ground truth.

lookAlikes: Soybean looper or another plusiine looper
Hail, wind, handling, or training tear
Spray or contact injury that later tears
confirmation: Capture whole-plant and row views and record affected and unaffected plants, upper/middle/lower canopy zones, leaf age, both leaf surfaces, and flower involvement; do not infer a universal lower-canopy preference from one Missouri guide or a detached-leaf assay.
At the fresh feeding front, record the larva and damage in the same uninterrupted sequence, then obtain dorsal, lateral, and ventral macro views with a millimeter scale.

Record video of the larva moving so the looping gait is observed, not reconstructed from a still pose; show two abdominal proleg pairs on segments five and six and retain the terminal anal pair in view.

Preserve a representative larva or rear it to an adult and seek Extension-entomologist or diagnostic-laboratory identification when soybean looper, another plusiine, or incomplete morphology remains plausible.
Mark plants and repeat counts and fixed-view imaging to separate expanding injury from old residual holes; log eggs, larvae, frass, cocoons, adults, and damaged area as separate observations.

Keep damage-only, frass-only, egg-only, adult-only, cocoon-only, non-Cannabis, detached-leaf-only, generated, vendor, anecdotal, unverified, low-resolution, and organism/injury-unlinked samples out of the confirmed Trichoplusia ni Cannabis class.

Retain the Stack et al. detached-leaf assay as direct host-feeding evidence but flag it as a model-herbivore laboratory result: the study did not observe Trichoplusia ni in its field plots and does not supply a hemp action threshold, field distribution, or universal cultivar response.
immediateActions: Flag the plant and preserve the organism-to-damage link before moving, collecting, or treating the larva.
Inspect both surfaces of lower, middle, and upper leaves plus flowers; count larvae and map fresh versus old injury across several plants and locations.
Quarantine collected larvae with plant and location identifiers for expert review or rearing when species morphology is incomplete.
correctivePlan: Base any intervention on confirmed active larvae, observed injury trend, crop stage, local Extension advice, and products currently legal and labeled for hemp in the jurisdiction.
Do not apply Virginia cole-crop thresholds, laboratory chemotype effects, or non-Cannabis treatment results as hemp thresholds.
Revisit fixed plants after intervention because holes and missing flower tissue will not reverse and cannot alone demonstrate current control.
prevention: Include leaf-underside, whole-canopy, flower, larval dorsal/ventral/lateral macro, gait video, frass, and fixed-site progression views in routine scouting.
Record nearby crops and weeds, weather, crop stage, cultivar, and cannabinoid chemotype when known without assuming those variables predict infestation.
Conserve predators and parasitoids where compatible with local IPM guidance, while recording parasitized or diseased larvae separately from healthy active feeders.
warnings: Chewing morphology is shared by many insects and physical injuries; species-level ground truth requires a diagnostic larva linked to fresh Cannabis feeding.
Looping gait and a green striped body are not independently unique to Trichoplusia ni; soybean looper and other plusiines may require microscopic or expert determination.

The direct Cannabis study used Trichoplusia ni as a model generalist in detached-leaf assays and did not observe it in the field experiment; it cannot establish field prevalence, progression, distribution, yield loss, or thresholds.

Cannabinoid-free and CBD-dominant F2 genotypes differed in feeding and larval growth in one controlled study, but genotype, chemotype, and trichome context prevent a universal cultivar or severity rule.
Virginia and Florida timing, crop injury, generation, and management statements are non-Cannabis transfer evidence only; no validated hemp economic or treatment threshold was found.

The licensed University of Georgia organism image shows a non-Cannabis larva only. It is useful for morphology review but cannot label Cannabis injury, host use, severity, location, or progression and must remain outside Cannabis training and evaluation splits.
All damage-only, incomplete-morphology, detached-tissue, organism-only, non-Cannabis, unlinked, rights-unclear, and low-resolution samples require human review.

supportedClaims: Spotted cucumber beetle adults feed on hemp foliage and floral tissue, producing holes and ragged edges, while larvae can feed on root hairs and root tips.

The Missouri Extension guide lists chlorotic spots, curling, terminal stunting, distorted buds, and bud abortion as possible tarnished plant bug injury on hemp; these institutional symptom claims conflict with earlier hemp literature that had not documented foliar symptoms and therefore require organism-linked human review.

sources.title: Cannabinoids function in defense against chewing herbivores in Cannabis sativa L.
sources.publisher: Oxford University Press on behalf of Nanjing Agricultural University
supportedClaims: In a controlled detached-leaf assay, single Trichoplusia ni neonates fed for six days on leaves from 12 cutting-propagated Cannabis sativa F2 genotypes: six CBD-dominant and six cannabinoid-free genotypes.
Trichoplusia ni larvae consumed more leaf area and reached greater final mass on cannabinoid-free Cannabis genotypes than on CBD-dominant genotypes in the detached-leaf assay.

The detached-leaf assay establishes that Trichoplusia ni can consume Cannabis leaf tissue, but the species was not observed in the study field plots and was used as a model generalist herbivore; the experiment therefore does not establish field prevalence, canopy distribution, progression, injury thresholds, or yield loss on hemp.

Larvae in the detached-leaf assay were more often observed on the abaxial surface of cannabinoid-free leaves, but this laboratory behavior must not be converted into a universal field location or diagnostic threshold.

Cannabinoid chemotype, genotype, and trichome morphology affected feeding context, so severity or susceptibility observed in this limited F2 population must not be generalized across Cannabis cultivars.

sources.title: Cabbage Looper
sources.publisher: Virginia Tech and Virginia State University
supportedClaims: Cross-crop identification guidance describes cabbage looper larvae as pale green, relatively smooth, thinly white-striped caterpillars that arch or loop while crawling and can reach approximately 1.5 inches long.

Two pairs of abdominal prolegs on abdominal segments five and six help distinguish cabbage looper larvae from imported cabbageworm larvae, which have four pairs; incomplete or obscured ventral views cannot support that exclusion.
In non-Cannabis crops, early instars feed from leaf undersides and may leave the opposite epidermis intact, while later instars chew through leaves and sticky frass can occur near feeding sites.
Virginia cabbage, broccoli, and cauliflower thresholds are crop-specific and must not be transferred to Cannabis or hemp.

sources.title: Cabbage Looper, Trichoplusia ni (Hübner) (Insecta: Lepidoptera: Noctuidae)
sources.publisher: University of Florida Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences Extension
supportedClaims: Institutional morphology guidance describes mature larvae as predominantly green, usually with a distinct white stripe on each side and faint dorsal white stripes, with a narrower anterior and broader posterior body that loops during movement.

Cabbage looper can be confused with soybean looper; dark thoracic legs and microscopic body microspines favor soybean looper, so a dorsal photograph or looping gait alone is insufficient for species confirmation.
Eggs are small, ridged, yellowish-white to green, and can occur on either leaf surface; eggs alone require rearing or expert identification because their appearance is not a Cannabis injury label.

A thin white fragile cocoon can occur under foliage or in debris, and the gray-brown adult has a central silvery U-shaped mark and dot that may be connected; an adult or cocoon not linked to a damaged Cannabis plant does not prove larval injury.
Geographic activity, generation time, host suitability, and crop management vary substantially; non-Cannabis timing, host, threshold, and treatment statements are transfer context only.

The oblique dorsal view does not fully document the ventral proleg pattern or a looping gait and cannot by itself exclude soybean looper or another plusiine in a new observation.
Keep organism-only media outside Cannabis condition training and evaluation splits even though the license permits reuse; require a plant-linked diagnostic sequence and human label review.

name: Dectes stem-borer injury
summary: A documented industrial-hemp stem-borer differential. Hemp evidence supports pith galleries, wilt, dieback, swollen or split stems, and breakage; species-level confidence requires a compatible larva or identified adult linked to the affected plant because those injury signs overlap disease, other borers, and mechanical failure.
affectedParts: leaf petiole as an early scouting location
central pith and internal stem gallery
individual leaf or branch above the entry site
whole plant secondarily after structural failure
indicators: A symptomatic hemp stem contains a longitudinal gallery through the central pith rather than only superficial bark injury
A legless cream to yellow larva with an orange-red head and accordion-like, rear-tapering body is recovered within the gallery
A dark-bodied adult covered by dense gray pubescence has very long, black-and-gray banded antennae and is linked to the affected plant or local infestation
One leaf or branch wilts or dies while surrounding canopy tissue remains initially greener, prompting inspection of its petiole and connected stem
The hemp stem is locally swollen, split, weakened, or broken and the internal gallery continues through the damaged region
Serial stem dissections show pith tunneling progressing toward lower stem tissue rather than a static wound cavity
exclusions: No internal pith gallery is present and wilt follows measured drought, waterlogging, heat, or root-zone failure
Vascular discoloration, crown lesions, root rot, or laboratory evidence supports Fusarium, Rhizoctonia, Pythium, or another vascular/root pathogen without a compatible larva
A clean fracture, training wound, wind split, or equipment injury has healthy intact pith on both sides and no tunnel, frass, or insect
The recovered larva has legs or morphology inconsistent with a cerambycid stem borer
The adult is an ashgray blister beetle or another gray beetle and lacks compatible longhorn morphology
A hollow or senescent stem is labeled from appearance alone without an active gallery, larva, adult association, or expert identification
Soybean-only basal girdling, frass-plug, field-edge, seasonal, or lodging patterns are transferred to hemp without Cannabis observations
Adult presence alone is used to infer that a photographed Cannabis stem is internally infested

progression.description: Adults may be observed on vegetation, but published Cannabis evidence does not establish a universal hemp emergence or oviposition calendar. Record local date, geography, weather, plant stage, and direct plant association.

A single leaf, petiole, or branch may wilt while nearby canopy tissue remains greener. This sequence is characterized in soybean and is a hemp scouting hypothesis, not Cannabis ground truth until the connected tissue is dissected.
Larvae feed within the central pith. On hemp, document gallery direction, length, fresh frass, larval position, stem diameter, and the external tissue directly connected to the tunnel.
Hemp stems may swell or split and connected tissue may wilt or die back as boring disrupts internal tissues and weakens the stem.

Affected hemp stems can break under mechanical stress. Mature-stem basal girdling and overwintering chambers are well described in soybean and sunflower but require direct Cannabis documentation before being used as hemp labels.

lookAlikes: Mechanical training split or wind breakage
Other stem-boring beetle or moth larva
Normal mature hollow-stem or post-harvest decay
confirmation: Capture a whole-plant and row view before cutting, showing affected and unaffected plants and the precise canopy position of wilt or breakage.
Record a continuous video from the external symptom to the connected petiole or stem, then split the stem lengthwise on camera so the gallery-to-symptom relationship is preserved.
Photograph the intact stem exterior, entry or swelling site, cross-section, full longitudinal gallery, frass if present, and larva in situ with a metric scale and color reference.
Obtain dorsal, lateral, antenna, head-capsule, and full-body macro views of recovered adults or larvae; do not identify Dectes from a damaged stem alone.
Sample several symptomatic and asymptomatic stems across several field locations because one adult, one wilted leaf, or one gallery cannot establish field distribution.
Submit the organism and connected stem section to an Extension entomologist or diagnostic laboratory when morphology is incomplete or another borer/blister beetle is plausible.
Pair insect confirmation with vascular and root-zone inspection when wilt, dieback, or crown decline could represent a co-occurring pathogen.
immediateActions: Flag affected plants and preserve the symptom-to-stem connection before pruning, disposal, or destructive sampling.
Quarantine removed stem material from clean production areas until the insect and any co-occurring disease are evaluated.
Map plants with fresh wilt, stem swelling, galleries, larvae, adults, and breakage as separate observations rather than one combined severity label.
correctivePlan: Base any response on confirmed Cannabis infestation, local Extension guidance, crop stage, and products or cultural practices currently legal for hemp in the jurisdiction.
Remove or manage confirmed infested residues only when compatible with local agronomic, sanitation, erosion, and regulatory requirements.
Continue fixed-plant monitoring after intervention because existing galleries, wilted leaves, and broken stems will not reverse and cannot alone measure current control.
prevention: Add stem exterior, petiole, split-stem, larva/adult macro, and whole-row views to routine outdoor scouting records.
Record adjacent soybean, sunflower, ragweed, and cocklebur context as potential regional reservoirs without assuming those host relationships predict Cannabis infestation.
Retain specimens and source-grouped sequences so future expert review can keep plants, stems, organisms, dates, and field locations together.
warnings: Wilt, dieback, swollen stems, splits, galleries, and breakage are not independently species-specific; Dectes ground truth requires organism evidence linked to the affected hemp stem.

Published Cannabis evidence is currently much thinner than soybean and sunflower evidence. Non-Cannabis leaf-age, canopy, seasonal, girdling, lodging, yield, and management claims are transfer context only.
An organism-only adult image teaches morphology but cannot establish Cannabis host use, an internal larva, active injury, severity, or field distribution.
The Dectes texanus versus historical Dectes sayi boundary includes ambiguous morphology; incomplete adult views require expert or molecular review rather than a forced species label.
Adult counts do not reliably predict infested-stem frequency in soybean and no validated hemp action threshold or symptom-to-yield relationship was found.
The institutional video is soybean-focused and has no verified reusable license; it is reference metadata only and must not enter Cannabis training or evaluation splits.
All damage-only, gallery-only, organism-only, unlinked specimen/stem, non-Cannabis, and unresolved-taxonomy samples require human review.

sources.title: Profile of the Dectes stem borer (Coleoptera: Cerambycidae) in sunflower and soybean
sources.organization: Journal of Integrated Pest Management (Varenhorst et al.)
sources.publisher: Oxford University Press for the Entomological Society of America
supportedClaims: In sunflower and soybean, adults are dark brown to black under dense light-gray pubescence, measure 6 to 11 mm long, and normally hold curved antennae forward with the tips directed downward.
Larvae are legless, have an orange-red head capsule and accordion-like body tapering toward the rear, and range from approximately 1.5 mm in early instars to 12.5 mm when mature.

The reviewed non-Cannabis sequence is egg deposition in petiole tissue, larval pith tunneling, movement toward the stem base, internal girdling, a frass-plugged overwintering chamber, and possible lodging; Cannabis timing and frequencies have not been established.
Adult abundance does not reliably predict the percentage of infested stems, and internal feeding requires stem dissection for confirmation.
Dectes adults may be confused with ashgray blister beetle, while historical Dectes texanus versus Dectes sayi species boundaries contain morphological ambiguity that may require molecular analysis.
Management timing and efficacy vary by geography and season, and the review does not establish a hemp economic threshold or a hemp-labeled treatment.

sources.title: Dectes Stem Borer Management in Soybeans (FS-1196)
supportedClaims: The peer-reviewed soybean factsheet describes gray adults with black-and-gray banded antennae and creamy white to yellow, legless, accordion-like larvae.
Petiole pith feeding can produce a single wilted leaf before larvae tunnel into the main stem; later internal girdling can predispose mature plants to basal breakage and lodging.
Regional occurrence and lodging losses are variable, so soybean severity, yield, and management values must not be transferred directly to Cannabis.

sources.title: Dectes Stem Borer (Dectes texanus)
sources.organization: Kansas State University Department of Entomology
sources.publisher: Kansas State University Research and Extension
supportedClaims: In soybean, eggs are usually laid in mid-canopy leaf petioles; larvae tunnel down the petiole into the stem and generally move downward.
An individual wilted or drying leaf above the normal lower-canopy senescence zone is a useful scouting cue but is not diagnostic without stem tunneling and a larva.
Representative confirmation requires carefully splitting stems from several field locations and documenting tunnels and live larvae.

name: Japanese beetle feeding injury
summary: A documented outdoor-hemp defoliator and flower feeder. Fresh skeletonization plus an adult with metallic-green head/thorax, copper-bronze wing covers, and twelve white abdominal hair patches is strong field evidence; feeding damage without the adult is only a low-specificity chewing-injury label.
affectedParts: major and minor veins left after feeding
indicators: Adults on hemp have a metallic-green head and thorax with copper-bronze wing covers
Five white hair patches along each abdominal side plus two posterior patches form twelve visible tufts when the adult is photographed from above and slightly behind
Fresh chewing removes interveinal leaf tissue while leaving a lace-like network of veins
Adults are present on the same leaf, shoot, or developing flower as fresh feeding injury
Multiple adults and newly expanding damage occur in a localized plant or field cluster
Flower feeding is directly observed rather than inferred from missing or browned floral tissue
exclusions: No adult or specimen is recovered after repeat scouting and another defoliator is found at the fresh feeding front
The beetle lacks the twelve discrete white abdominal hair patches or morphology supports green June beetle, another scarab, or a metallic beetle
Holes contain caterpillars, silk, or frass and do not preserve the characteristic interveinal lace pattern
Small round shot holes with flea beetles support flea-beetle injury
Irregular holes or ragged margins occur with spotted cucumber beetles rather than Japanese beetles
Damage is mined within intact epidermis rather than removed from the leaf surface
Skeletonization is old, dry, and unchanged across serial observations, with no active organism established
Root decline is attributed to Japanese beetle solely because adults occur above ground; hemp-root grub feeding has not been confirmed

progression.description: One or more adults occupy exposed foliage or developing flowers; small fresh interveinal feeding windows begin near the occupied tissue.
Interveinal tissue is progressively removed and intact veins create a lace-like pattern; neighboring leaves or flowers should be checked to map whether injury is clustered.
More adults and fresh injury may accumulate on a subset of plants or canopy positions. Record actual adult counts and new injury because a single frame cannot establish temporal growth.

Large populations can remove substantial leaf area or completely defoliate plants, but serious hemp defoliation was rare in the early multi-state literature and no universal loss threshold was established.
Skeletonized tissue persists after adults leave. Old lace-like leaves without adults or newly expanding injury must not be labeled as a current Japanese beetle infestation.

lookAlikes: Green June beetle or another scarab beetle
confirmation: Capture a whole-plant or row view to show the distribution of affected and unaffected plants, then record upper, middle, and lower canopy zones separately; published hemp sources do not establish a preferred leaf age or canopy position.
Photograph fresh injury and the adult together before disturbance, then obtain dorsal, lateral, and posterior macro views with a scale reference.
Verify the metallic-green head/thorax, copper-bronze wing covers, and twelve discrete white abdominal hair patches; preserve a representative adult when morphology is unclear.
Revisit marked leaves or plants and record new feeding and adult counts so old residual skeletonization is separated from an active infestation.
For image/video datasets, require an organism-level frame linked to the damage sequence; do not use skeletonization-only frames as species-level ground truth.
Submit an intact adult to an Extension entomologist or diagnostic laboratory when a similar scarab, green June beetle, or incomplete view prevents confident identification.
Do not infer larval root injury from adult canopy presence; confirm grubs in the root zone and identify them separately if root damage is suspected.
immediateActions: Mark sampled plants, count adults, estimate current defoliation, and record whether flowers are being fed on before choosing an intervention.
Scout several plants across several locations so one conspicuous aggregation is not treated as a field-wide population estimate.
Preserve pre-intervention photographs and a representative specimen when the diagnosis or future label review depends on species identity.
correctivePlan: Use an IPM response based on confirmed adults, fresh injury, crop stage, local pressure, and products currently legal for hemp in the jurisdiction.
Track new injury and adult counts at fixed plants; old skeletonized tissue will not recover and should not be used alone to judge control.
Protect pollinators and flowering-crop quality when evaluating any response on developing flowers.
prevention: Include adult-morphology and fresh-damage views in routine outdoor scouting records.
Map clusters and repeat counts through the adult activity period instead of relying on cumulative season-long damage.

warnings: Skeletonization, irregular holes, or flower injury alone are not Japanese beetle ground truth; species-level image labels require the adult and diagnostic morphology.

Published hemp observations do not establish a preferred leaf age or canopy position, so those fields must be recorded from the sampled plant rather than imputed.

name: Spotted cucumber beetle feeding injury
scientificName: Diabrotica undecimpunctata species and subspecies complex
summary: A documented adult chewing pest of field hemp. Adults can make irregular holes in leaves and flowers and may prefer floral tissue, but damage is usually reported as minor. Authoritative hemp sources conflict on larval root feeding, so roots and soil larvae are excluded from confirmed Cannabis injury unless future plant-linked evidence resolves the conflict.
affectedParts: soil and roots only as a disputed differential, not confirmed hemp injury
indicators: A compatible adult is photographed or collected on the same hemp plant and date as fresh chewing injury; an organism from an unrelated trap, crop, weed, or date is occurrence evidence only.
The general species profile describes adults as 5.2 to 7.5 mm long, yellow to yellowish green, with a black head, long dark antennae, and black elytral spots.
Eastern and western subspecies differ in leg and abdominal coloration, and institutional sources describe 11 or 12 wing spots; spot count alone is not a safe subspecies or species label.
Hemp leaf injury consists of small or irregular holes and ragged chewing margins while an adult is actively feeding; hole morphology without the beetle is nonspecific.
Adults can occupy and feed on hemp flowers, and the 2019 hemp synthesis reported an apparent flower preference, but one beetle on a flower does not establish reproductive loss.
A useful capture set includes the whole plant, upper/middle/lower canopy, intact damaged organ, dorsal and lateral adult macros, metric scale, and a short video linking the insect to active feeding.
Repeat observations distinguish fresh expanding injury from old static holes, weather damage, or an incidental beetle resting after damage occurred.
Pacific Northwest and Utah guidance characterize mature-hemp or field injury as minor; severity must be measured locally rather than inferred from non-Cannabis crops.
exclusions: No beetle is linked to fresh injury and another caterpillar, beetle, slug, snail, grasshopper, or earwig is present with compatible feeding signs.
The adult is metallic green with copper-brown wing covers and abdominal white hair patches, supporting Japanese beetle rather than spotted cucumber beetle.
The yellow-and-black adult has striping, different spot geometry, or morphology consistent with striped cucumber beetle, western corn rootworm, northern corn rootworm, or another chrysomelid.
Silk, frass, caterpillar body or proleg evidence, or edge-to-interior skeletonization supports caterpillar feeding.
Damage consists mainly of stippling, silvering, mines, galls, rasping scars, honeydew, sooty mold, or sap-feeding distortion rather than fresh chewing holes.
Torn tissue follows hail, wind, training, handling, equipment, or contact points and lacks missing tissue associated with an observed feeding event.
Root decline, weak anchorage, wilt, or stunting occurs without direct Cannabis-specific larval feeding evidence; inspect drought, hypoxia, compaction, root binding, nematodes, and pathogens instead.
An adult is present but serial images show no new injury, or injury continues after the beetle is absent and another causal pathway is better supported.

progression.description: Record cultivar, plant stage, field position, canopy level, nearby hosts, recent weather and injury-free comparison plants before assigning a beetle label.
Capture dorsal, lateral, head, antenna, leg, abdomen, and elytral views with a scale; record whether the beetle is feeding, resting, or flying away.
Video the adult contacting the exact leaf or flower and photograph the intact organ before and after feeding so new missing tissue remains plant-linked.
Reinspect tagged plants and matched controls to quantify new holes, affected organs, beetle counts, and whether injury remains minor or progresses.
Retain the adult or diagnostic images for expert or validated-key identification; keep root-larval and subspecies conclusions separate from adult hemp feeding.

lookAlikes: Other spotted or striped leaf beetle
Hail, wind, handling, equipment, or training tear
Leaf-spot center loss or shot hole
Root disease, root-zone stress, or nematode injury
confirmation: Record a linked evidence sequence: whole plant and row, affected organ, both leaf surfaces when applicable, dorsal and lateral adult macros, metric scale, and video of the insect on the exact injury site.
Sample multiple affected and unaffected plants across field edge and interior on at least two dates; record adults, fresh holes, flowers, crop stage, and neighboring hosts separately.
Identify a collected adult or complete diagnostic image set with an entomologist or validated regional key; do not assign species or subspecies from yellow-green color or spot count alone.
Require active feeding or temporally linked new injury on the same hemp plant for a Cannabis injury label; an organism-only image supports morphology, not Cannabis causation.

Treat soil larvae and root symptoms as unresolved because Utah guidance says larvae are not known to feed on hemp roots while Missouri Extension states they can; require future Cannabis-specific plant linkage before confirming root injury.
Do not transfer bacterial-wilt vector status, root-feeding injury, thresholds, severity, or yield effects from cucurbits, corn, peanut, beans, or sweet potato to Cannabis.

Keep damage-only, organism-only, trap-only, root-only, larva-only, incomplete-morphology, low-resolution, generated, vendor, anecdotal, forum, and unverified samples out of confirmed ground truth and route them to human review.
immediateActions: Preserve linked organism and plant-injury evidence before removing beetles or damaged tissue.
Scout nearby hemp plants, field edges, flowers, leaves, and alternate hosts with a repeatable method while recording adults and fresh injury separately.
Avoid species-specific treatment or root-injury claims until the organism, plant linkage, severity, crop stage, and local legal options are established.
correctivePlan: Use an integrated pest-management response only when locally confirmed adult pressure and measured Cannabis injury justify action; follow current hemp labels and local regulations.
Do not transfer numeric triggers from Utah or non-Cannabis crops as universal thresholds, and account for flowering-stage pollinators and beneficial insects before intervention.
Reinspect tagged plants after any response and evaluate new injury rather than expecting old holes to repair.
prevention: Maintain consistent field-edge and interior scouting records from small-plant through flowering stages.
Track nearby cucurbits, corn, legumes, grasses, weeds, crop harvest, and adult movement without treating proximity as proof of source.
Retain paired healthy and affected plant sequences plus identified adult vouchers so future review can separate occurrence, feeding, and consequential injury.
warnings: Chewing holes and a yellow-green spotted beetle are not individually diagnostic of Diabrotica undecimpunctata.

Hemp sources conflict on root feeding: Missouri Extension lists larval root-hair and root-tip feeding, while Utah State says larvae are not known to feed on hemp roots; root injury remains unconfirmed and requires human review.
Pacific Northwest and Utah minor-pest conclusions, seasonality, morphology descriptions, and numeric guidance are regional and must not become universal Cannabis thresholds.
The peer-reviewed species profile is primarily cross-crop biology; its larval injury, disease-vector, timing, and management claims do not establish Cannabis ground truth.
The CC BY-SA 4.0 adult image is organism-only, non-Cannabis, visually identified media and requires scientific review; it is excluded from Cannabis condition training.
No licensed, plant-linked hemp feeding progression or verified diagnostic video was found for this batch.
