sources.title: Spotted cucumber beetle/southern corn rootworm: profile of a polyphagous native pest
sources.publisher: Oxford University Press for the Entomological Society of America
supportedClaims: Adults are 5.2 to 7.5 mm long, yellow to yellowish green, with a black head, dark antennae longer than half the body, and 12 black elytral spots; eastern and western subspecies differ in leg and abdominal coloration.

Larvae are soil-dwelling, yellowish-white and wormlike with brown legs and dark head, thoracic, and anal plates, but their economically important root feeding is documented on non-Cannabis crops rather than hemp.
The species feeds on more than 200 plant species and can occur on hemp, but damage on many hosts is cosmetic or inconsequential and action thresholds are not well developed.
Adults are mobile and populations can increase into late summer, but geography, subspecies, climate, host, and crop context prevent a universal Cannabis timing or severity rule.
General species biology and non-Cannabis injury examples are identification and transfer context only; they do not prove that a photographed hemp root, leaf, or flower was injured by this beetle.

sources.title: Hemp-Cucumber beetle
sources.publisher: Oregon State University, Washington State University, and University of Idaho Extension
supportedClaims: The Pacific Northwest hemp guide describes the western spotted cucumber beetle as yellowish green, approximately 0.25 inch long, and bearing 11 black spots on the wing covers.
Adults eat small holes in leaves and flowers and are commonly found feeding on hemp.
Damage to mature hemp is usually minor, and the regional guide states that scouting thresholds are unnecessary because it treats the beetle as a minor hemp pest.
This western regional description and management conclusion must not be generalized to other subspecies, seedling stages, climates, or production systems.

sources.title: Spotted Cucumber Beetle
sources.organization: Utah State University Extension Integrated Pest Management
authors: Utah State University Extension Integrated Pest Management Program
supportedClaims: Utah hemp guidance describes adults as ovoid yellow-green beetles with a black head, legs, antennae, and 12 black wing spots; listed look-alikes include western and northern corn rootworms and other yellow-and-black chrysomelids.
On hemp, the damaging life stage is the adult, which chews irregular holes in leaves; damage is characterized as minor and adults can also be scouted on stems and flowers.
The guide explicitly states that soil larvae are not known to feed on hemp roots, conflicting with a Missouri Extension statement that larvae can feed on hemp root hairs and tips.
The reported Utah seasonality, low threat rating, and numeric treatment trigger are regional guidance rather than validated universal Cannabis thresholds.

name: Tarnished plant bug occurrence and possible feeding injury
scientificName: Lygus lineolaris and other Lygus spp.
summary: Lygus adults and nymphs are documented residents of field hemp and can breed on the crop, but organism presence is not proof that a photographed symptom was caused by tarnished plant bug. Earlier peer-reviewed hemp observations and current Utah guidance report no documented foliar symptoms, while Missouri Extension lists chlorotic spotting and terminal or bud distortion. Treat foliar and reproductive injury as compatible, contested evidence until a correctly identified insect is repeatedly linked to fresh injury; hemp economic thresholds remain unestablished.
affectedParts: whole plant and canopy for organism scouting
upper and expanding foliage as a contested symptom location
shoot tips and terminals as a contested symptom location
flowers and inflorescences for adult and nymph scouting
developing seeds and seed heads in seed hemp
nearby weeds, alfalfa, quinoa, and field-edge vegetation as possible source habitat
indicators: A captured adult is 4.4 to 6.3 mm long, light green to mottled brown or black, and has a V-shaped or triangular mark on the scutellum; the mark supports genus-level screening but is not sufficient for Lygus lineolaris identification
A compatible nymph is green or yellow-green, wingless or developing wing pads, rounded, and marked by dark dorsal spots; direct macro views must separate it from aphids and beneficial big-eyed bugs

Adults and multiple nymph sizes are recovered repeatedly from the same hemp area by direct inspection, sweep net, beating tray, or vacuum sampling, supporting residency or breeding rather than a transient single-insect observation

Counts are mapped across field edge and interior, upper and lower canopy, nearby alternate hosts, crop stage, and date because Lygus distribution can reflect colonization from weeds, alfalfa, quinoa, or other hosts

Shriveled or deformed developing seed, flower or bud loss, and abortion are compatible reproductive-tissue observations only when fresh injury is linked to feeding insects; appearance alone does not establish Lygus causation

Chlorotic spots, leaf curling, terminal stunting, and distorted buds are low-specificity, source-conflicted hemp observations: Missouri Extension lists them, whereas the 2019 peer-reviewed synthesis and Utah Extension state that foliar symptoms had not been documented

In Pacific Northwest context only, counts may rise from late July to mid-August near flowering; calendar timing must not be transferred to other regions, environments, or cultivars as a diagnostic feature
exclusions: Repeated sweep, beating-tray, vacuum, flower, and direct visual sampling finds no compatible adults or nymphs while symptoms continue to progress
The insect is Lygus hesperus, Lygus elisus, another mirid, or remains genus-only; do not assign Lygus lineolaris from a pale triangular mark alone
A beneficial big-eyed bug, false chinch bug, stink bug, aphid, or another seed or plant bug better matches the captured organism
Aphids with cornicles and colonies, honeydew, or cast skins explain the observation rather than fast-moving Lygus nymphs
Magnification confirms broad mite or hemp russet mite populations on the distorted tissue
Chewing holes, frass, silk, mines, galleries, or recovered larvae support a caterpillar, beetle, leafminer, or borer instead of piercing-sucking injury
A spray, herbicide, heat, wind, hail, training, or mechanical exposure pattern explains the distortion without organism-linked fresh injury
Boron or another nutrient/root-zone disorder is supported by measured inputs, root-zone pH or EC, tissue analysis, and a distribution pattern independent of Lygus counts
Flower or seed injury is assigned from one late-season frame without paired healthy tissue, repeated insect counts, crop-use context, or exclusion of pollination, pathogen, and abiotic causes

progression.description: Adults may move from weeds, alfalfa, quinoa, or other hosts into field hemp. Record first detection date, plant stage, field edge versus interior, alternate hosts, and sampling method instead of inferring damage from presence.
Repeated recovery of adults plus multiple nymph sizes on hemp supports residency or breeding. A single adult frame supports occurrence only, not causal injury or population severity.

Lygus lineolaris can occur from emergence onward and Lygus species can breed on vegetative hemp, yet the strongest early hemp synthesis documented no visible leaf injury. Foliar spotting, curling, or terminal distortion therefore remains contested and low confidence.

Some regions report higher counts after flowering. Capture flower or seed-head context and record whether seed hemp, fiber hemp, or unpollinated cannabinoid hemp is being observed because reproductive targets differ.

Seed shriveling, deformation, flower abortion, or bud drop may be compatible with heavy feeding, but hemp-specific economic significance and universal causal morphology are unestablished. Link the insect, active feeding site, and fresh injury across time before using a causal label.

lookAlikes: False chinch bug or another seed bug
Aphid nymph or cannabis aphid colony
Boron deficiency or another root-zone nutrient disorder
Herbicide, spray, heat, hail, wind, training, or mechanical injury
Pollination, flower pathogen, or normal seed-development variation
confirmation: Record a linked capture set: whole plant, upper/middle/lower canopy, terminal or flower/seed-head context, dorsal and lateral insect macro views, a size scale, and a short video showing movement and the exact plant part occupied.

Sample multiple symptomatic and asymptomatic plants across field edge and interior on at least two dates using the same sweep-net, beating-tray, vacuum, or timed-inspection method; retain counts by adult and nymph stage.

Identify a captured adult or diagnostic later instar with an entomologist or validated regional key. Keep triangular-mark-only, low-resolution, nymph-only, and genus-only observations out of the Lygus lineolaris confirmed class.

Link the identified organism to fresh injury on the same plant and tissue over time. A specimen from an unrelated weed, trap, plant, date, or field supports local occurrence but not Cannabis causation.

For reproductive injury, compare affected and unaffected flowers or seeds from the same cultivar and stage, document pollination and crop-use context, and exclude pathogens, caterpillars, stink bugs, nutrition, and abiotic injury.

For foliar or terminal symptoms, retain a source-conflict flag and cap image/video-only confidence at 0.30 because authoritative hemp sources disagree and two sources report no documented foliage symptoms.
Keep symptom-only, insect-only, detached-tissue-only, stock, vendor, generated, unverified, and rights-unclear captures out of automated training and confirmed ground truth.
immediateActions: Pause species-specific treatment decisions while collecting repeatable organism and injury evidence; isolate the label from other distorted-growth records.
Scout flowers, terminals, whole plants, nearby weeds, and field margins with a documented method, while preserving representative adults or nymphs for identification.
Record cultivar, crop use, plant sex, flowering or seed stage, location, date, weather, recent sprays, root-zone measurements, and other organisms before interpreting injury.
correctivePlan: Use an integrated pest-management response only after local identification, repeated population assessment, and plant-linked injury justify action; follow current hemp labels and local regulations.
Do not use an unvalidated numeric threshold or transfer seed-crop, regional, or non-Cannabis injury assumptions to cannabinoid, fiber, indoor, or other production systems.
prevention: Maintain a repeatable field-edge and interior scouting record from emergence through harvest, with added flower and seed-head sampling when those tissues develop.
Track nearby weeds, alfalfa, quinoa, and other possible source hosts without removing flowering vegetation impulsively; account for beneficial insects and local habitat-management guidance.
Retain paired healthy and affected captures so future review can distinguish occurrence, breeding, active feeding, and confirmed injury.
warnings: Lygus presence on hemp is documented, but presence alone does not prove that a visible Cannabis symptom was caused by tarnished plant bug.

Authoritative hemp sources conflict on foliar injury: Missouri Extension lists spotting, curling, stunting, and distortion, while the 2019 peer-reviewed synthesis and Utah Extension report no documented foliage symptoms.
A pale V-shaped or triangular scutellar mark is shared across Lygus species and cannot establish Lygus lineolaris without an adequate specimen and expert or key-based identification.
No validated hemp economic or treatment threshold is available, and reproductive injury significance varies with seed, fiber, and cannabinoid production context.
The public-domain USDA image is an organism-only laboratory nymph reference on a non-Cannabis plant; it is not Cannabis damage ground truth and is excluded from automated training.
No licensed, plant-linked Cannabis Lygus injury image or verified diagnostic video was located for this batch.

sources.title: Lygus Bug (Tarnished Plant Bug)
sources.organization: Utah State University Extension Integrated Pest Management
supportedClaims: Adult Lygus vary from brown with yellow, black, or red markings and a yellow or green triangle on the upper center of the back; nymphs are lighter, dark-spotted, wingless, and rounded.
The hemp guidance states that seed feeding can produce shriveling and heavy flower feeding may cause bud drop or flower abortion, while symptoms on foliage have not been documented.
Utah scouting guidance recommends visual or sweep-net sampling of hemp and nearby weeds plus repeated examination of flowers for adults and nymphs.

sources.publisher: Oregon State University, Washington State University, and University of Idaho Extension
supportedClaims: The regional hemp profile includes Lygus hesperus, Lygus elisus, and Lygus lineolaris and cautions that Lygus hesperus and Lygus elisus are the most common PNW species.
Adults are 4.4 to 6.3 mm long, range from light green to brown or black, and bear a V-shaped or triangular scutellar mark; nymphs are green or yellow-green with black dorsal spots.
In the Pacific Northwest, Lygus can occur throughout the hemp growing season and higher counts may occur from late July to mid-August near flowering; this timing is regional rather than universal.
Beating sheets or trays, vacuum sampling, and direct observation can recover mixed adult and nymph stages, while no hemp treatment threshold or established economic-damage relationship exists.
Alfalfa, quinoa, weeds, and other hosts may produce populations that later colonize hemp, so nearby-host context and field distribution should be recorded.

name: Thrips feeding injury
summary: Onion thrips and western flower thrips are documented on hemp; feeding can produce vein-associated white flecks or irregular silvery scars, dark fecal spots, and distortion of leaves damaged while expanding, but symptoms alone cannot identify the insect or its species.
indicators: Irregular white flecks or silvery scarred patches, often following or crossing veins
Small dark fecal spots occur within or beside fresh feeding scars
Minute elongated yellow, tan, or yellow-brown insects are recovered from symptomatic tissue
Wingless creamy-yellow larvae or slender adults with narrow fringed wings are visible under magnification
Leaves fed on while developing later expand with localized distortion or uneven scarred areas
Indoor or protected-crop injury increases over serial observations while matched uninfested plants remain unchanged
exclusions: No thrips, larvae, shed skins, or dark fecal spots are found after repeat inspection, foliage tapping, and sticky-card monitoring
Fine webbing, round eggs, and two-spotted mites are present
Microscopic cigar-shaped mites with two pairs of legs are present
Only residue is visible and it wipes or dissolves without damaged epidermal tissue beneath it
The pattern follows a nutrient-mobility gradient by leaf age rather than localized feeding scars
Circular or angular lesions enlarge independently and have halos, fungal growth, bacterial streaming, or pathogen-positive laboratory results
Distortion is restricted to the newest protected tissue and broad mites or dotted broad-mite eggs are confirmed
Abrasion aligns uniformly with a fan, rubbing surface, spray event, or physical contact and no organisms are recovered

progression.description: Small white flecks or short irregular silver scars appear, commonly along veins; a single image may omit the tiny insect and remains low confidence.
Fresh scars accumulate on multiple leaves with dark fecal spots, and larvae or adults can be recovered by direct inspection or tapping.
Tissue fed on while young expands unevenly, leaving localized distortion and larger scarred areas even if insect abundance later changes.

In one preliminary indoor Cannabis experiment, plants begun with five onion thrips produced less fresh yield than uninfested plants; this does not define a universal visual severity scale or action threshold.

confirmation: Inspect both leaf surfaces, veins, folds, growing tips, and flowers with at least a 10× hand lens; record whether scars, dark fecal spots, larvae, adults, and shed skins occur together.
Tap symptomatic foliage and flowers over white paper or a collection tray, then preserve representative insects for magnified examination.
Use blue or yellow sticky cards as population and movement monitors, not as proof that a particular damaged leaf was caused by thrips.

For species-level labels, submit intact adults to an entomology or plant diagnostic laboratory for morphological or validated molecular identification; color and a routine phone photograph are insufficient.
Capture serial whole-plant, leaf-surface macro, opposite-surface, vein-level, and organism-magnification views with scale and production context; compare with a matched healthy plant.
immediateActions: Separate or clearly mark suspect plants and inspect neighboring propagation material, young growth, flowers, weeds, and sticky cards before moving plants.
Preserve representative insects and pre-treatment images before intervention when species or causal confirmation is needed.
Avoid applying an unverified pesticide or coating simply because silver injury is present.
correctivePlan: Use only a control program legal for Cannabis or hemp, the jurisdiction, production system, and growth stage, following the current product label and worker-safety requirements.
Track fresh scars and organism counts at fixed sampling sites; old silver scars and distorted leaves will not heal and should not be used alone to judge control.
Address confirmed entry or reservoir points such as infested transplants, weeds, crop debris, flowers, or unscreened openings while conserving identified beneficial thrips and other natural enemies.
prevention: Quarantine and hand-lens inspect incoming clones and transplants.
Scout representative plants and canopy zones on a fixed schedule, including young leaves and flowers rather than relying only on sticky cards.
Maintain clean plant and weed-free buffer practices appropriate to the production system and record thrips detections by stage and location.
warnings: Silver flecks, black specks, or distorted leaves alone are not thrips ground truth; confirm the organism and feeding context.

A group-level thrips label does not establish onion thrips, western flower thrips, tobacco thrips, or another species; species identification requires suitable adult specimens and specialist examination.
The controlled yield study was preliminary and used defined indoor infestation treatments; it does not establish a universal economic threshold or symptom-to-yield conversion.
Predatory thrips can be beneficial, so the presence of a thrips-shaped insect is not sufficient to assign a damaging-pest label.
The two institutional Cannabis images below have no explicit reuse license; they are hidden metadata references, not copied assets or training samples.

sources.title: Onion thrips, Thrips tabaci (Thysanoptera: Thripidae), reduces yields in indoor-grown cannabis
supportedClaims: A controlled preliminary study identified onion thrips, Thrips tabaci, proliferating on indoor-grown Cannabis and compared plants initially receiving zero, one, or five thrips.

Plants initially receiving five thrips had lower fresh yield than plants receiving zero thrips; the result supports monitoring but does not establish an image-only diagnosis or a general action threshold.
The experiment was limited to defined indoor conditions and infestation treatments, so yield effects and severity must not be generalized across cultivars, production systems, or thrips species.

sources.title: Thrips
sources.organization: Utah State University Extension, Utah Plant Pest Diagnostic Laboratory
supportedClaims: Onion thrips and western flower thrips occur on field- and greenhouse-grown hemp; adults are minute, elongated, yellow to yellow-brown insects with fringed wings and larvae are creamy yellow and wingless.
Feeding on hemp produces white flecks or silvery scars with dark fecal spots, often along veins, and feeding on developing leaves can distort them.
Field injury is usually minor in Utah, economic damage is more likely indoors, and no industrial-hemp treatment threshold is established.
The two hemp symptom photographs on the page are credited collectively to the USU Extension IPM Program, while the page provides no explicit reuse license.

sources.title: Developing Insect Pest Management Systems for Hemp in the United States: A Work in Progress
sources.organization: Journal of Integrated Pest Management (Cranshaw et al.)
sources.publisher: Oxford University Press for the Entomological Society of America
supportedClaims: Onion thrips was the species commonly found on hemp foliage in eastern Colorado and could cause serious foliage damage during indoor production, while outdoor populations generally failed to reach damaging levels.
Western flower thrips was also identified on Colorado hemp but was associated mainly with flowers and pollen; tobacco thrips was reported on young plants in an earlier Mississippi survey.
Thrips on hemp remained incompletely characterized, so visual injury cannot safely assign species or predict economic impact without organism sampling and production context.

name: Broad mite
summary: A microscopic tarsonemid mite that hides in protected young tissue; feeding injury appears later as hardened, puckered, cupped, or strap-like new leaves, bronzing, short internodes, and deformed buds.
indicators: Warped, puckered, or hardened newest leaves
Cupped or strap-like new growth
Bronze, copper, or dark discoloration on young tissue
Short internodes and stunted growing tips
Deformed or aborted flower buds
Oval mites or dotted translucent eggs under magnification
exclusions: Cigar-shaped mites with only two pairs of legs are present instead
Fine webbing and round spider-mite eggs are present
Only older leaves follow a mobile-nutrient symptom pattern
Injury is uniform on the brightest upper canopy and measured leaf temperature or light is excessive
No mites or dotted eggs are found after repeat sampling of adjacent fresh growth and protected sites

progression.description: Tiny mites and eggs occupy leaf undersides, axils, buds, and other protected young tissue; visible injury may be absent or lag behind feeding.
Expanding leaves become puckered, cupped, hardened, strap-like, or bronze while internodes shorten and growing tips slow.
New growth is markedly stunted, buds deform or abort, and damaged tissue can remain symptomatic after mites move to fresher growth.

confirmation: Inspect fresh expanding tissue adjacent to the worst damage, including undersides, axils, growing tips, and buds, at about 20× or with a dissecting microscope.
Confirm translucent oval adults and clear oval eggs bearing raised pale dots; adult females may show a pale dorsal stripe.
Separate broad mite from cigar-shaped, two-pair-legged russet mites and from cyclamen mites, whose eggs lack the characteristic dotted surface.
Treat a negative sample cautiously because injury can persist after mites leave badly damaged tissue; repeat sampling across plants and time when suspicion remains.
immediateActions: Quarantine suspect plants and stop moving cuttings or shared tools into clean areas.
Microscope-screen neighboring plants before choosing any control.
correctivePlan: Use only controls legal for the crop, jurisdiction, and growth stage, following the current label.
Track mites or eggs on fixed fresh-growth sampling sites; do not judge response from old distorted leaves.
Remove severely infested material without spreading mites and sanitize shared tools between plants.
prevention: Start with inspected propagation material.
Quarantine and magnification-screen incoming clones.
Include protected new-growth sites in routine scouting rather than inspecting only mature fan leaves.
warnings: Leaf distortion, bronzing, or short internodes alone are not diagnostic.
The two media assets below show the organism without a host and are morphology references, not cannabis symptom ground truth.
Although their licenses permit reuse, both remain reference-only and excluded from automated training pending a separate training and dataset-split review.

sources.title: Broad Mite
sources.organization: Utah State University Extension, Utah Plant Pest Diagnostic Laboratory
supportedClaims: Broad mite (Polyphagotarsonemus latus) is documented on hemp and occupies shaded, protected leaf surfaces and crevices.
Adults are extremely small, oval to round, and light yellow to green; eggs are laid on leaf undersides.
Feeding can produce malformed, warped, or hardened young leaves and flower buds, bronzing, stunting, and aborted growth.

sources.title: Assessing the impact of piercing-sucking pests on greenhouse-grown industrial hemp (Cannabis sativa L.)
sources.publisher: Oxford University Press for the Entomological Society of America
supportedClaims: Broad mites are recognized among the most significant piercing-sucking pests of greenhouse-grown hemp.

Piercing-sucking pest injury in hemp can overlap visually with cupping, yellowing, leaf loss, and reduced reproductive performance, so pest presence must be confirmed rather than inferred from canopy symptoms.

sources.title: Broad Mite
supportedClaims: Broad mites prefer young, protected tissue and may no longer be present on the most damaged tissue because visible injury can persist after feeding.
Clear oval broad-mite eggs have raised pale dots, while cyclamen-mite eggs are smooth and russet mites have a narrow, conical body form.
Broad-mite injury can resemble plant-growth-regulator herbicide injury, nutrient problems, and other abiotic disorders; inspection at about 20× or by microscope is recommended.

name: Hemp russet mite
summary: A microscopic eriophyid mite whose feeding can cause localized bronzing, brittle or reduced leaves, distorted edges, stunting, and suppressed floral growth without the webbing typical of spider mites.
indicators: Dull gray or bronzed foliage
Brittle or reduced leaf size
Leaf edges curl upward or downward
Stem or petiole bronzing
Stunted growing tips
No webbing despite mite-like damage
exclusions: Fine webbing and round spider-mite eggs are present
Only interveinal chlorosis follows an older-leaf nutrient pattern
Damage is restricted to the hottest or brightest canopy surface
No cigar-shaped mites are found after adequate microscope sampling

progression.description: Visible injury may be absent; mites occupy protected sites around veins, trichomes, petioles, and leaf undersides.
Fine spotting, dull gray-green tissue, bronzing, edge curl, and reduced or brittle leaves become apparent on affected shoots.
Stunting, stem bronzing, deformed growing tips, and reduced or dwarfed flower buds can develop; dense mites or cast skins may resemble tan powder.

confirmation: Sample both symptomatic and adjacent apparently healthy leaves; inspect undersides, midribs, petioles, and protected trichome zones with a dissecting or digital microscope.
Confirm pale, cigar-shaped eriophyid mites with only two pairs of legs; ordinary phone or whole-plant images are not sufficient.
For repeatable image counts, photograph multiple leaflet sections under microscope magnification rather than relying on a single field of view.
immediateActions: Quarantine suspect plants and stop moving cuttings, tools, clothing, or plant debris into clean areas.
Inspect nearby plants under adequate magnification before choosing a treatment.
correctivePlan: Use only controls legal for the crop, jurisdiction, and growth stage, following the current product label.
Track mite counts on fixed leaf positions after intervention; visible injury can lag behind population change.
Remove severely infested material without spreading mites and clean shared tools between plants.
prevention: Start with inspected, mite-free propagation material.
Quarantine and microscope-screen incoming clones.
Maintain routine microscope scouting because low populations can be visually silent.
warnings: Leaf curl or bronzing alone is not diagnostic.
Do not confuse tan cast-skin accumulations with fungal powder.
CC BY 4.0 permits reuse with attribution, but these hashed reference images remain excluded from model training until a separate training and dataset-split review is completed.

sources.title: Hemp Russet Mite
sources.organization: Utah State University Extension, Utah Plant Pest Diagnostic Laboratory
supportedClaims: Hemp russet mites are microscopic, cigar-shaped eriophyid mites usually found on leaf undersides and best identified with high magnification.
High populations can cause fine spotting, bronzing, reduced leaf size, brittle foliage, upward edge curl, and stem bronzing.
Spider mites, thrips, and physiological leaf curl or yellowing are documented look-alikes.

sources.title: Hemp Russet Mite in Industrial Hemp
supportedClaims: The absence of webbing helps distinguish hemp russet mite from spider mites, but microscopy is necessary because injury resembles disease and abiotic stress.
Stem, petiole, and leaf feeding can cause stunting, smaller leaves, dull gray or bronzed tissue, and suppressed or dwarfed buds.
The two referenced photographs are credited to Whitney Cranshaw, Colorado State University, Bugwood.org, under CC BY 4.0.

sources.title: Novel Approach to Tally Aculops cannabicola (Acari: Eriophyidae) Using Photographs of Hemp Leaves
sources.organization: Journal of Economic Entomology (Falcon-Brindis et al.)
sources.publisher: Oxford University Press for the Entomological Society of America
supportedClaims: Hemp russet mites are approximately 160–210 micrometres long and are easily missed with standard low-power hand lenses.
Image-based counts require microscope photographs of multiple leaflet sections; ordinary whole-plant photographs cannot confirm the pest.
Feeding is associated with chlorosis, stunting, brittle leaf breakage, and reduced flower-bud size or resin production at high populations.

name: Two-spotted spider mites
summary: Twospotted spider mites feed mainly from leaf undersides, producing upper-surface stippling that can progress to chlorosis, necrosis, leaf loss, and silk webbing. Injury alone is nonspecific and can persist after mites leave, so an active label requires direct organism evidence.
indicators: Paired-leaf view: fine pale stippling or speckling on the upper surface corresponds to a colony, eggs, cast skins, or debris on the lower surface.
Adults are tiny, oval, pale yellowish to greenish mites whose two dark body spots may be visible in a sharp macro view; round translucent eggs occur near veins and webbing below the leaf.
Damage can expand from localized stippled leaves to bronze or yellow tissue, dry brown margins or whole leaves, premature leaf drop, and reduced vigor or flower growth.
Fine silk first appears in protected leaf regions and can bridge leaves, stems, or flowers when populations are high; visible webbing generally indicates an established infestation.
Hot, dry, dusty, or water-stressed zones can develop faster or denser hotspots, including field edges near dusty paths, but this spatial association is contextual evidence only.
exclusions: Silvery scraped streaks with black fecal specks and slender insects support thrips rather than spider mites.
Distorted newest growth with no webbing and mites too small for a hand lens supports hemp russet or broad-mite triage, not a two-spotted spider-mite label.
Fast-moving, long-legged, pear-shaped mites may be beneficial predators; do not label every visible mite as Tetranychus urticae.
Spray or mineral residue may wipe away and lacks eggs, moving life stages, cast skins, and silk anchored to the leaf.
Nutrient, root-zone, or water stress can produce chlorosis or necrosis but should not produce a matched underside colony or mite webbing.
Leafhopper injury can cause pale stippling without an underside mite colony; inspect for hoppers and the distribution of feeding marks.

progression.description: In the two-cultivar flowering-hemp study scale, no visible stippling, chlorosis, or webbing was present.
Slight stippling on a few leaves increased to moderate stippling across multiple leaves.
Heavy stippling was accompanied by early chlorosis.
Extensive chlorosis developed with patchy webbing.
Severe chlorosis and necrosis occurred with dense silk webbing.

confirmation: Do not confirm an active infestation or species from stippling, chlorosis, or webbing in an image or video alone; capture the whole-canopy distribution plus paired upper- and lower-leaf views.

Inspect several symptomatic and adjacent apparently healthy leaf undersides with at least 10x magnification; record eggs, larvae or nymphs, adults, cast skins, fecal debris, and silk with a scale reference.
Tap suspect leaves or stems over clean white paper and record close video of moving organisms; distinguish slow plant-feeding mites from faster, longer-legged predatory mites.
For species-level ground truth, retain a specimen and obtain qualified entomologist or diagnostic-laboratory identification when morphology is not resolved by the capture.
Record cultivar, growth stage, canopy position, site or room, first-observed date, repeat counts from fixed leaves, temperature, humidity, dust, and water-stress context.
immediateActions: Separate or clearly flag affected plants and inspect neighboring plants before moving people, tools, or plant material through the area.
Preserve representative leaves or specimens for confirmation and record the pre-intervention organism count and visual distribution.
correctivePlan: Use a legal, crop- and stage-appropriate integrated pest-management plan selected for the production system; protect beneficial predators and follow all label restrictions.
Reinspect the same marked leaves and nearby plants at fixed intervals; use live-organism counts rather than persistent old stippling to judge whether the active population changed.
Reduce avoidable dust and water stress and examine weeds or adjacent host plants where relevant, while treating these as risk factors rather than diagnostic proof.
prevention: Quarantine and inspect incoming plants, especially leaf undersides, before they enter production.
Scout fixed leaves across canopy zones and field edges consistently, documenting both direct organisms and injury over time.
warnings: The published 0-to-5 visual scale came from one evaluator, two hemp cultivars, naturally occurring background mite populations, and flowering plants; it is an observational study reference, not a universal severity or treatment threshold.
No research-based action threshold has been established for North Carolina hemp across fiber, seed, and cannabinoid markets.
Injury-only imagery is not species-level ground truth: stippling is nonspecific, webbing is usually a later sign, and old injury can remain after mites have left.
Cultivar, canopy, environment, and production system can alter visible severity, and predatory mites or other pest mites can be confused with Tetranychus urticae in low-resolution media.
The linked CC BY 4.0 damage-scale figure is a mixed-grade composite; it remains training-ineligible and its panels are not independent samples without crop geometry, source-group, and label review.
Avoid applying any product unless it is legal for the crop, site, growth stage, and jurisdiction, especially on flowers.

sources.title: Cultivar Identity and Spider Mite Herbivory Shape Rhizosphere Bacteria in Hemp (Cannabis sativa L.)
supportedClaims: A trained evaluator scored naturally occurring Tetranychus urticae injury on flowering BaOx and Cherry Citrus hemp under the same greenhouse conditions with a standardized 0-to-5 scale: 0, no visible stippling, chlorosis, or webbing; 1, slight stippling on a few leaves; 2, moderate stippling across multiple leaves; 3, heavy stippling with early chlorosis; 4, extensive chlorosis with patchy webbing; and 5, severe chlorosis and necrosis with dense silk webbing.

Cherry Citrus had significantly less visual damage than BaOx despite similar measured growth traits, showing that cultivar identity can alter symptom severity and limiting generalization of a single image progression.

The study used background mite populations rather than experimentally manipulating herbivore pressure and reported associations rather than proof of causality; its two-cultivar flowering-stage score is a study-specific reference, not a universal diagnostic or intervention threshold.

Figure 1 is a CC BY 4.0 composite reference for the 0-to-5 visual damage scale and should not be split into independent training examples without panel-level cropping, source grouping, and label review.

sources.title: Twospotted Spider Mite in Industrial Hemp
supportedClaims: Twospotted spider mites occur on greenhouse and field hemp; at least 10x magnification is recommended because mites and eggs occur mainly on leaf undersides while feeding injury appears as pale speckling on the upper surface.

High infestations can produce yellow, dry leaves, premature leaf drop, reduced flower growth, and webbing that can cover much of a plant; hot, low-humidity conditions can shorten a generation to roughly one to two weeks.
Water-stressed or dusty plants and field edges near dusty paths can have greater risk, but exposure context is not proof of the causal organism.

No research-based action threshold was established for North Carolina hemp across fiber, seed, and cannabinoid production, so visible damage grades or mite counts must not be presented as universal treatment thresholds.

sources.title: Spider Mites
sources.organization: University of California Statewide IPM Program
sources.publisher: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources
supportedClaims: Spider-mite feeding can cause stippling, bronzing or yellowing, leaf drop, and fine silk webbing; damage can remain visible after mites have left, so injury alone does not establish an active infestation.

Diagnosis should include leaf-underside inspection with a hand lens and tapping suspect foliage over white paper to look for moving mites; eggs, mites, and webbing provide stronger evidence than leaf color alone.
Predatory mites are typically more active and have longer legs than plant-feeding spider mites, so visible mite-like organisms are not automatically pests.

Do not treat the six severity panels as independent training examples until panel-level crop, source-group, and label review are complete.

The publisher has served visually identical PNG encodings with different cryptographic hashes; dHash remained stable. Treat SHA-256 as the observed source-byte hash, not a permanent publisher identifier.

name: Root-knot nematodes
summary: A Cannabis root-parasitic nematode complex in which small, firm, whitish root galls are the strongest visible cue. Gall morphology can support a root-knot differential, but species, race, burden, and causality require plant-linked root/soil nematode evidence because canopy effects and cultivar responses are nonspecific.
indicators: Small, firm, whitish localized galls are integrated into Cannabis root tissue; M. hapla, M. incognita, and M. javanica galls are often no more than about 4 mm
An intact washed root system shows the distribution and burden of true galls rather than an isolated swelling
Adult females within roots, associated egg masses, extracted juveniles, or quantified eggs accompany compatible galling
Root systems may show reduced development, lateral-root growth, or root weight as burden increases
Above-ground growth may become stunted or chlorotic, but no consistent leaf-age or canopy-position pattern is established
Morphology plus validated species-specific PCR or sequence evidence identifies Meloidogyne when a species-level label is required
exclusions: Root swellings are normal lateral-root branch points or other root anatomy rather than firm integrated galls
Circling, matted roots and container-wall geometry support root binding without plant-linked nematode recovery
Soft, water-soaked or sloughed roots plus oomycete evidence support Pythium or another water mold
Necrotic root or crown lesions plus fungal isolation or molecular evidence support Rhizoctonia, Fusarium, or another root pathogen
No galls or nematodes are found and measured drought, hypoxia, salinity, pH, or nutrient conditions explain the canopy response
Only canopy stunting, yellowing, wilt, or low vigor is visible without an intact root-system inspection
A detached or cropped gall close-up cannot be linked to the sampled Cannabis plant and surrounding soil
Root-knot species or race is inferred from gall size, color, cultivar response, or geography without organism-level testing

progression.description: Root-knot juveniles establish feeding sites; early infection may have little or no discriminating canopy signal.
Small, firm, whitish galls become visible on fine and lateral roots; record their distribution across the intact washed root system.
Females, egg masses, eggs, or juveniles can accompany galling and provide stronger organism-linked evidence than root shape alone.
Root development, lateral roots, or root weight may decline, with magnitude varying by species, isolate, cultivar, inoculum, and time.
Stunting, chlorosis, poor growth, or wilt may appear across the plant, but these responses are not leaf-age-specific and remain nonspecific.

lookAlikes: Normal lateral-root branch points or root primordia
Pythium or other oomycete root rot
confirmation: Capture the same plant at whole-canopy scale, then recover and gently wash the complete root system; photograph the intact root architecture and gall distribution with a scale before making close-ups or sections.
Collect representative galled roots and surrounding soil under the same plant identifier; keep canopy, root, soil, date, cultivar, substrate, and treatment metadata linked.
Extract and quantify juveniles or eggs from a defined soil volume and females or egg masses per defined root mass; absence from one cropped close-up does not establish absence from the root system.

Use adult-female and juvenile morphology together with a validated species-specific PCR or sequence assay when assigning a Meloidogyne species; gall appearance alone supports at most a root-knot complex label.

For high-confidence causal ground truth, require a plant-linked diagnostic result and compatible root signs; controlled pathogenicity or a documented reproduction factor is stronger than field association alone.
Record cultivar, nematode species or isolate, inoculum or starting population where known, sampling interval, and root-washing method because all can change visible burden and reproduction.
Keep canopy-only, symptom-only, detached-root-only, unlinked soil/root assay, species-from-gall, low-resolution, stock, forum, vendor, or generated captures out of the confirmed root-knot class.
immediateActions: Quarantine the sampled root-zone material and prevent movement of potentially infested soil, roots, runoff, tools, or containers into clean production areas.
Preserve representative galled roots and paired surrounding soil for nematode analysis before destructive treatment or disposal.
Measure root-zone moisture, pH, and EC and inspect for root binding and rot concurrently so a coincident abiotic or pathogen problem is not missed.
correctivePlan: Base any intervention on confirmed nematode identity, burden, crop stage, production system, and locally legal options; this record does not convert laboratory hemp-seed-extract assays into field treatment guidance.
Track response with repeated plant-linked canopy, root, and nematode-count observations rather than assuming visual recovery proves eradication.
prevention: Use clean planting material and media and avoid moving infested soil or root debris on tools, footwear, containers, or equipment.
When unexplained patches of poor growth occur, compare complete root systems and paired soil samples from affected and nearby apparently healthy plants.
Retain cultivar and source-lot metadata because susceptibility and reproduction vary materially among hemp cultivars and Meloidogyne species or isolates.
warnings: Above-ground chlorosis, wilt, and stunting are nonspecific and should receive very low diagnostic weight without linked root and organism evidence.
Small white hard galls support a root-knot differential but do not identify species or race; M. enterolobii can also produce larger galls.
Cultivar, Meloidogyne species or isolate, inoculum, pot size, and observation interval can alter gall burden, reproduction, and growth effects, so one image cannot define universal severity.
The Alabama field evidence was region-, cultivar-, and race-specific; do not generalize M. incognita Race 3 to every Cannabis root-knot case.
The 2025 article figures plot seed-extract bioassays rather than infected-root symptoms and are not diagnostic image ground truth.
Cannabis yield-loss thresholds and clean, cultivar-diverse, laboratory-linked image or video sequences remain incomplete.

sources.title: Surveying for Potential Diseases and Abiotic Disorders of Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa) Production
supportedClaims: A North Carolina 2017–2018 hemp diagnostic survey identified 16 diseases caused by fungi, bacteria, oomycetes, and nematodes; the study used clinic diagnostics, morphology, sequence data for representative organisms, and pathogenicity testing for its confirmed disease set.

Fusarium foliar and flower blight was common in submitted samples and involved F. equiseti and F. graminearum; flowers developed surface hyphae and light-brown necrotic tips while leaves developed circular light-brown lesions about 1 cm wide with dark margins and gray-brown aging centers.
Exserohilum rostratum leaf spot occurred on leaves and stems as round brown-to-black lesions with darkened margins and abundant conidia, with ITS1/RPB2 evidence supporting the identification.

Rhizoctonia solani was found on roots and crowns with plant wilting and necrotic lesions just above the soil line; pigmented septate hyphae showed characteristic right-angle branching and sequence evidence supported R. solani.

Southern blight caused whole-plant wilt in reproductive hemp during hot midseason conditions, with abundant hyphae and russet-brown sclerotia on roots/lower stems and sequence/phylogenetic evidence supporting Athelia rolfsii/Sclerotium rolfsii.
Meloidogyne incognita was identified from galled hemp roots with females and egg masses; affected plants had some associated stunting.

The survey documented Serratia-associated, vein-limited angular hemp lesions and red bacterial ooze emerging from punctured lesions, while emphasizing that hemp leaf diseases overlap visually and require diagnostic separation.

sources.title: Root-Knot Nematodes
supportedClaims: Infection of hemp by root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne spp.) is established, although the extent of Cannabis yield loss is not well quantified.
Organism confirmation and root signs are required; above-ground stunting or chlorosis alone is nonspecific.

sources.title: Review of Nematode Interactions with Hemp (Cannabis sativa)
supportedClaims: The review found that Meloidogyne is the most frequently reported plant-parasitic nematode genus on hemp, while stressing that only a small primary literature supports hemp-specific host and damage conclusions.

Galls induced on hemp by M. hapla, M. incognita, and M. javanica are described as small, whitish, and hard, generally not exceeding about 4 mm in diameter; M. enterolobii can form both small and large galls.
Its Figure 2 shows a controlled M. incognita inoculation on Cannabis sativa cultivar Cherry as an entire root system and close-up of small white galls with a 5 mm scale.

Hemp susceptibility and nematode reproduction vary substantially with cultivar, Meloidogyne species or isolate, inoculum, pot size, and evaluation time, so gall burden or canopy severity must not be generalized across cultivars or studies.

sources.title: First Report of Meloidogyne incognita Infecting Cannabis sativa in Alabama
supportedClaims: Field-grown Alabama hemp in symptomatic areas showed stunted growth, poor root development, and numerous root galls, with Meloidogyne recovered from associated soil.
The nematode was identified as M. incognita using morphology and species-specific PCR; a greenhouse host-differential assay supported Race 3.
A modified Koch-postulates test reproduced galling and nematode reproduction on hemp, providing plant-linked pathogenicity evidence rather than a symptom-only association.

sources.title: Virulence of Five Root-Knot Nematodes (Meloidogyne spp.) on Nine Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa L.) Varieties and Nematicidal Potential of Hemp Seed Extracts Against Meloidogyne javanica
supportedClaims: A controlled greenhouse experiment found M. javanica, M. incognita, M. arenaria, M. hapla, and M. luci pathogenic across nine tested industrial-hemp varieties, with all inoculated treatments showing reduced shoot weight relative to controls.

M. incognita produced the lowest mean root weight among the tested species, while M. javanica and M. luci produced the lowest mean shoot weights, demonstrating that root and canopy effects differ by species.

Females per gram of root, egg masses per gram of root, and fecundity differed by both hemp variety and Meloidogyne species; Futura 75 carried the lowest overall nematode numbers, whereas USO 31, Fedora 17, Ferimon 12, and Zenit were among the more susceptible varieties in this experiment.
The article figures concern laboratory seed-extract effects on juvenile mobility and egg hatch rather than visual diagnosis of infected Cannabis roots, so those graphs are not symptom ground truth.

media.alt: Two-panel controlled reference showing an entire Cannabis sativa Cherry root system and a close-up of small white Meloidogyne incognita galls with a 5 mm scale.
media.caption: Figure 2 from Bernard, Chaffin, and Gwinn: controlled M. incognita galling on Cannabis sativa cultivar Cherry after an initial inoculum of 10,000 eggs. Panel A shows the full root system; panel B shows small white galls.
media.creator: Angel G. Chaffin, University of Tennessee (image credit); Ernest C. Bernard and Kimberly D. Gwinn (figure coauthors)
media.requiredAttribution: Bernard, Ernest C.; Chaffin, Angel G.; Gwinn, Kimberly D. (2021), Figure 2 in Review of nematode interactions with hemp (Cannabis sativa), Zenodo, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.11644653. Licensed under CC BY 4.0.
media.diagnosticLabel: root-knot-nematodes — controlled M. incognita galling on Cannabis sativa Cherry, whole-root and close-up composite
useLimitations: Two-panel composite from one cultivar and a controlled initial inoculum of 10,000 eggs; it is not a panel-level training sample or a universal severity reference.
The image supports small white Cannabis root-gall morphology but does not establish species from appearance alone; retain the article-linked M. incognita inoculation context.
Do not crop away the scale, panel relationship, cultivar, inoculum, or source metadata; expert panel separation and label review are required before any automated training use.

name: Late-cycle leaf aging / senescence context
summary: Cannabis and hemp leaves can lose chlorophyll and photosynthetic capacity as foliage ages and flowering advances, with stronger age and canopy-position effects in older or lower leaves; visible yellowing is neither required nor sufficient to classify the change as normal senescence.
affectedParts: whole canopy only as a mapped age gradient
inflorescences and sugar leaves as exclusion-check tissue
stages: flowering time series; strongest Cannabis evidence compares weeks 1, 5, and 9 after transition to a 12-hour photoperiod
indicators: Change is gradual across serial observations rather than abrupt between captures
Older or lower-position fan leaves change before recently expanded upper-canopy leaves
Chlorophyll index or photosynthetic capacity declines with documented leaf age even when a leaf remains visibly green
The same cultivar and production cohort shows a repeatable late-cycle age and canopy-position gradient
Inflorescences, recently expanded leaves, stems, and roots lack independent evidence of a spreading disorder
Color assessment is made under calibrated or repeatable lighting with healthy same-cultivar references
exclusions: Visible yellowing alone is used as proof of senescence or harvest readiness
Recently expanded or upper-canopy leaves decline first or as strongly as older lower leaves without an established age gradient
Chlorosis begins early, progresses rapidly, reduces whole-plant vigor, or spreads independently of leaf age
Interveinal chlorosis, marginal scorch, discrete lesions, rings, mosaic, distortion, brittle growth, webbing, feeding scars, frass, or visible organisms are present
Root-zone pH, EC, water content, oxygenation, root appearance, or irrigation history is abnormal
Feed composition, tissue or solution analysis, or response to correction supports nitrogen or another nutrient disorder
Inflorescence mold, necrosis, odor, collapse, or laboratory evidence supports a pathogen
A lamp, spray, heat, cold, drought, salinity, or other exposure gradient explains the distribution better

progression.description: At flowering transition, map leaf node, canopy position, cultivar, photoperiod, PPFD, root-zone measurements, color reference, and a matched healthy plant.

Leaf chlorophyll index and photosynthetic capacity may decline with physiological age. In one Stillwater trial, upper- and lower-canopy chlorophyll indices were lower at weeks 5 and 9 than week 1, while a separate hemp study found declining photosynthetic capacity over 42 days even though leaves stayed green.

Document whether pale green, yellow, anthocyanin-associated red or purple, necrosis, or abscission develops and whether it follows leaf age and canopy position. Published Cannabis evidence does not establish a mandatory color or timing sequence.
Rapid spread, new-growth involvement, lesions, distortion, root abnormalities, pest signs, or inflorescence decline moves the sample out of the normal-development reference class pending diagnosis.

lookAlikes: Nitrogen deficiency or under-supply during flowering
Magnesium, potassium, phosphorus, sulfur, or micronutrient disorder
Water shortage or excessive vapor demand
Pythium, Phytophthora, Fusarium, or other root disease
Beet curly top virus or unresolved systemic mosaic syndrome
Powdery mildew, Botrytis, or leaf-spot disease
Hemp russet mite, broad mite, spider mite, or thrips injury
High-light, heat, cold, spray, or plant-growth-regulator injury
Cultivar pigmentation or camera color artifact
confirmation: Do not label “normal fade,” senescence, ripeness, harvest readiness, nutrient depletion, or plant health from color in one photograph or video.
Record leaf node, leaf age, upper versus lower canopy, cultivar, flowering day, photoperiod, PPFD, temperature, humidity or vapor-pressure deficit, irrigation, and serial rate of change.
Capture whole-plant, canopy, branch, upper-leaf-surface, lower-leaf-surface, root-zone, and inflorescence views under repeatable lighting with a color reference and scale.

Measure root-zone pH, EC, water content or container weight, and inspect roots; review feed composition and, when consequential, use calibrated solution or tissue analysis rather than assuming remobilization.
Inspect both leaf surfaces and protected growth with magnification for mites, thrips, webbing, eggs, cast skins, frass, and feeding scars.
Use a plant diagnostic laboratory when lesions, systemic distortion, vascular or root decline, inflorescence disease, or virus/viroid signs remain plausible.
Compare several healthy same-cultivar plants from the same propagation cohort; an age-position gradient that repeats across serial observations is contextual support, not causal proof.
immediateActions: Keep the sample labeled “late-cycle leaf aging—cause unresolved” until exclusion checks are complete.
Preserve serial images and measured root-zone, environment, and nutrition records before changing the program.
Isolate or pause propagation from plants with systemic, pest, pathogen, or viroid warning signs.
correctivePlan: Correct only measured nutrient, pH, EC, irrigation, environment, pest, or pathogen problems; do not force yellowing or apply nitrogen solely from camera color.
Reassess recently expanded leaves, roots, and inflorescences after any evidence-based correction while recognizing that old yellow or necrotic tissue will not become a clean health indicator.
Retain the normal-development label only when progression remains slow, age-positioned, cultivar-consistent, and unsupported by competing diagnoses.
prevention: Maintain same-cultivar flowering timelines with leaf-node and canopy-position annotations.
Keep calibrated pH and EC records, irrigation history, environmental logs, pest scouting, and laboratory results linked to image and video samples.
Create healthy reference captures under fixed lighting and camera settings rather than relying on internet photographs or a universal week-of-flower chart.
warnings: A hemp leaf-aging study found photosynthetic capacity could decline while leaves remained green, so visible yellowing is not required for senescence.

The Stillwater flowering study found temporal and canopy-position changes but did not resolve how much was caused by leaf age versus whole-plant ontogeny and did not validate a universal visible fade.
Flowering Cannabis still responds materially to nitrogen and phosphorus supply; withholding nutrients to manufacture a fade is not evidence of normal development.
Color is not a validated harvest-maturity marker and this record does not recommend harvest timing, flushing, or a universal feeding concentration.
The source experiments used limited cultivars and defined production systems; their weeks and nutrient concentrations must not be generalized as thresholds.

No authoritative Cannabis photograph or video with adequate longitudinal measurements and causal exclusion was admitted; media remain empty rather than treating vendor, forum, anecdotal, or generated imagery as ground truth.
All symptom-only samples remain low confidence and require human review.

sources.title: Cannabis Yield, Potency, and Leaf Photosynthesis Respond Differently to Increasing Light Levels in an Indoor Environment
sources.organization: Frontiers in Plant Science (Rodriguez-Morrison et al.)
supportedClaims: Indoor-grown Cannabis sativa Stillwater was exposed during flowering to average canopy PPFDs from 120 to 1,800 micromoles per square metre per second.
Dry inflorescence yield increased linearly through the highest tested PPFD even though leaf-level photosynthesis saturated below 1,800 micromoles per square metre per second.

The high-light experiment did not establish a universal PPFD injury threshold or validate cupping, bleaching, or edge necrosis as light-specific visual symptoms; light exposure must be interpreted with cultivar, acclimation, canopy position, temperature, carbon dioxide, and water status.

In Stillwater during the 12-hour flowering phase, chlorophyll-content index was higher in week 1 than weeks 5 and 9 and was consistently higher in upper- than lower-canopy fan leaves; the authors described evidence of early senescence but stated that the contributions of leaf age and plant ontogeny to diminished week-9 photosynthesis were unresolved.
The study measured chlorophyll index and physiology rather than validating a yellow-leaf appearance, harvest date, or universal late-flower-fade sequence.

sources.title: Leaf Age and Position Effects on Quantum Yield and Photosynthetic Capacity in Hemp Crowns
supportedClaims: Hemp leaves at three crown positions were followed from full expansion for 42 days; photosynthetic capacity declined with leaf age regardless of crown position, light intensity, or photoperiod.
The measured leaves remained green while photosynthetic capacity declined, demonstrating that physiological aging is not equivalent to visible yellowing.

The experiment evaluated aging leaves before abscission in hemp crowns and did not establish a drug-type Cannabis harvest cue, a cultivar-independent color sequence, or proof that visible chlorosis is normal.

sources.title: Optimisation of Nitrogen, Phosphorus, and Potassium for Soilless Production of Cannabis sativa in the Flowering Stage Using Response Surface Analysis
sources.organization: Frontiers in Plant Science (Bevan et al.)
supportedClaims: A high-THC Cannabis cultivar grown in deep-water culture during flowering showed quadratic inflorescence-yield responses to nitrogen and phosphorus, with predicted optima near 194 mg per litre nitrogen and 59 mg per litre phosphorus under the tested conditions.

Inflorescence yield decreased markedly outside approximately 160–230 mg per litre nitrogen and 40–80 mg per litre phosphorus, demonstrating that flowering plants still respond materially to nutrient supply.
Those solution concentrations are experiment- and cultivar-specific and must not be converted into universal feed targets, tissue sufficiency ranges, or visual thresholds.

name: Cannabis reproductive sex expression
summary: An organ-level developmental classification, not a whole-plant silhouette diagnosis: pistillate expression requires visible stigma-bearing flowers, staminate expression requires anther-bearing flowers, and co-sexual expression requires both organ types linked to the same plant. Seedling morphology, plant habit, a single negative view, or a sex-linked marker alone cannot establish the expressed phenotype across the plant or over time.
affectedParts: several upper and lower leaf axils and nodes
whole plant only for spatial mapping, not organ classification
stages: pistillate maturation and possible seed development
indicators: Seedling height, leaf size, vigor, branching, and internode length provide no reliable cross-cultivar image-only sex distinction
The first visible reproductive expression can be a solitary flower at a leaf axil rather than a dense terminal inflorescence
Pistillate flowers show bifurcate protruding white to yellowish-white stigmas with the attached flower, carpel, and bract context visible
Staminate flowers occur in short-stalked or pedicillate clusters and open to expose five stamens or anthers
Co-sexual expression is established only when anthers or staminate flowers and pistillate structures are linked to the same plant
In predominantly pistillate tissue, co-sexual expression can appear as a few bright-yellow 2–3 mm anthers embedded in bract tissue among stigmas
Staminate expression may be spatially sparse or concealed within dense pistillate inflorescences, so several organs and repeated dates are needed to map distribution
During pistillate maturation, stigmas may curl and brown or redden while carpels and surrounding bracts swell; this is maturity context, not evidence of staminate expression
Video evidence is most useful when an uninterrupted sequence links the plant identifier to node or branch position and then to a focused macro view of organ attachment
exclusions: A seedling or vegetative plant is labeled male, female, or co-sexual from overall habit, height, leaf morphology, vigor, branching, or internode length alone
Only stipules, reduced leaves, new axillary shoots, subtending bracts, or undifferentiated primordia are visible
Apical solitary stigmas are counted as a developed terminal inflorescence without showing the surrounding branching and flower distribution
An unopened or swollen pistillate bract is labeled as a staminate pollen sac without a visible pedicel, tepals, stamens, or anthers
Senescent stigmas, necrotic floral tissue, pollen, trichomes, yellow plant debris, or an organism are called anthers from color alone
A single node, one inflorescence surface, one date, or a whole-canopy view is used to exclude sparse or concealed co-sexual expression
Anther-like material is blurred, compressed, scale-free, detached, or not visibly attached to the photographed plant
A Y-linked marker result is used to claim that female versus monoecious expression has been distinguished or that future expression is guaranteed
Cultivar-specific days after a photoperiod change, plant height, or inflorescence architecture are treated as universal sex or maturity thresholds

progression.description: Male, female, and co-sexual outcomes cannot be separated consistently by gross morphology across cultivars. Keep image and video labels indeterminate until reproductive organs are in focus.

The first visual indication can be one or two solitary flowers and bracts at a leaf axil, including under long photoperiod. Show the full node because stigmas near an apex can be mistaken for a developed terminal inflorescence.

Pedicillate staminate clusters open to expose anthers, while short-photoperiod pistillate inflorescences condense branching, reduced leaves, bracts, flowers, and axillary shoots. Classify visible organs rather than overall cluster shape.

A few 2–3 mm bright-yellow anthers may emerge within bract tissue among stigmas, or anther clusters may replace part of a pistillate inflorescence. Sparse concealed organs may become visible only on later, multi-surface inspection.

Pistillate stigmas can curl and shift toward brown or red as carpels and bracts swell; staminate flowers can release pollen. Update the label only for mapped organs and dates rather than treating maturation color or an earlier negative view as proof of future expression.

lookAlikes: Yellow plant debris inside an inflorescence
Pollen dust without a linked source flower
Aphids, mites, eggs, cast skins, frass, or webbing
Mechanical injury or split bract tissue
confirmation: Do not assign male, female, monoecious, or co-sexual ground truth from a seedling, vegetative silhouette, whole-canopy view, or reproductive-organ-free clip; use visually indeterminate.
Capture a plant identifier and whole-plant view, then uninterrupted branch-to-node or branch-to-inflorescence context, followed by focused macro views with scale under repeatable lighting.

Record several upper and lower nodes plus multiple surfaces of terminal and lateral inflorescences; preserve the surrounding bract, stigma, pedicel, tepal, stamen, and anther context needed to distinguish organs.

Confirm pistillate expression from attached stigma-bearing flowers and staminate expression from attached opened anther-bearing flowers; yellow color, round shape, pollen dust, or a closed bract alone is insufficient.
Repeat inspection of the same mapped nodes and inflorescences through flowering because sparse staminate organs can be hidden and may appear after an earlier negative observation.
State the observation as expressed floral phenotype at the recorded organ, location, and date; do not infer chromosomal sex, plant-wide distribution, or future stability from one visual sample.

When pre-flower genetic sex is operationally important, use a validated Y-linked assay and retain sample-to-plant identity; interpret a negative result as female-or-monoecious genotype rather than proof of exclusively pistillate future expression.
Record cultivar, seed or clonal origin, plant age, propagation cohort, photoperiod history, treatment history, node or branch location, observation date, and any pollen or seed development.
Require human review for detached, scale-free, single-view, low-resolution, organ-ambiguous, genetically discordant, generated, stock, anecdotal, or plant-unlinked samples.
immediateActions: Keep the visual label indeterminate when reproductive organs are not yet visible.
If pollen release matters to the production objective, isolate a plant with confirmed anthers while identity and facility-specific disposition are reviewed.
correctivePlan: Treat sex expression as a monitored developmental classification, not a nutrient or pesticide diagnosis.
Use serial, multi-location inspection to document whether staminate organs are isolated, plant-wide, or embedded within pistillate inflorescences.
Apply only the facility’s lawful crop-management protocol after expressed flower type is confirmed.
prevention: Include multiple-node macro imagery and time-series flowering views in capture protocols.
Maintain cultivar, propagation, photoperiod, treatment, and genetic-test records so expressed phenotype is not confused with genetic assay status.
Continue inspection of nominally female or marker-screened populations through flowering because co-sexual expression is not excluded by a single early observation.
warnings: Image/video-only confidence is capped at 0.40 because visible organs can support a local expressed-phenotype label but cannot establish chromosomal sex, future stability, or absence elsewhere on the plant.
Seedling silhouette, height, leaf number, leaf size, vigor, branching, and internode length are not reliable ground-truth sex labels across cultivars.
A photograph of reproductive organs describes expressed floral phenotype at that place and time; it does not by itself establish chromosomal sex or guarantee future expression elsewhere on the plant.
A solitary stigma-bearing flower at an apical node is not automatically a developed terminal inflorescence, and cultivar-specific flowering days are not universal maturity thresholds.
The cited Y-linked assay separates Y-bearing males from female or monoecious plants but cannot distinguish the latter outcomes or guarantee future organ expression.
Use organ-specific terms and mapped distribution; a blanket whole-plant label is inappropriate when only one flower, node, or inflorescence surface was observed.

The three CC BY figures are lawful reference displays, but each is a multi-panel composite and remains excluded from automated training until panel-level annotation, identity-preserving split, crop, and leakage review.
Every detached, single-view, low-resolution, organ-ambiguous, plant-unlinked, genetically discordant, generated, anecdotal, or stock sample requires human review and is not ground truth.

sources.title: Dioecious hemp (Cannabis sativa L.) plants do not express significant sexually dimorphic morphology in the seedling stage
supportedClaims: In a study of 112 dioecious hemp plants, seedling morphology did not consistently distinguish male, female, and co-sexual plants across cultivars.
The researchers assigned expressed sex after flowering from floral morphology; 10 plants were co-sexual, defined as predominantly female flowering with at least one male flower.
Male flowers on co-sexual plants may be concealed within dense female inflorescences and may not be found until after pollen release, so one early view is not an adequate exclusion check.

sources.title: Development and validation of genetic markers for sex and cannabinoid chemotype in Cannabis sativa L.
supportedClaims: Male and female Cannabis plants are phenotypically difficult to distinguish before flowering, while DNA from young plants can be used for genotype assays.
The validated CSP-1 Y-chromosome assay separated male plants from female and monoecious plants across 2,170 plants, but it did not separate female from monoecious expression.

Sex-linked genotype and expressed floral phenotype are not interchangeable because female-genotype plants can express monoecious flowers and hormonal manipulation can induce male flowers on XX plants.

sources.title: Hermaphroditism in Marijuana (Cannabis sativa L.) Inflorescences – Impact on Floral Morphology, Seed Formation, Progeny Sex Ratios, and Genetic Variation
supportedClaims: Young pistillate inflorescences developed protruding white hair-like stigmas that later became yellowish-white, then curled and browned or reddened as carpels and surrounding bracts swelled during maturation.
Staminate flowers formed in pedicillate clusters at leaf axils, opened five tepals, exposed five stamens, and released pollen through a longitudinal anther groove.

In predominantly female inflorescences, co-sexual expression appeared as bright-yellow 2–3 mm anthers within bract tissue among stigmas; expression ranged from a few anthers to replacement of much of the female inflorescence and progressed over weeks.
The study figures are original Cannabis photographs and microscopy distributed with the article under the Creative Commons Attribution license.

sources.title: Architecture and Florogenesis in Female Cannabis sativa Plants
supportedClaims: In three female medical-Cannabis cultivars, solitary flowers and their subtending bracts occurred at leaf axils under long photoperiod, so visible reproductive organs can precede formation of a dense terminal inflorescence.
The authors identified solitary flowers as the first visual indication of sex and warned that stigmas from solitary flowers in the apical zone can be mistaken for inflorescence flowering.

Under short photoperiod, the female inflorescence developed as condensed branchlets containing reduced leaves, bracts, solitary flowers, and axillary shoots; these neighboring structures are relevant visual confounders in node-scale imagery.
Flowering timing and inflorescence architecture differed among the three cultivars, so the study-specific days after photoperiod change and plant habit are not universal sex or maturity thresholds.

One cultivar produced terminal flowers with both pistils and anthers under the experiment conditions, supporting organ-level documentation instead of inferring the whole plant’s future expression from an earlier or distant view.

media.alt: Composite research figure showing indoor Cannabis plants and sequential pistillate inflorescence development from white stigmas to mature swollen bracts
media.caption: Figure 1 documents pistillate Cannabis inflorescence development across several cultivars; panels include whole-canopy context and close views from young protruding stigmas through mature curled stigmas and swollen carpels.
media.creator: Zamir K. Punja and Janesse E. Holmes
media.requiredAttribution: © 2020 Punja and Holmes; cite Frontiers in Plant Science 11:718, DOI 10.3389/fpls.2020.00718, and provide the CC BY license notice.
useLimitations: Composite figure with different cultivars and stages; preserve panel labels and caption context.
Whole-plant panels do not independently establish sex; use the visible reproductive-organ panels.
Reference-only pending a separate training, crop, and dataset-split review.

media.alt: Composite research figure showing bright-yellow anthers emerging among brown stigmas in co-sexual Cannabis inflorescences and releasing pollen
media.caption: Figure 2 shows bright-yellow anther clusters formed within pistillate bract tissue beside stigmas, including a close view of pollen release along the anther groove.
media.creator: Zamir K. Punja and Janesse E. Holmes
media.requiredAttribution: © 2020 Punja and Holmes; cite Frontiers in Plant Science 11:718, DOI 10.3389/fpls.2020.00718, and provide the CC BY license notice.
useLimitations: Composite close-up from one study strain; it does not represent every co-sexual presentation.
The label requires visible anthers among pistillate structures and must not be inferred from yellow color alone.
Reference-only pending a separate training, crop, and dataset-split review.

media.alt: Composite research figure showing stalked male Cannabis flower clusters at leaf axils, opened flowers, five stamens, and pollen release
media.caption: Figure 6 follows genetically male Cannabis flowers from pedicillate axillary clusters through opening tepals, exposed stamens, and pollen release.
media.creator: Zamir K. Punja and Janesse E. Holmes
media.requiredAttribution: © 2020 Punja and Holmes; cite Frontiers in Plant Science 11:718, DOI 10.3389/fpls.2020.00718, and provide the CC BY license notice.
useLimitations: Composite includes macro and electron-microscope panels; preserve panel and scale context.
Pollen and microscopic anther details are confirmation context, not features expected in ordinary phone imagery.
Reference-only pending a separate training, crop, and dataset-split review.
media.stage: staminate flower development and pollen release

name: Boron deficiency
summary: A measurement-dependent Cannabis differential centered on shoot and root meristems. In one controlled T1 withholding study, new-growth distortion progressed to marginal necrosis, growing-tip and root-tip death, and wilt; those images support a sequence, not image-only ground truth.
affectedParts: stems, calyxes, and bracts as provisional institutional context
whole plant secondarily after severe root loss
stages: reproductive tissue context requires human review
indicators: Slight whole-plant stunting begins at growing tips while older foliage can remain comparatively normal in the controlled sequence
Youngest and newly expanding leaves cluster, twist, or fail to expand normally around affected shoot tips
New leaflets are smaller and distorted, with the leaflet base narrower than the distal portion
Progressing leaves curl inward, downward, or at irregular angles rather than following one uniform curl direction
Advanced new growth develops necrotic margins and thick, brittle, or malformed tissue
Growing tips can become necrotic and die, leaving a localized dead apex rather than an older-leaf-first fade
Root growth slows and root tips can swell, discolor, die, and lose biomass; whole-plant droop or wilt is secondary and nonspecific
A repeated new-growth-plus-root-tip pattern linked to low boron in correctly sampled tissue and a plausible supply or availability problem is stronger evidence than morphology alone
exclusions: Broad mites or hemp russet mites, eggs, cast skins, bronzing, or characteristic feeding injury are found on magnified growing-point and leaf-underside inspection
Calcium or copper evidence better explains the new-growth distortion and correctly positioned tissue and root-zone results do not support low boron
Older leaf margins yellow and necrose first under excessive boron or high-EC conditions while new meristems lack the controlled deficiency sequence
Root-zone pH, EC, saturation, drought, temperature, oxygenation, or root disease is abnormal enough to explain impaired uptake or wilt without deficient boron supply
Damage maps to spray droplets, a growth-regulator or herbicide exposure, a lamp-facing surface, a heat event, rubbing, pruning, or another localized injury
Mosaic, vein clearing, brittle growth, asymmetrical spread, vascular discoloration, lesions, pathogen structures, or laboratory evidence supports a virus, viroid, phytoplasma, or other pathogen
The same leaf geometry is stable in healthy clones or a cultivar reference, or appears only under altered white balance, grow-light color, glare, compression, or occlusion
Correctly positioned tissue boron is adequate for the cultivar, stage, sampled organ, laboratory method, and production system, or another measured nutrient disorder explains the syndrome better

progression.description: A supply, pH, root-health, or analytical abnormality may exist before a reliable visual label; do not manufacture a positive image class from exposure history alone.
After six weeks of complete boron withholding in one Cannabis sativa T1 experiment, plants were slightly stunted from the growing tips; the timing is study-specific.
