New and expanding leaflets become smaller, distorted, and narrow at their bases while older foliage is less dominant in the frame.
New leaves become severely distorted, curl inward or downward or at odd angles, and develop marginal necrosis; shoot tips can die.
Root-tip death and root-biomass loss can accompany whole-plant wilt. Capture roots and root-zone measurements because canopy wilt alone cannot identify boron deficiency.

lookAlikes: Waterlogging, root-zone hypoxia, or root rot
Camera white-balance, grow-light, focus, or compression artifact
confirmation: Do not confirm boron deficiency from twisted tips, narrow leaflet bases, marginal necrosis, wilt, one photograph, or one video; retain a suspected label until analytical and root-zone evidence is linked to the imaged plant.

Capture serial whole-plant and matched upper-, middle-, and lower-canopy views, apical and axillary tips, both surfaces of new leaves, leaflet bases and margins, stems and reproductive tissue when present, washed roots and root tips, and the root zone under neutral repeatable lighting with scale and a healthy same-cultivar reference.

Record cultivar, stage, days since onset, boron concentration and formulation in fertilizer and source water, complete nutrient recipe, recent product changes, irrigation and dryback history, substrate or soil type, and any spray, heat, light, pruning, or mechanical event.
Measure root-zone pH, EC, water content, temperature, drainage, and oxygenation as appropriate to the system, and inspect roots before changing boron supply.

Submit correctly positioned most-recently-mature leaves plus matched symptomatic and healthy material and an appropriate solution, substrate, soil, leachate, or water sample to an agricultural or plant diagnostic laboratory; document sample position, contamination controls, and method.

Inspect growing points and both leaf surfaces with sufficient magnification for broad and russet mites, and use a plant diagnostic laboratory when root pathogens, viruses, viroids, phytoplasmas, or mixed disorders remain plausible.

Interpret 2.46 mg/kg from the controlled T1 study and the NC survey range only within their methods and populations; correction response in subsequent growth is supporting evidence and does not retroactively make the original image ground truth.
immediateActions: Mark affected and matched healthy plants and preserve pre-treatment images, roots, root-zone measurements, feed and water records, and representative tissue before changing nutrition.
Quarantine or separate suspect plants when mites or transmissible pathogens remain plausible, and inspect meristems before nutrient correction.
Correct documented drainage, pH, EC, moisture, temperature, oxygenation, or root-health problems before assuming boron concentration is inadequate.
correctivePlan: Only when testing supports inadequate boron supply or availability and roots are functional, restore a balanced crop- and system-appropriate micronutrient program gradually under current local agronomic guidance.
Track new meristem geometry, new necrosis, root-tip growth, turgor, root-zone measurements, and follow-up tissue results; old deformed leaves and dead tips will not recover.
If boron status is adequate or the pattern continues, reopen calcium, copper, zinc, mite, pathogen, pH, EC, salinity, hypoxia, exposure, environmental, and genetic differentials.
prevention: Verify boron in fertilizer and source water and maintain calibrated pH and EC monitoring without using a generic internet deficiency chart as a feed target.
Use consistent most-recently-mature-leaf sampling, contamination controls, and same-cultivar references linked to plant, stage, and image identifiers.
Maintain root-zone moisture, drainage, temperature, and oxygenation records so impaired uptake is separated from inadequate supply.
warnings: The direct progression evidence came from one Cannabis sativa T1 cultivar grown in silica sand with boron completely withheld; six weeks, 2.46 mg/kg tissue boron, 96% reduction from control, and 28% less dry biomass are experiment-specific, not universal thresholds.

The NC State 30 to 90 ppm interval is a survey-based floral-hemp reference range, not a causal deficiency cutoff, and must not be transferred uncritically across cultivar, stage, plant part, production system, crop purpose, or laboratory method.
Stem corking and reproductive-tissue signs are institutional hemp observations rather than a controlled Cannabis progression and require human review.

The licensed Figure 4 asset is already indexed once under manganese deficiency because it contains manganese, boron, and copper classes; the center boron panels remain reference-only until panel crops, coordinates, labels, provenance, and dataset splits are reviewed.
USU page images have mixed institutional and vendor credits without item-level reuse licenses and are excluded from media indexing and ground truth.
Do not apply a generic boric-acid or borax dose from visual suspicion: the same source distinguishes boron excess, and an unmeasured correction can create toxicity or salinity-like injury.
All image-only, root-unlinked, unmatched, method-unknown, contaminated, cross-crop-threshold, mixed-disorder, or analytically discordant samples require human review.

sources.title: Characterization of Nutrient Disorders of Cannabis sativa
supportedClaims: Single-element withholding in Cannabis sativa T1 documented boron deficiency, manganese toxicity, and the absence of a visible molybdenum-deficiency phenotype during the nine-week experiment.
Boron-deficient plants developed growing-tip stunting, distorted new leaves, marginal necrosis, death of growing tips, root-tip loss, and severe wilting in advanced stages.

Boron-withheld plants first showed slight whole-plant stunting from growing tips after six weeks; new and expanding leaflets were smaller and distorted, with bases narrower than tips, before margins became necrotic and leaves curled inward, downward, or at irregular angles.

At first boron-deficiency symptom expression, boron-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 2.46 mg/kg boron compared with 58.58 mg/kg in controls, 96% lower under the experiment conditions, and treated plants produced 28% less dry biomass.

Figure 4 is a CC BY 4.0 nine-panel composite: manganese, boron, and copper deficiency occupy the left, center, and right columns respectively, with initial, intermediate, and advanced rows; only the center column represents boron deficiency.

In Cannabis sativa T1, manganese-toxicity symptoms appeared seven weeks after treatment: marginal yellowing began on lower leaves, intensified inward toward the midrib, and advanced to marginal necrosis, severe chlorosis, and occasional leaf abscission.

The manganese-toxicity treatment used a tenfold increase over the complete formula (180 micromolar Mn versus 18 micromolar), but treated foliar Mn was 47.88 mg/kg, within the cited 41–93 mg/kg survey range; dry weight did not differ significantly from controls and the authors called for higher-concentration work to refine the threshold.
Figure 5 is a six-panel composite: manganese toxicity occupies the left column and boron toxicity the right, with initial, intermediate, and advanced symptom rows.

Molybdenum-withheld plants had foliar Mo 96% lower than controls yet developed no visual symptoms and no significant dry-weight difference by nine weeks, so a camera-visible Mo-deficiency phenotype was not established.
The experiment used one cultivar and complete withholding or tenfold treatments; tissue values and timing are experimental observations rather than universal Cannabis thresholds.

sources.title: Nutrient Deficiencies
sources.organization: Utah State University Extension, Utah Plant Pest Diagnostic Laboratory
supportedClaims: USU describes hemp boron-deficiency context as stunted, twisted, clustered new tip growth that does not expand properly, with shoots that can appear burned.

The guide describes slow root growth with swollen or discolored root tips, thickened brittle distorted leaves, interveinal necrotic spots, stem corking, underdeveloped calyxes or bracts with small brown spots, and overall droop; these institutional observations are not a controlled progression sequence.
USU distinguishes excess boron as an older-leaf-first marginal yellowing and necrosis pattern that can resemble salinity injury, supporting separation of deficiency from toxicity and high-EC stress.
The page mixes institutional and commercial-vendor photographs and provides no item-level reuse license, so none of its images are admitted as dataset media or ground truth.

sources.title: Hemp Leaf Tissue Nutrient Ranges: Refinement of Reference Standards for Floral Hemp
sources.publisher: North Carolina Cooperative Extension and North Carolina Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services
supportedClaims: The reference ranges were derived from 6,119 floral-hemp samples representing more than 100 varieties from field and greenhouse production in 76 North Carolina counties between 2017 and 2020.

For diagnostic hemp sampling, the publication recommends the most recently mature leaf, generally the third through fifth leaf below the growing point, using one or two leaves from 10 to 20 representative plants.
The adopted 30 to 90 ppm boron range is a survey-based floral-hemp reference interval rather than a causal deficiency threshold; the authors state that rate studies and further refinement are needed.
The survey does not establish universal boron thresholds for every cultivar, plant part, growth stage, production system, grain or fiber crop, or laboratory method.

name: Calcium deficiency
summary: A calcium-supply or transport disorder that can damage meristems, newly expanding leaves, roots, fan leaves, and sugar leaves. Controlled Cannabis studies produced different canopy-onset patterns, so spotting, curled tips, or marginal necrosis require feed, water, root-zone, tissue, stage, and cultivar evidence.
affectedParts: growing tips and newly expanding leaves in vegetative T1
lower fan leaves at flowering-stage onset in Gelato 29
upper fan leaves and sugar leaves as the Gelato 29 sequence advanced
leaflet bases, interveinal tissue, serrations, margins, and tips
developing inflorescences and bracts for differential inspection
stages: chronic insufficient supply or impaired transport
indicators: Vegetative T1: growing tips and new leaves become stunted and irregular while leaflet bases stay narrow and paler than tips
Vegetative T1 progression: basal yellowing intensifies into interveinal chlorosis, distorted new leaves, marginal necrosis, growing-tip death, and increased axillary branching
Flowering Gelato 29: lower fan leaves begin with interveinal yellow rings around necrotic brown centers during week three of withholding
Flowering Gelato 29 progression: spotting concentrates near margins and tips, coalesces into irregular marginal necrosis, and browns serration points
Later flowering progression: injury moves upward into younger fan and sugar leaves, with upward curling of upper fan-leaf tips
A calcium deficit or impaired calcium delivery is supported by input, root-zone, water, tissue, and plant-stage measurements linked to the imaged plant
exclusions: Spots, edge burn, or curl occur without a documented calcium-supply or transport problem
Root-zone EC is high and broad multi-ion salt injury explains the tip and margin damage
Roots are saturated, oxygen-limited, drought-stressed, temperature-injured, mechanically damaged, or diseased and calcium analysis does not support a deficit
Young-growth distortion is accompanied by mites, thrips, insects, webbing, eggs, fecal spots, or feeding scars
Discrete expanding lesions, halos, fungal structures, or laboratory results support a pathogen
Injury is limited to the hottest, brightest, sprayed, or contact-exposed canopy surfaces
Older-leaf marginal injury follows a potassium- or magnesium-type pattern and tissue/root-zone evidence supports that alternative
Yellowing is consistent with measured nitrogen deficiency or late-cycle senescence and no calcium evidence is present
Color or spotting is visible only under altered lighting, white balance, residue, dust, or compression artifact

progression.description: Calcium supply or delivery becomes inadequate because of formulation, water, root-zone, transport, or root-function context; a photograph cannot establish which mechanism is responsible.
After five weeks of withholding in T1, growing tips and newly expanding leaves were slightly stunted and irregular, with narrow pale leaflet bases.
By week three of withholding in Gelato 29, lower fan leaves developed interveinal spots with yellow rings around necrotic brown centers.
Depending on study context, basal and interveinal chlorosis, distorted new leaves, or lower-leaf spotting intensified and developed margin or serration necrosis.
T1 growing tips became necrotic and axillary shoots proliferated; Gelato 29 injury spread upward across fan and sugar leaves with marginal necrosis and upward-curled upper tips.
Evaluate new meristem quality, new root tips, lesion rate, canopy expansion, and follow-up analyses; existing necrosis and distorted leaves will not recover.

confirmation: Do not confirm calcium deficiency from rust-colored spots, curled leaf tips, distorted new growth, marginal necrosis, one photograph, or one video.

Capture serial whole-plant, growing-tip, upper/middle/lower-canopy, fan-leaf, sugar-leaf, leaf upper-surface, underside, cleaned-root, and root-tip views under repeatable lighting with scale and a matched same-cultivar plant.
Record the first affected node and leaf age, cultivar, stage, days since symptom onset, irrigation and dryback, root-zone water content, temperature, pH, EC, and dissolved oxygen where relevant.

Measure calcium and competing ions in source water, fertilizer stocks, final solution, root-zone extract, substrate or soil, and representative leaf tissue from defined upper and lower canopy positions.
Interpret tissue results using plant part, node, stage, cultivar, method, and system context; neither 0.39% from T1 nor the Gelato 29 upper/lower relationship is a universal threshold.
Inspect roots for active white tips, discoloration, softness, odor, lesions, binding, and mechanical damage; use a plant diagnostic laboratory when root pathogens or leaf lesions remain plausible.
Inspect distorted growth and both leaf surfaces with magnification for broad mites, russet mites, thrips, eggs, webbing, and feeding evidence.
Retain a suspected label until a calcium-supply or transport problem, compatible progression, and exclusion evidence are linked to the photographed plant.
immediateActions: Preserve pre-treatment images, nutrient labels, mixing records, solution and water samples, root-zone readings, and representative tissue before changing the program.
Verify meter calibration, formulation calculations, source-water mineral content, root health, pH, EC, water status, and temperature before adding calcium or flushing.
Remove symptom-only samples from training-ground-truth collections until analytical and exposure evidence is reviewed.
correctivePlan: Correct the verified supply, pH, salinity, irrigation, temperature, oxygen, drainage, or root-health cause using crop-, medium-, and stage-appropriate agronomic guidance.
Restore a balanced nutrient solution rather than stacking unmeasured calcium-magnesium products; account for calcium already present in source water and fertilizers.
Track new growth, new roots, lesion rate, root-zone pH and EC, and follow-up tissue results; reopen potassium, magnesium, boron, pest, pathogen, and environmental differentials if response is absent.
prevention: Test source water and complete fertilizer for calcium and competing ions and document all calcium-containing inputs.
Use calibrated root-zone pH, EC, moisture, temperature, and irrigation monitoring appropriate to the production system.
Maintain same-cultivar healthy references and consistent upper/lower canopy tissue-sampling and serial imaging procedures.
warnings: Controlled Cannabis studies disagreed on first affected canopy location: vegetative T1 began at growing tips and new leaves, while flowering Gelato 29 began on lower fan leaves; location alone is not ground truth.
The T1 five-week timing, 0.39% most-recent-mature-leaf value, and growing-tip sequence are experiment-specific.
The Gelato 29 three-week onset, upper/lower tissue relationship, and biomass response came from three deep-water-culture plants per treatment and must not be generalized.
Calcium can be present in the root zone while water status, salinity, temperature, oxygen, damaged roots, or transport conditions limit delivery; adding calcium does not correct those causes.
The CC BY figure is a single-treatment progression, but remains excluded from automated training until panel annotations, source grouping, and a leakage-safe dataset split are assigned.
The NC State e-GRO page requires author permission for its separate images; those assets were not copied or admitted.
All symptom-only samples remain low confidence and require human review.

sources.title: Characterization of Nutrient Disorders of Cannabis sativa
supportedClaims: Cannabis sativa T1 plants were grown in silica sand with a complete modified Hoagland solution or a solution withholding one nutrient, observed daily, photographed through initial, intermediate, and advanced symptoms, and sampled at first symptom expression for most-recent-mature-leaf tissue analysis.

Nitrogen-withheld plants developed symptoms after six weeks: slight stunting and lower-foliage paling progressed upward into middle foliage, then affected leaves became fully yellow, necrotic, and abscised.

At first symptom expression, nitrogen-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 1.62% nitrogen dry weight compared with 4.28% in controls, and treated plants produced 50% less dry biomass under the experiment conditions.
Only the left column of Figure 2 represents nitrogen deficiency; the center and right columns are phosphorus and calcium deficiency and must retain separate labels.
The one-cultivar, silica-sand, complete-withholding experiment does not establish universal onset timing, tissue thresholds, production symptoms, or response to partial nitrogen limitation.

Phosphorus-withheld plants first showed slight stunting and irregular olive-green spots on lower and older leaflets after seven weeks; spots enlarged, appeared sunken and almost wet, developed some marginal necrosis, and advanced to extensive olive spotting and large necrotic portions.

At first phosphorus-deficiency symptom expression, phosphorus-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 0.09% phosphorus dry weight compared with 0.43% in controls, a 79% difference under the experiment conditions.

The study used one cultivar, began nutrient withholding at transplant, and reported no statistically significant biomass difference for phosphorus-withheld plants at the symptom-onset harvest, so its timing, tissue value, and appearance are not universal diagnostic thresholds.
Figure 2 is a CC BY 4.0 composite showing initial, intermediate, and advanced nitrogen-, phosphorus-, and calcium-deficiency phenotypes in Cannabis sativa T1.

In calcium-withheld T1 plants, symptoms appeared after five weeks as slight stunting and irregular growing tips and newly expanding leaves; leaflet bases stayed narrow and paler than tips, then basal and interveinal chlorosis, marginal necrosis, distorted geometry, growing-tip death, and axillary branching developed.

At first calcium-deficiency symptom expression, most-recent-mature leaves contained 0.39% calcium dry weight compared with 3.73% in controls, but the one-cultivar silica-sand withholding experiment does not establish a universal tissue threshold or field sequence.

Iron-withheld T1 plants first developed symptoms after nine weeks: slight marginal yellowing, especially near leaflet bases, progressed to interveinal chlorosis on growing-tip and newly expanding leaves and spread through the upper half while middle and lower foliage remained healthy dark green.

At first iron-deficiency symptom expression, iron-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 60.08 mg/kg iron compared with 111.75 mg/kg in controls, 46% lower under the experiment conditions; biomass did not differ significantly from the control at that harvest.
Figure 6 is a CC BY 4.0 composite with initial, intermediate, and advanced iron-deficiency images in its left column and zinc-deficiency images in its right column.

Manganese-withheld T1 plants developed bright-yellow netted interveinal chlorosis on upper and central foliage after six weeks; the netting began near leaflet midribs, spread toward margins, retained green veins, and later developed small tan necrotic regions.

At first manganese-deficiency symptom expression, manganese-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 7.56 mg/kg manganese compared with 29.40 mg/kg in controls, 74% lower under the experiment conditions; dry biomass did not differ significantly at that harvest.

The control manganese concentration was itself below the cited general crop survey range, and the study used one cultivar in silica sand with complete withholding, so neither treatment value is a universal Cannabis diagnostic threshold.

Figure 4 is a CC BY 4.0 composite showing initial, intermediate, and advanced manganese-, boron-, and copper-deficiency phenotypes in Cannabis sativa T1; only its left column represents manganese deficiency.

Copper-withheld T1 plants first developed visible symptoms after nine weeks, beginning with slight whole-plant stunting and mild distortion of newer and expanding leaves, especially narrowed and slightly yellow leaflet bases.

As copper-withholding symptoms advanced, basal narrowing and distortion intensified, marginal interveinal chlorosis developed, and the whole leaf progressed to fine interveinal chlorosis with slightly inward- and downward-curled margins and reduced turgidity.

At first copper-deficiency symptom expression, copper-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 1.41 mg/kg copper compared with 4.65 mg/kg in controls, 70% lower under the experiment conditions; treated plants produced 45% less biomass.

The control copper concentration of 4.65 mg/kg was itself slightly below the general crop survey range cited by the authors, and the one-cultivar complete-withholding result does not establish a universal Cannabis threshold.

The published Figure 4 caption and column labels identify initial, intermediate, and advanced copper-deficiency panels in the right column, although the copper subsection text cites Figure 5; Figure 5 is captioned as manganese- and boron-toxicity progression, so this source-level numbering inconsistency must remain attached to copper panel review.

Magnesium-withheld T1 plants first developed slight interveinal yellowing on lower and older foliage after seven weeks; the contrast between green veins and yellow interveinal tissue intensified and some regions became necrotic.

At first magnesium-deficiency symptom expression, magnesium-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 0.12% magnesium compared with 0.61% in controls, 80% lower under the experiment conditions; biomass did not differ significantly at that harvest.

Figure 3 is a CC BY 4.0 composite showing initial, intermediate, and advanced sulfur-, magnesium-, and potassium-deficiency phenotypes in Cannabis sativa T1; only its center column represents magnesium deficiency.

Potassium-withheld T1 plants first developed yellowing at leaflet margins and saw-tooth serrations on lower and older foliage after nine weeks; yellowing intensified and moved inward toward the midrib, followed by tan necrosis concentrated along serrated margins.

At first potassium-deficiency symptom expression, potassium-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 0.41% potassium compared with 2.85% in controls, 86% lower under the experiment conditions; treated plants produced 27% less biomass.

Figure 3 is a CC BY 4.0 composite whose right column shows initial, intermediate, and advanced potassium-deficiency phenotypes; the sulfur and magnesium columns are separate diagnoses and the asset is indexed once under the magnesium record to avoid duplicate media hashes.

Zinc-withheld T1 plants first developed symptoms after nine weeks as marginal yellowing on newer and expanding leaves, concentrated along leaflet margins and toothed portions; tan, irregularly shaped marginal necrosis developed as the disorder progressed.

At first zinc-deficiency symptom expression, zinc-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 10.70 mg/kg zinc compared with 25.33 mg/kg in controls, 58% lower under the experiment conditions; biomass did not differ significantly from the control at that harvest.

Sulfur-withheld T1 plants first developed symptoms after seven weeks as slight overall yellowing, especially in the middle canopy and at leaflet bases; yellowing intensified at leaflet bases and on newly expanding leaves, then advanced to very pale yellow tissue around the midrib and leaflet bases.

At first sulfur-deficiency symptom expression, sulfur-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 0.11% sulfur compared with 0.41% in controls, 73% lower under the experiment conditions; biomass did not differ significantly from the control at that harvest.

sources.title: Foliar Symptomology, Nutrient Content, Yield, and Secondary Metabolite Variability of Cannabis Grown Hydroponically with Different Single-Element Nutrient Deficiencies
supportedClaims: Three Gelato 29 plants per treatment were grown in aerated deep-water culture; single-element withholding began with the switch to a 12-hour flowering photoperiod, plants were examined daily and photographed weekly, and upper- and lower-canopy foliage was laboratory analyzed at symptom onset.
Nitrogen-withheld plants showed reduced vegetative expansion before foliar symptoms; during week three, very slight yellowing began at leaflet tips of lower-canopy fan leaves.

By week four, most fan leaves in the lower two-thirds were yellowing; chlorosis was initially strongest between veins before broad whole-leaf yellowing, and severity within leaflets progressed from base toward tip.

By week five, nearly all fan leaves were yellow with severity increasing from bottom to top; petioles became red-brown, some fan leaves browned and senesced, stems began yellowing, and sugar-leaf chlorosis began.

By weeks six and seven, most fan leaves had senesced, older and lower-position sugar leaves progressively yellowed or browned, and stems became brown; the authors considered this prolonged severe endpoint commercially damaging.

At symptom onset, upper- and lower-canopy foliar nitrogen concentrations did not differ and overlapped the control and other treatments, illustrating limitations of a single tissue analysis later in production.

Healthy control plants developed lower-fan-leaf chlorosis in weeks six through eight despite adequate nutrient solution and foliar concentrations, demonstrating that natural late-flower senescence can visually confound nitrogen deficiency.

Nitrogen-withheld plants had 73% less aboveground vegetative fresh mass and approximately 72% less fresh inflorescence mass than controls under this three-plant treatment; these are experiment-specific loss estimates, not universal predictions.

Figure 2 is a CC BY 4.0 four-panel flowering-stage nitrogen-deficiency progression spanning lower-canopy onset, detached fan-leaf severity, canopy distribution, fan-leaf senescence, stem color, and beginning sugar-leaf chlorosis.

In the calcium-withheld treatment, lower fan leaves developed interveinal spots with yellow rings and necrotic brown centers in week three; by week four symptoms occupied mostly the lower two-thirds and were concentrated near leaflet margins and tips.

By week five, spots coalesced into irregular marginal necrosis, serration points browned, injury moved upward into younger fan and sugar leaves, and upper fan-leaf tips curled upward; by week six most fan and sugar leaves were affected.

The flowering-stage lower-leaf onset differed markedly from the vegetative-stage T1 study and from the usual expectation for an immobile nutrient; lower-canopy foliage also contained almost three times the calcium of upper-canopy foliage at symptom onset.

Calcium-withheld plants averaged 621 g fresh inflorescence mass compared with 1110 g in controls under this three-plant-per-treatment experiment; those values do not establish a universal yield-loss estimate.
Figure 5 is a CC BY 4.0 five-panel Cannabis calcium-deficiency progression from week-three spotting through widespread marginal necrosis and upward curling in week six.

Despite foliar iron concentrations less than half those of controls, iron-withheld flowering Gelato 29 plants showed no visible deficiency symptoms and no significant aboveground biomass reduction by the end of the 7.5-week treatment.

The symptom-negative flowering result came from three plants in one cultivar and one deep-water-culture experiment; it demonstrates that absence of a visible syndrome cannot exclude inadequate iron status, not that flowering Cannabis never shows iron-deficiency symptoms.

In sulfur-withheld flowering Gelato 29, recently developed upper sugar leaves yellowed in week four; by week five upper fan leaves angled upward and lower fan leaves developed interveinal chlorosis from midrib to margins, later progressing through fan leaves to total yellowing and senescence while early sugar-leaf chlorosis changed little except for browned tips and marginal teeth.

Sulfur-withheld foliage had substantially lower sulfur than all other treatments, with no significant upper-versus-lower canopy concentration difference; inflorescence yield was 34% lower than control while vegetative biomass, root biomass, and cannabinoid concentrations showed no major effect in the three-plant treatment.

Figure 7 is a CC BY 4.0 four-panel sulfur-deficiency progression showing younger sugar-leaf yellowing, upward-angled upper fan leaves, a fan-leaf chlorosis sequence, and the later whole-plant distribution.

The flowering study contrasted with the vegetative T1 study in first described canopy location and progression direction, and cautioned that late-flower nutrient symptomology can be confounded with natural foliar senescence.

No visually obvious manganese-deficiency signs developed in the manganese-withheld flowering Gelato 29 plants; at week seven their apical inflorescences were similar to controls in size, shape, and color, and the treatment did not reduce biomass or cannabinoid concentrations.

At harvest, manganese-withheld upper-canopy foliage was extremely low in manganese relative to lower-canopy foliage and other treatments, yet the plants remained visually similar to controls, so a symptom-negative image cannot exclude low manganese status.

The authors state that nutrient diagnosis should integrate fertilizer and leachate composition, symptomology, and strategically timed and positioned foliar analysis because cultivar, environment, maturity, and sample location affect tissue concentrations.

Figure 9 is a CC BY 4.0 side-by-side comparison of manganese-withheld and control apical inflorescences during week seven; it is a controlled symptom-negative reference rather than a visible-deficiency example.

Magnesium-withheld flowering Gelato 29 plants had no visible symptoms for three weeks; mild interveinal chlorosis began on lower fan leaves in week four between the midrib and margins, then rapidly predominated on smaller, younger fan leaves while older fan leaves and inflorescence sugar leaves were less affected.

Severely affected flowering leaves developed interveinal necrosis that increased from leaflet bases toward tips; by week five symptoms were widespread except at apical inflorescences, and by week six most smaller fan leaves and sugar leaves were yellow except at the midrib and extreme margins while some older fan leaves remained largely unaffected.

At symptom onset, lower-canopy foliage in the magnesium-withheld treatment contained about one-third the magnesium of upper-canopy foliage; the treatment averaged 748 g fresh inflorescence mass versus 1110 g in controls, approximately 30% lower in this three-plant-per-treatment experiment, while cannabinoid concentrations were not significantly affected.

Figure 6 is a CC BY 4.0 five-panel flowering-stage magnesium-deficiency progression spanning the first mild lower-fan-leaf chlorosis, whole-plant distribution, detached-leaf severity, inflorescence context, and advanced whole-plant symptoms.

Potassium-withheld flowering Gelato 29 plants had no visible symptoms for two weeks; in week three, larger sugar leaves developed dark-brown lesions around secondary branch veins, while lower fan leaves developed lighter browning at leaflet tips and marginal teeth one week later.

By week five both potassium-deficiency pathways appeared on the same plant: sugar-leaf lesions predominated near the top and fan-leaf injury was strongest in the middle third, with light-brown fan-leaf injury moving inward especially through interveinal tissue.

By week six, green tissue was largely limited to inflorescences, sugar-leaf midribs, and some lower fan leaves; by week seven most non-inflorescence leaves were brown, curled, and dry, and some inflorescence leaves developed tip browning.

Potassium-withheld plants averaged 535 g fresh inflorescence mass compared with 1110 g in controls and had the second-lowest root dry mass in this three-plant-per-treatment experiment; higher THCA concentration did not offset the lower plant-level yield.
Figure 4 is a CC BY 4.0 four-panel flowering-stage potassium-deficiency progression showing distinct sugar-leaf and fan-leaf symptoms at week four and their middle-canopy distribution by week five.

sources.title: Nutrient Deficiencies
sources.organization: Utah State University Extension, Utah Plant Pest Diagnostic Laboratory
supportedClaims: USU describes hemp phosphorus-deficiency context as slowed growth with bluish-green foliage, purple petioles, copper to purplish-brown lower-leaf blotches, contortion or downward curl, and bronze or purple necrosis in heavily affected leaves.

USU states that high-pH soil above 7, cold soil, and clayey, poorly drained, soggy conditions can limit phosphorus uptake, so tissue appearance cannot distinguish inadequate supply from impaired root-zone availability.
The page recommends soil and nutrient analysis to guide amendments and states that excess phosphorus can resemble iron or zinc deficiency, supporting measurement before corrective fertilization.
The phosphorus photographs on the page have mixed USU and commercial-vendor credits and no explicit reuse license, so they are not admitted as verified media or ground truth.

USU describes hemp calcium-deficiency context as contorted or curled leaves, irregular yellow-brown spotting while intervening tissue remains green, slowed flower-bud development, and root-tip dieback, and states that excess water, salinity, or root damage can impair calcium transport.

The USU calcium page localizes pictured spotting to lower leaves, which is compatible with a flowering-stage hydroponic study but differs from the newly expanding growth sequence in the vegetative T1 study; canopy location alone is therefore not diagnostic.

USU describes hemp boron-deficiency context as stunted, twisted, clustered new tip growth that does not expand properly and root tips that can swell and discolor, while excess boron begins on older leaf margins and can resemble salinity injury.
The page mixes institutional and commercial-vendor photographs and provides no item-level reuse license, so none of its images are admitted as dataset media or ground truth.

media.alt: Five-panel Gelato 29 Cannabis calcium-deficiency progression showing lower fan-leaf spotting, marginal necrosis, upward spread, and upper-leaf curling
media.caption: Controlled flowering-stage calcium-withholding sequence: lower-fan-leaf yellow-ringed necrotic spots progress toward marginal necrosis, then upper fan and sugar leaves become affected and upper tips curl upward.
media.creator: David Llewellyn, Scott Golem, A. Maxwell P. Jones, and Youbin Zheng
media.requiredAttribution: Llewellyn D, Golem S, Jones AMP, Zheng Y (2023), Plants 12(3):422, Figure 5, CC BY 4.0; link the source and license and indicate modifications.
useLimitations: One cultivar, three plants per treatment, flowering-stage deep-water culture, and complete calcium withholding do not establish universal field symptoms or timing.
The five panels are a temporal sequence from the same experimental treatment; preserve panel order and source grouping and do not split panels across train and evaluation sets.
Reference display only until each panel is bounded, stage-annotated, scientifically reviewed, and assigned a leakage-safe dataset split.

name: Copper deficiency
summary: A controlled vegetative Cannabis copper-withholding response characterized by late-onset stunting, basal narrowing and yellowing of newer leaflets, progressive new-leaf distortion, fine interveinal chlorosis, slight inward/downward margin curl, and reduced turgidity. The evidence comes from one cultivar and requires tissue and root-zone confirmation.
affectedParts: most-recent-mature leaves for source-comparable tissue analysis
roots and root zone for availability checks
stages: advanced distortion and fine interveinal chlorosis
indicators: Slight whole-plant stunting relative to a matched healthy plant
Newer and expanding leaves show mild distortion concentrated near leaflet bases
Leaflet bases become narrower than the distal leaflet and slightly yellow
Basal narrowing and distortion become more pronounced as the sequence advances
Marginal interveinal chlorosis develops on new and expanding leaves
Advanced leaves show fine interveinal chlorosis across much of the blade
Leaf margins distort and curl slightly inward and downward
New and expanding leaves show mildly reduced turgidity
Low copper is documented in correctly positioned foliage and linked to supply or root-zone availability
exclusions: New-leaf interveinal chlorosis occurs without basal narrowing or distortion and iron, manganese, or zinc evidence is stronger
Growing-tip distortion, narrow leaflet bases, root-tip loss, severe wilting, or tip death follows a boron-deficiency pattern and boron analysis supports it
Newest leaves are puckered, bronzed, hardened, or strap-like and broad mites are found under adequate magnification
Uniform wilting or reduced turgidity follows irrigation, drought, heat, root hypoxia, salinity, or root disease rather than the published leaf sequence
Fine stippling, silver scars, webbing, eggs, mites, thrips, or fecal spots are present on magnified inspection
Mosaic, vein clearing, brittle growth, asymmetrical distortion, or molecular evidence supports a virus or viroid
Discrete lesions, halos, surface growth, vascular discoloration, root decay, or laboratory evidence supports a pathogen
Damage maps to a lamp-facing surface, heat event, spray droplets, residue, rubbing point, pruning event, or other documented exposure
Color or distortion appears only under grow lights, altered white balance, glare, shadow, compression, residue, or a stable inherited leaf form
Correctly positioned tissue copper is adequate for the cultivar, stage, method, and production system or another nutrient result explains the syndrome better

progression.description: Copper supply or availability may be low before a reliable image pattern appears; the controlled T1 study did not report visible symptoms until nine weeks after withholding began.
The plant becomes slightly stunted and newer or expanding leaves show mild distortion, narrowed leaflet bases, and slight basal yellowing.
Basal narrowing and distortion intensify and marginal interveinal chlorosis appears on new and expanding leaves.
Fine interveinal chlorosis extends across the leaf, margins become distorted with slight inward and downward curl, and newer leaves show mildly reduced turgidity.
Assess subsequent growth, new-leaf geometry, serial canopy views, root-zone measurements, and follow-up tissue analysis; established deformation or chlorosis may not reverse.

lookAlikes: Camera white-balance, exposure, or grow-light color shift
confirmation: Do not confirm copper deficiency from stunting, narrow leaflet bases, chlorosis, curl, reduced turgidity, one photograph, or one video; retain a suspected label until analytical and root-zone evidence is linked to the photographed plant.

Capture serial whole-plant and matched upper-, middle-, and lower-canopy views, growing tips, new and mature leaves of known node and physiological age, leaflet bases and margins, both leaf surfaces, internodes with scale, and roots under neutral repeatable lighting with a healthy same-cultivar reference.

Record cultivar, stage, days since onset, copper concentration and formulation, iron, manganese, zinc, boron, calcium, sulfur, phosphorus, and complete fertilizer inputs, source-water chemistry and alkalinity, irrigation history, substrate or solution type, and recent product changes.
Measure root-zone pH, EC, water content, temperature, drainage, and oxygenation as appropriate to the system, and inspect washed roots before changing copper supply.

Submit correctly positioned foliage plus appropriate solution, substrate, soil, leachate, or water samples to an agricultural or plant diagnostic laboratory; interpret copper with plant part, stage, cultivar, method, and competing elements rather than treating 1.41 mg/kg as a universal cutoff.

Inspect growing points and both leaf surfaces with magnification and use a plant diagnostic laboratory when broad mites, russet mites, thrips, root disease, viruses, viroids, or other pathogens remain plausible.
Treat response of subsequent growth as supporting evidence only; improvement after correcting a documented cause does not retroactively make the original image ground-truth copper deficiency.
immediateActions: Mark affected and matched healthy plants; preserve pre-treatment serial images, fertilizer and irrigation records, root-zone measurements, and representative tissue before changing nutrition.
Correct documented pH, salinity, saturation, drought, temperature, oxygenation, or root-health problems before assuming copper concentration is inadequate.
Avoid blind copper supplementation when boron, iron, manganese, zinc, mites, pathogens, spray injury, and genetic leaf form have not been excluded.
correctivePlan: When analytical and production records support inadequate copper supply or availability and roots are functional, restore a balanced crop- and system-appropriate micronutrient program gradually under current local agronomic guidance.
Track subsequent leaf geometry, chlorosis, turgidity, internode growth, roots, root-zone measurements, and follow-up tissue results rather than judging correction from old deformed leaves.
If copper status is adequate or the pattern continues, reopen boron, iron, manganese, zinc, calcium, root disease, arthropod, pathogen, environmental, exposure, and genetic differentials.
prevention: Record copper and competing micronutrients in fertilizer, source water, and representative tissue by plant part and stage rather than relying on a generic deficiency chart.
Calibrate pH and EC meters, monitor root-zone conditions and leachate where appropriate, and keep irrigation, dryback, temperature, and oxygenation records.
Maintain same-cultivar healthy references and consistent growing-tip, node-, and canopy-position sampling so developmental leaf shape is not mistaken for copper response.
warnings: The controlled sequence came from one Cannabis sativa T1 cultivar in silica sand with copper completely withheld; nine weeks, 1.41 mg/kg tissue copper, 45% lower biomass, and the pictured pattern are experiment-specific, not universal thresholds.
The control contained 4.65 mg/kg copper, slightly below the general crop survey range cited by the authors, which further limits conversion of either value into a Cannabis cutoff.

The source contains a figure-number inconsistency: its copper prose cites Figure 5, while the published Figure 4 caption and right-column label identify copper deficiency and Figure 5 is captioned manganese and boron toxicity. Copper panels require human verification against the original layout.

New-growth distortion, basal narrowing, chlorosis, curl, reduced turgidity, and stunting overlap nutritional, root-zone, arthropod, pathogen, environmental, exposure, genetic, and imaging conditions and are not image-only ground truth.

The CC BY Figure 4 asset is already hashed and indexed under manganese deficiency; it is cross-referenced rather than duplicated here because repository quality gates require unique verified media hashes.

No separate image or video is admitted for this record in this batch; all symptom-only samples and any derived copper-panel crops require human review and linked analytical evidence before ground-truth use.

sources.title: Characterization of Nutrient Disorders of Cannabis sativa
supportedClaims: Cannabis sativa T1 plants were grown in silica sand with a complete modified Hoagland solution or a solution withholding one nutrient, observed daily, photographed through initial, intermediate, and advanced symptoms, and sampled at first symptom expression for most-recent-mature-leaf tissue analysis.

Nitrogen-withheld plants developed symptoms after six weeks: slight stunting and lower-foliage paling progressed upward into middle foliage, then affected leaves became fully yellow, necrotic, and abscised.

At first symptom expression, nitrogen-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 1.62% nitrogen dry weight compared with 4.28% in controls, and treated plants produced 50% less dry biomass under the experiment conditions.
Only the left column of Figure 2 represents nitrogen deficiency; the center and right columns are phosphorus and calcium deficiency and must retain separate labels.
The one-cultivar, silica-sand, complete-withholding experiment does not establish universal onset timing, tissue thresholds, production symptoms, or response to partial nitrogen limitation.

Phosphorus-withheld plants first showed slight stunting and irregular olive-green spots on lower and older leaflets after seven weeks; spots enlarged, appeared sunken and almost wet, developed some marginal necrosis, and advanced to extensive olive spotting and large necrotic portions.

At first phosphorus-deficiency symptom expression, phosphorus-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 0.09% phosphorus dry weight compared with 0.43% in controls, a 79% difference under the experiment conditions.

The study used one cultivar, began nutrient withholding at transplant, and reported no statistically significant biomass difference for phosphorus-withheld plants at the symptom-onset harvest, so its timing, tissue value, and appearance are not universal diagnostic thresholds.
Figure 2 is a CC BY 4.0 composite showing initial, intermediate, and advanced nitrogen-, phosphorus-, and calcium-deficiency phenotypes in Cannabis sativa T1.

In calcium-withheld T1 plants, symptoms appeared after five weeks as slight stunting and irregular growing tips and newly expanding leaves; leaflet bases stayed narrow and paler than tips, then basal and interveinal chlorosis, marginal necrosis, distorted geometry, growing-tip death, and axillary branching developed.

At first calcium-deficiency symptom expression, most-recent-mature leaves contained 0.39% calcium dry weight compared with 3.73% in controls, but the one-cultivar silica-sand withholding experiment does not establish a universal tissue threshold or field sequence.

Iron-withheld T1 plants first developed symptoms after nine weeks: slight marginal yellowing, especially near leaflet bases, progressed to interveinal chlorosis on growing-tip and newly expanding leaves and spread through the upper half while middle and lower foliage remained healthy dark green.

At first iron-deficiency symptom expression, iron-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 60.08 mg/kg iron compared with 111.75 mg/kg in controls, 46% lower under the experiment conditions; biomass did not differ significantly from the control at that harvest.
Figure 6 is a CC BY 4.0 composite with initial, intermediate, and advanced iron-deficiency images in its left column and zinc-deficiency images in its right column.

Manganese-withheld T1 plants developed bright-yellow netted interveinal chlorosis on upper and central foliage after six weeks; the netting began near leaflet midribs, spread toward margins, retained green veins, and later developed small tan necrotic regions.

At first manganese-deficiency symptom expression, manganese-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 7.56 mg/kg manganese compared with 29.40 mg/kg in controls, 74% lower under the experiment conditions; dry biomass did not differ significantly at that harvest.

The control manganese concentration was itself below the cited general crop survey range, and the study used one cultivar in silica sand with complete withholding, so neither treatment value is a universal Cannabis diagnostic threshold.

Figure 4 is a CC BY 4.0 composite showing initial, intermediate, and advanced manganese-, boron-, and copper-deficiency phenotypes in Cannabis sativa T1; only its left column represents manganese deficiency.

Copper-withheld T1 plants first developed visible symptoms after nine weeks, beginning with slight whole-plant stunting and mild distortion of newer and expanding leaves, especially narrowed and slightly yellow leaflet bases.

As copper-withholding symptoms advanced, basal narrowing and distortion intensified, marginal interveinal chlorosis developed, and the whole leaf progressed to fine interveinal chlorosis with slightly inward- and downward-curled margins and reduced turgidity.

At first copper-deficiency symptom expression, copper-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 1.41 mg/kg copper compared with 4.65 mg/kg in controls, 70% lower under the experiment conditions; treated plants produced 45% less biomass.

The control copper concentration of 4.65 mg/kg was itself slightly below the general crop survey range cited by the authors, and the one-cultivar complete-withholding result does not establish a universal Cannabis threshold.

The published Figure 4 caption and column labels identify initial, intermediate, and advanced copper-deficiency panels in the right column, although the copper subsection text cites Figure 5; Figure 5 is captioned as manganese- and boron-toxicity progression, so this source-level numbering inconsistency must remain attached to copper panel review.

Magnesium-withheld T1 plants first developed slight interveinal yellowing on lower and older foliage after seven weeks; the contrast between green veins and yellow interveinal tissue intensified and some regions became necrotic.

At first magnesium-deficiency symptom expression, magnesium-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 0.12% magnesium compared with 0.61% in controls, 80% lower under the experiment conditions; biomass did not differ significantly at that harvest.

Figure 3 is a CC BY 4.0 composite showing initial, intermediate, and advanced sulfur-, magnesium-, and potassium-deficiency phenotypes in Cannabis sativa T1; only its center column represents magnesium deficiency.

Potassium-withheld T1 plants first developed yellowing at leaflet margins and saw-tooth serrations on lower and older foliage after nine weeks; yellowing intensified and moved inward toward the midrib, followed by tan necrosis concentrated along serrated margins.

At first potassium-deficiency symptom expression, potassium-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 0.41% potassium compared with 2.85% in controls, 86% lower under the experiment conditions; treated plants produced 27% less biomass.

Figure 3 is a CC BY 4.0 composite whose right column shows initial, intermediate, and advanced potassium-deficiency phenotypes; the sulfur and magnesium columns are separate diagnoses and the asset is indexed once under the magnesium record to avoid duplicate media hashes.

Zinc-withheld T1 plants first developed symptoms after nine weeks as marginal yellowing on newer and expanding leaves, concentrated along leaflet margins and toothed portions; tan, irregularly shaped marginal necrosis developed as the disorder progressed.

At first zinc-deficiency symptom expression, zinc-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 10.70 mg/kg zinc compared with 25.33 mg/kg in controls, 58% lower under the experiment conditions; biomass did not differ significantly from the control at that harvest.

Sulfur-withheld T1 plants first developed symptoms after seven weeks as slight overall yellowing, especially in the middle canopy and at leaflet bases; yellowing intensified at leaflet bases and on newly expanding leaves, then advanced to very pale yellow tissue around the midrib and leaflet bases.

At first sulfur-deficiency symptom expression, sulfur-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 0.11% sulfur compared with 0.41% in controls, 73% lower under the experiment conditions; biomass did not differ significantly from the control at that harvest.

name: Iron deficiency
summary: A context-dependent iron-status disorder that produced upper-canopy, new-leaf interveinal chlorosis in a controlled vegetative T1 study, but no visible syndrome in a controlled flowering Gelato 29 study despite substantially lower foliar iron. Images can support a differential, but cannot confirm or exclude iron deficiency.
affectedParts: growing tip and newly expanding leaves
leaflet margins and bases during the controlled early sequence
middle and lower foliage as distribution controls
roots and root zone for availability checks
stages: vegetative evidence from a transplant-onward withholding experiment
flowering evidence from a symptom-negative 7.5-week withholding experiment
indicators: Slight marginal yellowing, especially near leaflet bases, was the first controlled-study sign
Interveinal chlorosis develops on new and expanding leaves while veins remain relatively greener
Paling spreads through the upper half and is most apparent at the growing tip
Middle and lower foliage can remain healthy dark green during the vegetative controlled-study sequence
Serial upper-canopy images show progression rather than a fixed camera, lighting, or exposure artifact
Low foliar iron can occur with no visible syndrome, so a normal-looking canopy does not exclude inadequate iron status
exclusions: Older leaves are affected first with sharply interveinal chlorosis, favoring magnesium rather than the controlled iron sequence
Uniform lower-leaf yellowing or normal late-flower fade explains the pattern better
Chlorosis maps only to the lamp-facing canopy, a hot spot, bleaching, or a recorded heat or light event
Fine stippling, silver scars, webbing, eggs, mites, thrips, or fecal spots are found on magnified inspection
Mosaic, distortion, vein clearing, stunting, or laboratory evidence supports a virus, viroid, or other pathogen
Damage maps to spray droplets, residue, rubbing points, or another documented contact exposure
A stable cultivar pattern or sector follows the same tissue boundaries without progressive chlorosis
Root decay, saturation, hypoxia, abnormal temperature, salinity, pH, or irrigation history explains impaired uptake
Appropriately sampled tissue and root-zone testing support manganese, zinc, sulfur, nitrogen, calcium, or another diagnosis more strongly

progression.description: In flowering Gelato 29, foliar iron fell below half the control value without a visible syndrome during the 7.5-week treatment; absence of chlorosis is therefore not an exclusion test.
After nine weeks of iron withholding from transplant in Cannabis sativa T1, new upper foliage showed slight marginal yellowing, especially near leaflet bases.
New and expanding leaves at the growing tip developed interveinal chlorosis while middle and lower foliage remained healthy dark green.
Interveinal chlorosis spread through the upper half and remained especially prominent around the growing tip.
Track the color and expansion of subsequent leaves and the rate of new injury; old chlorotic tissue is not a clean visual measure of recovery.

lookAlikes: Nitrogen deficiency or normal late-flower senescence
Waterlogging, root-zone hypoxia, or root disease
Broad mite, spider mite, or thrips injury
Camera white-balance, exposure, or grow-light color shift
confirmation: Keep symptom-only image and video labels at low confidence: neither upper chlorosis nor a visually normal canopy confirms or excludes iron deficiency.

Capture serial whole-plant and matched upper-, middle-, and lower-canopy views, plus new and mature leaves on both surfaces, under neutral repeatable lighting with scale, leaf node, physiological age, and a healthy same-cultivar reference.

Record cultivar, stage, fertilizer iron concentration and chelate or formulation, source-water iron and alkalinity, irrigation history, substrate or solution type, and recent environmental or product changes.
Measure root-zone pH, EC, water content, temperature, drainage, and oxygenation as appropriate to the system, and inspect washed roots for decay or restricted growth before changing iron supply.

Submit correctly positioned leaf tissue and, where appropriate, solution, substrate, soil, or water samples to an agricultural or plant diagnostic laboratory; interpret iron and competing nutrients using crop-, organ-, stage-, and method-appropriate references.
Inspect both leaf surfaces and growing tips with magnification and use a plant diagnostic laboratory when arthropods, root disease, viruses, viroids, or other pathogens remain plausible.
Use subsequent new-leaf response only as supporting evidence; improvement after correcting an identified cause does not retroactively make the original image a ground-truth iron-deficiency sample.
immediateActions: Mark the plant and preserve pre-treatment serial images, feed and irrigation records, root-zone measurements, and representative tissue before changing nutrition.
Correct documented pH, salinity, saturation, temperature, oxygenation, or root-health problems before assuming the iron concentration is inadequate.
Avoid adding iron or changing chelates from color alone, especially when manganese, zinc, sulfur, pests, pathogens, or a lighting artifact have not been excluded.
correctivePlan: When analytical and production records support inadequate iron supply or availability and roots are functional, restore a balanced crop- and system-appropriate iron program gradually under current local agronomic guidance.
Track subsequent leaves, root growth, root-zone measurements, and follow-up tissue results; do not judge correction solely by old chlorotic leaves.
If iron status is adequate or the pattern continues, reopen manganese, zinc, sulfur, magnesium, root disease, arthropod, pathogen, light, heat, exposure, and genetic differentials.
prevention: Record the iron source, chelate or formulation, complete fertilizer composition, source-water chemistry, pH, EC, and irrigation conditions against plant and media identifiers.
Use routine same-position tissue sampling and production-system-appropriate root-zone or soil testing before visible injury.
Maintain healthy same-cultivar visual references and neutral-light serial imaging of upper, middle, and lower canopy positions.
warnings: The visible sequence came from one Cannabis sativa T1 cultivar grown in silica sand with iron withheld from transplant; nine weeks, 60.08 mg/kg tissue iron, and the pictured appearance are experiment-specific, not universal diagnostic thresholds.

A separate flowering study found no visible iron-deficiency symptoms in three Gelato 29 plants despite foliar iron below half the control value; symptom absence cannot rule out inadequate iron status, and this small experiment does not prove that flowering Cannabis never develops visible symptoms.
The controlled vegetative study found no significant biomass difference at the symptom-onset harvest, so visual severity must not be converted into a universal yield-loss estimate.
Upper interveinal chlorosis is shared by other nutritional, root-zone, biotic, environmental, genetic, and imaging conditions and is not image-only ground truth.

The CC BY figure contains both iron- and zinc-deficiency columns and three severity rows; it is excluded from automated training until panels are bounded, class- and stage-annotated, scientifically reviewed, and assigned a leakage-safe split.
All symptom-only and symptom-negative samples require human review and linked analytical evidence before ground-truth use.

sources.title: Foliar Symptomology, Nutrient Content, Yield, and Secondary Metabolite Variability of Cannabis Grown Hydroponically with Different Single-Element Nutrient Deficiencies
supportedClaims: Three Gelato 29 plants per treatment were grown in aerated deep-water culture; single-element withholding began with the switch to a 12-hour flowering photoperiod, plants were examined daily and photographed weekly, and upper- and lower-canopy foliage was laboratory analyzed at symptom onset.
Nitrogen-withheld plants showed reduced vegetative expansion before foliar symptoms; during week three, very slight yellowing began at leaflet tips of lower-canopy fan leaves.

By week four, most fan leaves in the lower two-thirds were yellowing; chlorosis was initially strongest between veins before broad whole-leaf yellowing, and severity within leaflets progressed from base toward tip.

By week five, nearly all fan leaves were yellow with severity increasing from bottom to top; petioles became red-brown, some fan leaves browned and senesced, stems began yellowing, and sugar-leaf chlorosis began.

By weeks six and seven, most fan leaves had senesced, older and lower-position sugar leaves progressively yellowed or browned, and stems became brown; the authors considered this prolonged severe endpoint commercially damaging.

At symptom onset, upper- and lower-canopy foliar nitrogen concentrations did not differ and overlapped the control and other treatments, illustrating limitations of a single tissue analysis later in production.

Healthy control plants developed lower-fan-leaf chlorosis in weeks six through eight despite adequate nutrient solution and foliar concentrations, demonstrating that natural late-flower senescence can visually confound nitrogen deficiency.

Nitrogen-withheld plants had 73% less aboveground vegetative fresh mass and approximately 72% less fresh inflorescence mass than controls under this three-plant treatment; these are experiment-specific loss estimates, not universal predictions.

Figure 2 is a CC BY 4.0 four-panel flowering-stage nitrogen-deficiency progression spanning lower-canopy onset, detached fan-leaf severity, canopy distribution, fan-leaf senescence, stem color, and beginning sugar-leaf chlorosis.

In the calcium-withheld treatment, lower fan leaves developed interveinal spots with yellow rings and necrotic brown centers in week three; by week four symptoms occupied mostly the lower two-thirds and were concentrated near leaflet margins and tips.

By week five, spots coalesced into irregular marginal necrosis, serration points browned, injury moved upward into younger fan and sugar leaves, and upper fan-leaf tips curled upward; by week six most fan and sugar leaves were affected.

The flowering-stage lower-leaf onset differed markedly from the vegetative-stage T1 study and from the usual expectation for an immobile nutrient; lower-canopy foliage also contained almost three times the calcium of upper-canopy foliage at symptom onset.

Calcium-withheld plants averaged 621 g fresh inflorescence mass compared with 1110 g in controls under this three-plant-per-treatment experiment; those values do not establish a universal yield-loss estimate.
Figure 5 is a CC BY 4.0 five-panel Cannabis calcium-deficiency progression from week-three spotting through widespread marginal necrosis and upward curling in week six.

Despite foliar iron concentrations less than half those of controls, iron-withheld flowering Gelato 29 plants showed no visible deficiency symptoms and no significant aboveground biomass reduction by the end of the 7.5-week treatment.

The symptom-negative flowering result came from three plants in one cultivar and one deep-water-culture experiment; it demonstrates that absence of a visible syndrome cannot exclude inadequate iron status, not that flowering Cannabis never shows iron-deficiency symptoms.

In sulfur-withheld flowering Gelato 29, recently developed upper sugar leaves yellowed in week four; by week five upper fan leaves angled upward and lower fan leaves developed interveinal chlorosis from midrib to margins, later progressing through fan leaves to total yellowing and senescence while early sugar-leaf chlorosis changed little except for browned tips and marginal teeth.

Sulfur-withheld foliage had substantially lower sulfur than all other treatments, with no significant upper-versus-lower canopy concentration difference; inflorescence yield was 34% lower than control while vegetative biomass, root biomass, and cannabinoid concentrations showed no major effect in the three-plant treatment.

Figure 7 is a CC BY 4.0 four-panel sulfur-deficiency progression showing younger sugar-leaf yellowing, upward-angled upper fan leaves, a fan-leaf chlorosis sequence, and the later whole-plant distribution.

The flowering study contrasted with the vegetative T1 study in first described canopy location and progression direction, and cautioned that late-flower nutrient symptomology can be confounded with natural foliar senescence.

No visually obvious manganese-deficiency signs developed in the manganese-withheld flowering Gelato 29 plants; at week seven their apical inflorescences were similar to controls in size, shape, and color, and the treatment did not reduce biomass or cannabinoid concentrations.

At harvest, manganese-withheld upper-canopy foliage was extremely low in manganese relative to lower-canopy foliage and other treatments, yet the plants remained visually similar to controls, so a symptom-negative image cannot exclude low manganese status.

The authors state that nutrient diagnosis should integrate fertilizer and leachate composition, symptomology, and strategically timed and positioned foliar analysis because cultivar, environment, maturity, and sample location affect tissue concentrations.

Figure 9 is a CC BY 4.0 side-by-side comparison of manganese-withheld and control apical inflorescences during week seven; it is a controlled symptom-negative reference rather than a visible-deficiency example.

Magnesium-withheld flowering Gelato 29 plants had no visible symptoms for three weeks; mild interveinal chlorosis began on lower fan leaves in week four between the midrib and margins, then rapidly predominated on smaller, younger fan leaves while older fan leaves and inflorescence sugar leaves were less affected.

Severely affected flowering leaves developed interveinal necrosis that increased from leaflet bases toward tips; by week five symptoms were widespread except at apical inflorescences, and by week six most smaller fan leaves and sugar leaves were yellow except at the midrib and extreme margins while some older fan leaves remained largely unaffected.

At symptom onset, lower-canopy foliage in the magnesium-withheld treatment contained about one-third the magnesium of upper-canopy foliage; the treatment averaged 748 g fresh inflorescence mass versus 1110 g in controls, approximately 30% lower in this three-plant-per-treatment experiment, while cannabinoid concentrations were not significantly affected.

Figure 6 is a CC BY 4.0 five-panel flowering-stage magnesium-deficiency progression spanning the first mild lower-fan-leaf chlorosis, whole-plant distribution, detached-leaf severity, inflorescence context, and advanced whole-plant symptoms.

Potassium-withheld flowering Gelato 29 plants had no visible symptoms for two weeks; in week three, larger sugar leaves developed dark-brown lesions around secondary branch veins, while lower fan leaves developed lighter browning at leaflet tips and marginal teeth one week later.

By week five both potassium-deficiency pathways appeared on the same plant: sugar-leaf lesions predominated near the top and fan-leaf injury was strongest in the middle third, with light-brown fan-leaf injury moving inward especially through interveinal tissue.

By week six, green tissue was largely limited to inflorescences, sugar-leaf midribs, and some lower fan leaves; by week seven most non-inflorescence leaves were brown, curled, and dry, and some inflorescence leaves developed tip browning.

Potassium-withheld plants averaged 535 g fresh inflorescence mass compared with 1110 g in controls and had the second-lowest root dry mass in this three-plant-per-treatment experiment; higher THCA concentration did not offset the lower plant-level yield.
Figure 4 is a CC BY 4.0 four-panel flowering-stage potassium-deficiency progression showing distinct sugar-leaf and fan-leaf symptoms at week four and their middle-canopy distribution by week five.

name: Potassium deficiency
summary: A stage- and leaf-type-dependent potassium-status disorder. Controlled vegetative plants developed older-leaf serration and margin yellowing followed by inward tan necrosis, while flowering plants showed an earlier sugar-leaf lesion pathway and a later fan-leaf tip-and-margin pathway. Edge burn alone is nonspecific and requires analytical and root-zone confirmation.
affectedParts: lower and older foliage in the vegetative T1 sequence
larger sugar leaves near flowering inflorescences
secondary branch veins within sugar leaves
lower fan-leaf tips and marginal teeth
middle-canopy fan leaves during flowering progression
interveinal fan-leaf tissue as browning expands inward
roots and root zone for availability checks
indicators: Burned leaf edges
Rust or tan spotting
Weak stems
Older leaves affected first
Vegetative T1 plants begin with yellowing along lower and older leaflet margins, especially saw-tooth serrations
Vegetative marginal yellowing intensifies and advances inward toward the midrib before tan marginal necrosis develops
Flowering sugar leaves can develop dark-brown lesions surrounding secondary branch veins before fan-leaf symptoms appear
Flowering lower fan leaves develop lighter browning at leaflet tips and marginal teeth
By week five, sugar-leaf injury predominates near the top while fan-leaf injury is strongest in the middle third
Advanced fan-leaf browning extends inward through interveinal tissue and leaves become curled and dry
A widespread serial pattern affects many leaves and is linked to low potassium in correctly positioned tissue and nutrient or root-zone evidence
exclusions: Only leaf tips burned immediately after a high-EC feed or fertilizer event and broad multi-ion salinity explains the pattern
Injury is confined to the hottest or brightest canopy face and measured light or leaf temperature explains it
Marginal chlorosis and necrosis are paired with elevated tissue boron or a verified boron exposure source
Interveinal yellowing retains strongly green veins without a serration-first pattern and magnesium evidence is stronger
Uniform yellowing follows nitrogen deficiency, sulfur deficiency, or normal late-flower senescence more closely
Dark sugar-leaf lesions are discrete, expanding, water-soaked, haloed, or associated with fungal structures or a positive laboratory pathogen result
Fine stippling, silver scars, webbing, eggs, mites, thrips, chewing, frass, or fecal spots are present
Damage follows a foliar spray, residue, fan abrasion, trellis contact, pruning, or another documented local exposure
