useLimitations: Multi-panel plant-and-organism figure; reference-only as a whole image.
Do not infer cannabis aphid from yellowing, wilting, or leaf distortion without directly observing aphids or other insect evidence.
Keep training-ineligible until panel-level source grouping and crop review are complete.

name: Fungus gnats / root-feeding Bradysia larvae
summary: A greenhouse root-zone pest complex in which adult fungus gnats are a population cue and dark-headed, translucent Bradysia larvae may feed on fine roots or young plant material. Hemp evidence supports the association but not a unique visual syndrome: a causal injury label requires plant-linked larvae, compatible root injury, and independent checks for wet-root disorders and pathogens.
affectedParts: seed, cutting base, and lower stem in susceptible propagation material
yellow sticky cards near the medium
indicators: Small, delicate, dark-bodied adults with long legs and antennae repeatedly emerge from or rest near the same plant's moist growing medium; a Y-shaped wing vein supports fungus gnat over shore fly when image resolution permits
Small translucent-to-white, slender, legless larvae with a distinct dark or black head capsule are found in the growing medium or at the root interface
Plant-linked larvae occur beside damaged fine roots, root hairs, a seed or cutting base, or lower-stem tissue in the same traceable plant
Dated low-position sticky-card or emergence observations show repeated adult activity near the affected container, but this is a population cue rather than proof of feeding injury
The affected zone has persistent surface moisture, algae, decomposing plant material, or poor drainage compatible with fungus-gnat habitat; habitat alone is not a positive label
Stunting, poor growth, yellowing, wilt, or seedling/cutting loss occurs only as a secondary supporting observation after larvae and root-zone injury have been documented
Repeated potato-piece or direct medium inspection recovers characteristic larvae and preserves the plant, container, location, and inspection interval
Root decline is mapped separately from Pythium, Fusarium, Rhizoctonia, hypoxia, pH, EC, drought, restriction, and nematode evidence because fungus gnats can coexist with those conditions
exclusions: Repeated, documented sticky-card, potato-piece, medium, and root inspection finds no compatible adults or dark-headed larvae
Adults are stout, short-antennaed shore flies with five pale wing spots rather than delicate long-legged gnats with a Y-shaped wing vein
Pear-shaped root-associated aphids, cornicles, aphid nymphs, or plant-linked alates establish rice root aphid rather than a fly larva
Observed organisms are springtails, soil mites, thrips, whiteflies, nematodes, or other arthropods without Bradysia-compatible morphology
Pythium, Fusarium, Rhizoctonia, or another root pathogen is confirmed while larval evidence is absent or insufficient to support a contributing fungus-gnat label
Measured hypoxia or waterlogging, drought, root binding, pH, EC, salinity, or nutrient evidence fully explains the root and canopy pattern without linked larvae
A sticky-card capture, flying-adult silhouette, dark head capsule, or generic larva alone cannot establish Bradysia species, plant injury, or causal severity
Detached roots, stock imagery, generated media, vendor material, anecdotes, forum posts, or specimens that cannot be linked to the affected plant are excluded from confirmed labels

progression.description: Delicate adults appear near moist media or on low sticky cards. Their presence triggers root-zone inspection but does not establish plant injury.
Immature stages develop in moist organic media; dark-headed translucent larvae become detectable by direct inspection or potato-piece monitoring.
Larvae are documented at the same plant's fine roots, root hairs, seed, cutting base, or lower-stem tissue with compatible localized injury.
Susceptible seedlings, cuttings, or plants may show poor growth, stunting, yellowing, wilt, or loss, but these canopy responses remain nonspecific.
Feeding and pathogen interactions may coexist as root function deteriorates. Cross-crop life-cycle timing must not be treated as a universal Cannabis progression clock.

lookAlikes: Springtails, soil mites, or other medium fauna
Thrips or whitefly adults on sticky cards
Pythium or another oomycete root rot
Root-zone pH, EC, salinity, or nutrient disorder
confirmation: Capture a traceable same-plant sequence: whole plant, labeled container, medium surface, low sticky card, exposed root ball, washed representative roots, and larval macro or microscope views with a scale.
Place dated sticky cards close to the medium and record repeated adult activity by plant and location; keep adult counts as a scouting cue, not a causal injury label.
Use standardized potato-piece and direct medium inspections, recording placement, exposure interval, plant ID, container, medium, moisture, and the number and location of recovered larvae.

Image larvae at sufficient resolution to show the legless translucent body and dark head capsule; image adult antennae, body form, and Y-shaped wing vein when possible, and explicitly exclude shore flies.
Map larval position against fine-root, root-hair, seed, cutting-base, or lower-stem injury in the same plant and include a similarly managed unaffected comparator where available.
Record root color, firmness, odor, moisture or oxygen status, pH, EC, drainage, root restriction, irrigation history, and laboratory pathogen or nematode results when root decline is present.

Require plant-linked larvae plus compatible injury for a confirmed injury label; require qualified entomological or validated molecular work for a species-level Bradysia label, and route adult-only, sticky-card-only, larva-only, unlinked-root, mixed-organism, low-resolution, non-Cannabis, stock, vendor, generated, anecdotal, forum, and unverified samples to human review.
immediateActions: Preserve plant-linked adult, larval, medium, and root evidence before treatment, root washing, or irrigation changes.
Inspect moisture, drainage, algae, decomposing debris, propagation material, and nearby containers using the same documented protocol.
Keep suspected pathogen or abiotic root-zone problems as separate concurrent labels until each has been evaluated.
correctivePlan: Use sanitation, moisture and drainage correction, physical or biological controls, and other locally legal integrated measures appropriate to the confirmed organism and production system.
Track adults and larvae separately during follow-up; fewer adults alone do not prove that larvae or root injury have resolved.
If root or canopy decline continues after larval pressure falls, continue the independent pathogen, irrigation, pH, EC, salinity, nutrition, and root-restriction workup.
prevention: Avoid chronic surface wetness while maintaining crop-appropriate root hydration and drainage.
Remove algae, decomposing roots, discarded media, and plant debris that support development without disturbing verified evidence before documentation.
Inspect incoming media, clones, rooted cuttings, and propagation areas, and use dated low-position monitoring before symptoms appear.
Retain plant- and location-specific records so recurring adults can be connected to direct larval and root inspections rather than treated as facility-wide injury proof.
warnings: Photo or video alone is capped at low confidence because adult fungus gnats, wet media, yellowing, wilt, and stunting do not prove that larvae caused plant injury.
A few adults or a sticky-card capture establish neither a plant link nor economic injury; the same-plant root zone must be inspected.

The University of Tennessee guide reports greenhouse-hemp root feeding and possible increased root-disease incidence but also identifies major hemp arthropod knowledge gaps; it does not supply a universal symptom, severity, threshold, or species diagnosis.

Cloyd and the Pacific Northwest guidance provide cross-crop greenhouse biology and morphology. Their host response and timing details must not be universalized to Cannabis cultivars or production systems.
Pathogen carriage or coexistence does not prove that fungus gnats caused a specific infection; pathogen and abiotic root-zone evidence must be labeled and confirmed independently.
No licensed, plant-linked Cannabis injury progression, verified diagnostic video, or species-vouchered Cannabis media is included, and no media is eligible for automated training.

sources.title: Ecology of Fungus Gnats (Bradysia spp.) in Greenhouse Production Systems Associated with Disease-Interactions and Alternative Management Strategies
supportedClaims: Bradysia fungus gnats are important greenhouse horticultural pests whose larvae feed on roots and may contribute to disease interactions.

The review describes adults as weak, delicate fliers associated with moist growing media and larvae as translucent to white, legless, dark-headed organisms in the medium; these organism traits are more useful than nonspecific canopy decline.

Larval feeding can damage roots and young plant material, while fungus gnats can participate in pathogen interactions; finding one component does not establish that it caused every observed root or canopy symptom.

This is cross-crop greenhouse evidence rather than Cannabis-specific symptom validation, so plant yellowing or stunting cannot identify fungus gnats without observing adults, larvae, or other root-zone evidence.

sources.title: Fungus Gnats fact sheet
sources.publisher: University of New Hampshire Cooperative Extension
supportedClaims: Greenhouse fungus-gnat larvae can feed on roots or inside stems and may be associated with poor plant growth, yellowing, and stunting.
Adults around moist growing media are a useful inspection cue, but above-ground plant symptoms remain nonspecific.

sources.title: Hemp Disease and Pest Management
supportedClaims: University of Tennessee Extension reports fungus-gnat larvae as a root-feeding pest of hemp grown under greenhouse conditions and states that they may increase root-disease incidence.

The guide also states that much remains unknown about arthropod pests in hemp; its report supports a greenhouse-hemp association but not a universal symptom, damage threshold, species label, or causal attribution from an adult capture alone.

sources.title: Greenhouse ornamental—Fungus gnat
supportedClaims: Institutional greenhouse guidance describes fungus-gnat larvae as small, white, legless maggots with black head capsules and adults as delicate, black-bodied flies with long legs and antennae.
A Y-shaped wing vein helps distinguish adult fungus gnats from shore flies, which are stouter, have short antennae, and have five white wing spots.

Larvae feed on decaying material and roots, high populations can kill seedlings, and both larvae and adults may move pathogen spores; these cross-crop statements do not prove Cannabis injury in a particular image.
Yellow sticky cards can monitor adults, potato pieces can monitor larvae, and roots of poorly performing plants should be inspected directly; wet conditions and poor drainage favor populations.
The page gives greenhouse life-stage timings, but those values are context-dependent cross-crop guidance and must not be treated as universal Cannabis progression intervals.

name: Rice root aphid on cannabis
summary: A primarily root-associated aphid of indoor Cannabis in North America. Direct, plant-linked root-colony evidence supports the pest class, while generalized decline, lower-leaf off-coloration, flying aphids, and sticky-card captures remain low-specificity cues. Species confirmation requires suitable intact specimens and expert morphology; root disease and irrigation stress must be evaluated independently.
affectedParts: stems and foliage during brief alate dispersal
upper-leaf trichomes that may trap dead alates
whole canopy for nonspecific secondary response
stages: post-harvest root system with living roots
indoor soil, aeroponic, coconut-coir, and rockwool production
indicators: Aphid colonies are visible on cannabis roots after careful root-zone inspection
Winged aphids emerge from or cluster around the growing medium while root colonies are present
Root-associated aphids are documented while stems and leaf undersides lack the typical cannabis-aphid colony pattern

Small temporary colonies may occur on stems or foliage after alates colonize a plant, but most observed offspring move downward toward roots and large persistent foliar colonies are atypical in the primary Cannabis account.
Dead alate aphids caught on upper-leaf hairs or low sticky cards can trigger root-zone inspection but cannot by themselves identify the infested plant or prove an active root colony.

Heavy infestation may coincide with generalized decline, reduced growth rate, or lower-leaf off-coloration; these canopy signs are supporting context only and have no unique rice-root-aphid morphology.
Root-associated aphids occur while leaf undersides, petioles, and stems lack the sustained foliar-colony pattern expected for cannabis aphid.
Repeated observations show colony or alate abundance changing on the same tagged plant; unrelated before-and-after images are not a progression series.
exclusions: Representative intact roots from the symptomatic plant are repeatedly inspected without aphids, cast skins, or a plausible colony while another measured cause explains the decline.
Dense persistent aphid colonies occupy stems, petioles, or leaf undersides and suitable morphology supports cannabis aphid or another foliar aphid.
A yellow sticky card contains a dark winged insect but the root zone is not linked, the specimen is too small for aphid morphology, or fungus gnats and other flyers are mixed on the card.
Small dark flies plus translucent, dark-headed larvae in moist media support fungus gnats rather than root aphids.
Springtails, soil mites, shore flies, thrips, whiteflies, or other root-zone arthropods are identified from the observed organisms.
Brown, slimy, sloughed, or odorous roots occur without plant-linked aphids and oomycete testing or root-zone oxygen evidence supports Pythium or hypoxia.
Root galls, cysts, females, or egg masses plus nematode evidence support root-knot nematodes rather than aphid feeding.
Canopy decline follows a measured pH, EC, moisture, temperature, root-restriction, nutrient, vascular, or pathogen pattern and the insects are absent or incidental.

progression.description: Record incoming plant lot, root condition, production medium, nearby crop age, sticky-card counts, and matched apparently unaffected plants before a colony is detected.
Aphids remain largely hidden on roots or near the stem base; canopy appearance may still be normal and canopy-only scouting can miss the infestation.
More root-associated nymphs, adults, and cast skins become visible across the tagged root zone; quantify inspected root area and organism counts instead of inferring density from one macro image.
Winged females may emerge from soil, particularly as Cannabis flowers or approaches maturity, and may appear on stems, foliage, trichomes, or low sticky cards before offspring move toward roots.

General decline, slower growth, or lower-leaf off-coloration may accompany high numbers, but root decay, pathogen involvement, yield loss, and causality remain separate questions requiring matched measurements.

lookAlikes: Bird cherry-oat aphid or another Rhopalosiphum species
Thrips or whitefly alates on sticky cards
Pythium or another oomycete root rot
Root binding, pH stress, or salinity / high EC
confirmation: Capture a traceable sequence from the same plant: whole canopy, labeled container and medium surface, root crown, representative exposed roots, colony overview, and macro or microscope views with a scale.

Record plant ID, cultivar, stage, production system, source lot, onset date, irrigation and root-zone history, root condition, inspected root area, aphid counts, alate counts, and sticky-card position and date.
Preserve intact apterous adults and representative alates in a manner suitable for entomological identification; do not rely on color, a single nymph, or a low-resolution sticky-card silhouette.
Use a qualified entomologist and appropriate morphological keys or validated molecular identification when a species-level Rhopalosiphum rufiabdominale label is required.
Inspect leaf undersides, petioles, and stems for sustained cannabis-aphid colonies, and compare fungus-gnat adults and larvae when flyers are the initial cue.

Assess root color, firmness, odor, oxygen/moisture status, pH, EC, root restriction, and representative pathogen or nematode samples independently; finding aphids does not prove they caused every root or canopy symptom.

Keep canopy-only, damage-only, sticky-card-only, alate-only, organism-only, unlinked-root, mixed-arthropod, low-resolution, stock, vendor, generated, anecdotal, forum, and unverified observations out of the confirmed class and route them to human review.
immediateActions: Preserve plant-linked root and insect evidence before treatment or destructive root washing.
Inspect nearby plants and incoming propagation lots using the same root-zone protocol and isolate confirmed infestations where practical.
Record root disease and irrigation evidence separately so concurrent problems are not collapsed into one label.
correctivePlan: Use an integrated root-zone pest-management response based on confirmed identity, population, production system, crop stage, and locally legal options.
Verify response by repeated plant-linked root inspection and alate counts; fewer flyers alone do not demonstrate that root colonies are absent.
If root or canopy decline continues after aphid numbers fall, continue the independent root-zone, nutrition, and pathogen workup.
prevention: Inspect roots of incoming clones, rooted cuttings, and retained mother material before integration.
Separate new plantings from older flowering or near-maturity plants that may be producing dispersing alates.
Use dated low-position sticky cards as an early cue while retaining scheduled direct root inspection as the confirmation method.
Avoid reusing containers or media with living roots from an infested crop without a validated sanitation process.
warnings: Photo or video alone cannot confirm rice root aphid to species; even a clear root-colony image needs a plant link and suitable organism evidence.
Generalized decline, slow growth, lower-leaf discoloration, and flying aphids are not unique symptoms and must not be used as ground truth without a documented root colony.
The primary Cannabis article states that increased pathogen susceptibility remains unconfirmed; root discoloration or decay must be labeled and tested independently.
The cited 2020 article and UNH guide reported indoor high-THC Cannabis associations and no North American outdoor-hemp records; that evidence gap does not prove outdoor infestation is impossible.

The existing CC BY 4.0 reference is one aeroponic root-crown figure. It remains training-ineligible pending source-group review and does not represent soil, coir, rockwool, cultivar, stage, geography, or severity diversity.
No verified diagnostic video or matched Cannabis progression series is included.

sources.title: Cannabis sativa as a Host of Rice Root Aphid (Hemiptera: Aphididae) in North America
sources.publisher: Oxford University Press on behalf of the Entomological Society of America
supportedClaims: Indoor Cannabis sativa has emerged as a common North American host of rice root aphid, Rhopalosiphum rufiabdominale.

The authors observed rice root aphid in Cannabis soil, aeroponic, coconut-coir, and rockwool systems, but had not found it in outdoor hemp plantings; the outdoor evidence gap must not be converted into an absence claim.

In indoor Cannabis the aphid is almost entirely root-associated; alate females can emerge from soil especially during flowering and near maturity, colonize new plants, and produce young on stems or foliage before most offspring migrate downward.
Dead alates trapped on upper-leaf hairs can be an early facility-level cue, but a sticky-card or canopy alate is not plant-linked confirmation of a root colony.
Heavy Cannabis infestations were associated with generalized decline, slower growth, and possible lower-leaf off-coloration, none of which is unique to rice root aphid.
The article explicitly states that a Cannabis association with increased pathogen susceptibility still requires confirmation; root discoloration or decay must therefore be diagnosed independently.

sources.title: Hemp Pests in New Hampshire
sources.organization: University of New Hampshire Cooperative Extension
sources.publisher: University of New Hampshire Cooperative Extension
supportedClaims: UNH Extension associates Rhopalosiphum rufiabdominale with indoor Cannabis sativa grown as a high-THC crop and reports observations from indoor cultivation across the United States.

The institutional guide reported no North American outdoor-hemp records and identified hemp soil-insect research as a gap; this supports an indoor-production scope flag rather than proof that outdoor infestation is impossible.

useLimitations: Reference-only until source-group and panel-level training review are complete.
The presence of rice root aphids is visible; generalized canopy decline is not uniquely diagnostic of this pest.
Do not use this asset to infer root disease, nutrient status, or above-ground symptom severity.

name: Hemp witches’ broom (phytoplasma-associated)
scientificName: Candidatus Phytoplasma trifolii and other phytoplasmas
summary: A leafhopper-associated systemic syndrome in which cannabis can develop shortened nodes, clusters of proliferating axillary or apical shoots, stunting, small distorted leaves, chlorosis, mottling, and curling; the same visual pattern can involve Beet curly top virus, Spiroplasma citri, or mixed infection.
stages: field-grown leaf-bearing plants; cannabis-specific stage effects are not established
indicators: Clusters of excessive apical or axillary shoots forming a broom-like tip
Shortened internodes and compact branch clusters
Small, distorted, curled, or upward-rolled leaves
Leaf chlorosis with mottling or mosaic
Vein-bounded green islands on the upper leaf surface
Interveinal discoloration with a pale pustule-like appearance from below
Whole-plant stunting with abnormal branching
exclusions: Validated testing identifies Beet curly top virus without detecting phytoplasma in properly sampled tissue
Validated testing identifies Spiroplasma citri or another agent and does not detect phytoplasma
Microscopy confirms broad mites or hemp russet mites in the distorted growing tips
Abnormal branching follows deliberate topping or training and subsequent leaves remain normal
Distortion maps to documented herbicide or plant-growth-regulator exposure
Short internodes and branching remain stable in healthy clones without chlorosis, mottling, progressive distortion, or pathogen detection

progression.description: Leaves may curl, roll upward, mottle, become chlorotic, or develop vein-bounded green islands above with pale interveinal discoloration visible below.
Internodes shorten while apical or axillary shoots proliferate into compact highly branched clusters; leaves on affected branches may remain small and distorted and the plant may become stunted.

Primary cannabis reports document variable symptoms during the growing season but do not establish a universal order or rate. Capture the same plant serially and do not infer infection age from one image.

confirmation: Do not confirm phytoplasma from witches’ broom architecture, a photograph, video, or leafhopper observation.
Submit the most symptomatic young leaves with petioles to a plant diagnostic laboratory using that laboratory’s current sampling and shipping protocol; include a healthy comparator when requested.

Use a validated phytoplasma molecular assay followed by sequence or classification evidence when group-level identity matters; the Nevada report combined real-time PCR, nested 16S rRNA PCR, Sanger sequencing, BLASTn, and iPhyClassifier analysis.
Request a differential panel that includes Beet curly top virus and Spiroplasma citri because the three agents can produce overlapping symptoms and can occur together.

Record whole-plant architecture, both leaf surfaces, affected shoot position, field location, onset date, and serial change to preserve image and video context without treating those observations as proof.
immediateActions: Flag suspect plants and pause distribution of their cuttings pending laboratory results.
Scout nearby plants and leafhoppers while keeping vector presence separate from pathogen confirmation.
Keep all symptom-only images out of phytoplasma, Spiroplasma, and BCTV ground-truth classes.
correctivePlan: Base removal and vector-management decisions on laboratory results, production policy, and locally legal recommendations.
If phytoplasma is not detected, continue testing or differential review for BCTV, Spiroplasma citri, mites, chemical injury, and physiological causes.
Continue serial observation because one plant or branch can combine architecture, foliar color, and distortion differently over time.
prevention: Use tested and traceable propagation material.
Monitor leafhoppers and regional alerts without assuming every vector carries the same pathogen.
Control weed reservoirs and vectors only with locally appropriate, crop-legal practices.
warnings: Witches’ broom is a syndrome, not a species-level visual diagnosis.
Cannabis symptom overlap and documented mixed infections make image-only ground truth unsafe.
The three institutional photographs below are metadata-only license-review candidates: no reuse license is stated, so they are hidden and prohibited from automated training.
Cannabis-specific evidence does not establish a universal symptom order, cultivar response, or infection-to-symptom interval.

sources.title: First Report of ‘Candidatus Phytoplasma trifolii’ Associated with a Witches’ Broom Disease in Cannabis sativa in Nevada, U.S.A
supportedClaims: Symptomatic Nevada cannabis had leaf curling, mottling, chlorosis, witches’ broom, stunting, and shortened nodes.
Upper leaf surfaces showed vein-bounded green islands while lower surfaces showed interveinal discoloration with a pale pustule-like appearance.

Phytoplasma was detected from petioles of the most symptomatic leaves by 23S rRNA real-time PCR; nested 16S rRNA PCR, Sanger sequencing, BLASTn, and iPhyClassifier analysis supported identification near Candidatus Phytoplasma trifolii.

sources.title: Hemp Abnormal Growth Is Attributed to Mono-, Di-, or Tri-Infections of Spiroplasma citri, Candidatus Phytoplasma trifolii, and Beet Curly Top Virus
supportedClaims: Across 67 symptomatic Nevada hemp samples, abnormal growth included stunting, yellowing, excessive apical branching, witches’ broom clusters, upward leaf rolling, mottling, and mosaic.
Candidatus Phytoplasma trifolii was detected in 14 samples, Beet curly top virus in 57, and Spiroplasma citri in two; dual and triple infections occurred.

The overlapping syndrome cannot assign one causal agent visually, so diagnostic testing should consider phytoplasma, Spiroplasma citri, and Beet curly top virus rather than treating witches’ broom as a species-specific image label.

sources.title: Hemp (Cannabis sativa)-Witches’ Broom
sources.publisher: Oregon State University, Washington State University, and University of Idaho Extension
supportedClaims: Cannabis witches’ broom expression varies with the phytoplasma involved; typical plants are stunted with highly branched stems, axillary shoot proliferation, and small, distorted, chlorotic leaves.
Phytoplasmas are leafhopper-transmitted, regional pathogen types vary, and vector presence or symptoms alone do not identify the phytoplasma involved.
The three cannabis symptom photographs are credited to C. M. Ocamb, Oregon State University, 2022; the landing page states copyright but supplies no reuse license.

name: Root binding / container-restriction stress
summary: Container restriction is documented in hemp transplants, but canopy stress is nonspecific and roots touching a pot are not sufficient evidence. A defensible label requires plant-linked views of the intact root ball, repeatable boundary-following deformation or dense matting, and exclusion of dry-center irrigation failure, salinity, hypoxia, transplant injury, nematodes, and root disease.
affectedParts: crown and lower stem for exclusions
indicators: Multiple roots follow the container wall or bottom in repeated arcs, coils, or a dense boundary mat rather than extending radially through available substrate.
The extracted intact root mass retains the container geometry and shows a tight root-dominant perimeter across more than one face; one exposed root or a cohesive nursery root ball is insufficient.

The root-ball center and perimeter differ visibly in moisture after a documented irrigation event, consistent with preferential flow or incomplete wetting; this supports a water-delivery mechanism but is not specific to root binding.
A plant-linked whole-canopy comparison may show reduced expansion or vigor relative to a matched same-cultivar, same-age, same-zone control, but canopy appearance is secondary evidence only.
In field-transplanted hemp, the original root architecture may remain constrained after transplant and poor establishment can coexist with secondary Fusarium or Pythium infection.

Time-matched root views show increasing wall-following deflection or matting before any post-transplant establishment failure, preserving the temporal link between container occupancy and later stress.
exclusions: Do not label a plant from canopy stunting, wilt, chlorosis, marginal browning, or reduced vigor without a plant-linked intact root-ball inspection.
Do not treat a small container, roots visible at drainage holes, one perimeter root, or normal root-ball cohesion as proof of pathological restriction.
Exclude drought or irrigation channeling with measured center-versus-edge moisture before and after irrigation and a documented wetting pattern.
Exclude salinity or fertilizer concentration with calibrated root-zone EC and input/runoff records.
Exclude overwatering or hypoxia with moisture history, aeration context, odor, root color, and tissue integrity rather than inferring it from wilt alone.
Escalate brown, water-soaked, sloughed, necrotic, lesioned, or foul-smelling roots for culture or molecular testing for Pythium, Fusarium, Rhizoctonia, and other root pathogens.
Inspect washed roots for discrete galls or abnormal swellings and obtain nematode confirmation when root-knot nematodes remain plausible.
Exclude transplant shock, torn roots, compressed plugs, buried crowns, stem girdling, and container heat injury using handling history and crown/root inspection.

progression.description: Root tips reach a physical boundary; contact or an occasional deflected root is normal and not diagnostic.
Repeated roots begin following the wall or bottom; record the number of affected faces and preserve an intact comparison root ball.
Wall-following roots become a tight root-dominant layer and may alter wetting, but moisture and EC measurements are still required to identify the stress mechanism.
Cannabis-specific survey evidence reports that some root-bound hemp transplants did not reliably overcome the bound architecture after field transplanting.
Poor establishment may overlap Fusarium or Pythium; later discoloration or decay must not be attributed to mechanical restriction alone.

lookAlikes: Normal cohesive nursery root ball or vigorous roots at drainage holes
Irrigation channeling or hydrophobic substrate without mechanical root restriction
Transplant shock or mechanical root tearing
Stem girdling, buried crown, or compressed propagation plug
Nutrient deficiency caused by pH or root-zone chemistry
confirmation: Before disturbing roots, record a plant identifier and capture the whole canopy, container size and shape, substrate surface, drainage openings, crown, and all accessible root-ball faces with a metric scale and neutral color reference.

Extract the root ball intact and photograph the top, bottom, and at least four side quadrants; then gently remove substrate and repeat the views so normal cohesion can be separated from repeated container-contour roots.
Capture a matched same-cultivar, same-age, same-substrate, same-irrigation comparison plant using identical views and exposure; do not infer restriction from an unmatched small-pot image.
Measure root-zone moisture at the center and perimeter immediately before and after a documented irrigation event, and record input and leachate EC plus pH with calibrated instruments.
Document root color, firmness, odor, lesions, sloughing, crown integrity, and discrete galls; submit representative plant-linked tissue for pathogen or nematode testing when those signs are present.

For a post-transplant sequence, keep plant identity linked across dates and include the original root-ball boundary plus new roots beyond it; do not use canopy recovery or failure alone as confirmation.

Keep canopy-only, detached-root-only, non-Cannabis transfer, unmatched, generated, vendor, anecdotal, unverified, and rights-unclear samples out of the confirmed class and all automated training splits.
immediateActions: Preserve and document at least one intact symptomatic root ball and one matched comparison before cutting, teasing, washing, transplanting, or changing irrigation.
Measure center/perimeter moisture, EC, pH, and drainage behavior while screening for root decay and galls; avoid assigning the cause from pot size or canopy appearance.
Quarantine or segregate plants with root lesions, decay, or galls until infectious and nematode differentials are evaluated.
correctivePlan: Use crop-stage- and production-system-appropriate transplant or root-management practices only after physical restriction is confirmed; the non-Cannabis sources do not validate a universal Cannabis root-pruning method.
Correct verified irrigation nonuniformity, salinity, hypoxia, or infection as separate coexisting problems rather than assuming that relieving container restriction resolves them.

Track new roots beyond the former container boundary and compare canopy development with matched controls; retain the record as uncertain if root expansion and plant response are not temporally linked.
prevention: Match container volume and transplant timing to cultivar growth rate and production duration, and audit representative intact root balls before transplant batches are moved.
Record container history, up-pot dates, irrigation delivery, substrate, cultivar, and plant age so boundary deformation can be interpreted against an appropriate comparison.
Reject or flag incoming transplants with severe repeated circling/matting, decay, galls, or an undocumented root-zone history for human review.
warnings: Photo or video alone cannot establish the physiological cause of canopy stress; root-ball morphology, plant linkage, measurements, and exclusion checks are required.

The controlled rooting-volume meta-analysis and University of Maryland morphology guide are non-Cannabis transfer evidence and do not establish Cannabis thresholds, universal symptoms, severity, or treatment efficacy.

The hemp evidence is a diagnostic survey rather than a controlled container-size trial, so cultivar response, incidence, timing, yield effect, and a pathological root-density threshold remain unresolved.
Root binding can coexist with Fusarium, Pythium, irrigation failure, or salinity; finding circling roots does not exclude a more proximate cause of decline.

No licensed, plant-linked Cannabis root-binding progression image or verified diagnostic video was located for this batch; media remains an explicit gap rather than using vendor, anecdotal, or non-Cannabis imagery as ground truth.

sources.title: Surveying for Potential Diseases and Abiotic Disorders of Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa) Production
supportedClaims: North Carolina hemp diagnostic submissions included root binding, excess water, nutrient disorders, and herbicide injury as important abiotic differentials.

Root-bound transplants were commonly reported and affected plants did not reliably overcome the bound root system after field transplanting; secondary Fusarium and Pythium infections were also observed.
Clomazone carryover caused bleaching of newly formed hemp tissue in a documented commercial field case and the plants did not recover.

Field and diagnostic observations also documented manganese toxicity as interveinal yellowing followed by interveinal necrosis, supporting it as a real hemp differential but not a camera-only diagnosis.

sources.title: Pot size matters: a meta-analysis of the effects of rooting volume on plant growth
supportedClaims: A meta-analysis of 65 plant studies found that doubling pot size increased biomass by 43% on average and that reduced growth in smaller pots was associated mainly with lower photosynthesis per unit leaf area.

The analysis establishes that rooting volume can materially alter plant growth, but it is not Cannabis-specific and does not validate a universal Cannabis container size, root-density threshold, visual symptom, or field diagnosis.

The authors caution that appropriate pot size depends on plant size; the paper's experimental biomass-per-volume proposal is research-design guidance and is not a diagnostic threshold for cultivated Cannabis.

sources.title: Pot-Bound Indoor Plants
sources.organization: University of Maryland Extension, Home & Garden Information Center
authors: University of Maryland Extension Home & Garden Information Center
supportedClaims: The institutional guide describes pot-bound morphology in non-Cannabis indoor plants as roots encircling the pot perimeter and forming a tight mass that can fill the pot or extend over its edge.
It also reports that water can pass through a pot-bound root mass too quickly while the root-ball center remains dry, and that resulting desiccation can produce tip dieback or marginal browning.

These morphology and watering observations are transfer context only: they support root-ball inspection and drought exclusion but do not establish Cannabis ground truth, severity, progression, or a camera-only diagnosis.

name: Fusarium crown and root rot / wilt complex
summary: A Cannabis crown/root/wilt disease complex associated with multiple Fusarium species. Yellowing and wilt are nonspecific; dark sunken crown tissue, root necrosis, and internal discoloration increase suspicion, while laboratory isolation or molecular work is required for organism-level confirmation.
indicators: Dark sunken crown lesions extend upward from the cannabis root zone
Reddish-brown or dark internal stem discoloration originates at the crown
Roots are necrotic while crown tissue is darkened or rotted
Canopy yellowing and wilt occur together with documented crown or internal stem decay
exclusions: Roots and crown are firm and healthy with no internal discoloration
Brown slimy roots occur without crown or internal stem lesions and Pythium or oxygen stress is better supported
Wilt resolves promptly after correcting a documented irrigation deficit without crown decay
Only one-sided mechanical stem injury explains the crown discoloration

progression.description: Root or crown tissue darkens and growth may slow before the canopy pattern is distinctive.
General or sometimes asymmetric yellowing and wilt develops as crown/root damage advances.
Internal decay may extend upward from the crown and plants can rapidly wilt, defoliate, collapse, or die.

confirmation: Inspect roots, crown, and a clean stem cross-section for the distribution of decay and internal discoloration.
Use a plant-diagnostic laboratory for isolation plus molecular or sequence-based identification when Fusarium confirmation changes management.
immediateActions: Quarantine severely affected plants and avoid moving contaminated root-zone material or runoff to clean plants.
Document crown/root/internal symptoms before destructive sampling and preserve representative tissue for diagnosis.
correctivePlan: Base sanitation, culling, irrigation-system, and crop-protection decisions on confirmed pathogen and production-system evidence.
Inspect propagation stock and adjacent plants because Fusarium can move through infected plant material and contaminated production environments.
prevention: Start with clean propagation stock and sanitized tools, containers, and root-zone systems.
Prevent recirculation or movement of contaminated irrigation water where pathogen spread is a concern.
warnings: A photograph of yellowing or wilt cannot confirm Fusarium.
Multiple Fusarium species and Pythium can occur in similar Cannabis crown/root disease complexes; do not make species-level claims without laboratory evidence.
The Fusarium species list on Cannabis continues to expand; a model should rank a Fusarium syndrome separately from a laboratory-confirmed species label.

sources.title: Root and crown rot pathogens causing wilt symptoms on field-grown marijuana (Cannabis sativa L.) plants
supportedClaims: Affected field-grown Cannabis plants showed general or one-sided yellowing, rapid wilting, and collapse, with dark sunken crown lesions and internal discoloration extending upward from the root/crown zone.

Fusarium oxysporum, F. brachygibbosum, F. solani, F. equiseti, and Pythium aphanidermatum were recovered from affected tissues; pathogenicity work demonstrates that visual wilt alone does not identify one causal species.
Darkened or necrotic roots, crown rot, and reddish-brown internal decay are more discriminating observations than general canopy yellowing.

sources.title: Diseases of Cannabis sativa Caused by Diverse Fusarium Species
supportedClaims: Multiple Fusarium species are associated with Cannabis root, crown, stem, wilt, and flower disease syndromes.
Reported Cannabis Fusarium diagnoses use culture and sequence-based or other laboratory identification together with pathogenicity evidence; symptom appearance is not species-level confirmation.

sources.title: First Report of Fusarium falciforme (FSSC 3 + 4) Causing Rot of Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa) in California
supportedClaims: Fusarium falciforme isolates caused internal hemp stem rot in pathogenicity work and were reisolated from inoculated stems.
Field root rot was associated with the same organism, but the report specifically confirmed stem-rot ability more directly than root-rot ability.

sources.title: First Report of Fusarium commune Causing Damping Off and Wilt in Cannabis sativa in Pennsylvania
supportedClaims: Fusarium commune was reported from indoor Cannabis with wilted yellowing foliage, browning stems and roots, and withering, expanding the documented Fusarium species associated with Cannabis wilt/root disease.
The case supports maintaining a Fusarium complex label unless laboratory work resolves the causal species.

media.alt: Multi-panel reference figure showing Fusarium-associated disease signs and pathogen evidence on greenhouse-grown Cannabis plants.
media.caption: Infection of greenhouse-grown Cannabis plants by Fusarium species, including yellowing, crown infection and decay, pith necrosis, crown rot, diseased cuttings, flower infection, cultures, and pathogenicity-test symptoms (Gwinn et al. 2022, Figure 4).
media.creator: Zamir Punja (photographs), published in Gwinn et al. 2022
media.requiredAttribution: Gwinn KD, Hansen Z, Kelly H, Ownley BH. 2022. Diseases of Cannabis sativa Caused by Diverse Fusarium Species. Frontiers in Agronomy 3:796062. Figure photographs courtesy of Zamir Punja. CC BY 4.0.
media.diagnosticLabel: fusarium-crown-root-rot — Fusarium-associated Cannabis crown/root/wilt disease composite
useLimitations: Multi-panel and multi-species composite: reference-only as a whole figure.
Do not treat the full composite as one single-class training example.
Do not visually confirm a Fusarium species in an unknown plant from resemblance to this figure.
Use the source article and laboratory confirmation guidance for causal identification.

name: Acidic or extreme substrate-pH root stress
summary: A measured root-zone condition in which persistently acidic peat-based substrate suppresses Cannabis shoot and root development, while either acidic or high-pH extremes can restrict visible root growth. There is no unique leaf appearance: cultivar, fertility, EC, substrate, and exposure duration materially change what a camera can see.
affectedParts: root tips and developing root system
lower foliage when low pH is combined with excessive micronutrient fertility in a susceptible cultivar
leaf tips and leaflet interior during treatment-associated bronzing and necrosis
root-zone solution and substrate for direct pH and EC measurement
indicators: Repeated calibrated substrate measurements remain at an extreme rather than a single irrigation or runoff reading
Root-tip development is reduced relative to matched healthy plants before a specific foliar pattern is reliable
Whole-plant diameter and accumulated shoot biomass lag despite plant height sometimes remaining similar
At acidic pH, leaf-tissue micronutrient concentrations may rise without visible toxicity
In the Sweetened pH 3.8 plus fourfold-micronutrient treatment, lower-leaf tips bronzed, became necrotic, spread inward, and developed chlorosis
The same low-pH and high-micronutrient treatment did not produce the same foliage response in Cherry Wine
exclusions: Only nutrient-solution input pH was measured and the actual substrate or root-zone pH is unknown
A single runoff, reservoir, or slurry reading is outside target but repeat representative measurements are not
High EC, fertilizer imbalance, or source-water alkalinity explains the response without a persistent measured substrate-pH extreme
Roots are restricted by saturation, compaction, container binding, drought, temperature, oxygen limitation, transplant damage, or root disease
Foliar bronzing or necrosis is localized to heat, light, spray, contact, pest feeding, or infectious lesions
Tissue analysis supports a specific nutrient deficiency or toxicity and measured root-zone pH is not outside the production-system target
Color differences appear only under altered lighting, white balance, cultivar pigmentation, senescence, or compression artifact

progression.description: Substrate pH persists outside the intended system range; solution pH alone does not establish the root-zone exposure.
Root-tip expansion can slow before a diagnostic foliage pattern appears. In Baox, separation at pH 3.1 and 7.1 was evident by 21 days after planting.
Plant diameter, root mass, or shoot dry mass can fall while height remains deceptively similar; compare serial whole-plant and root-zone measurements with matched controls.
Low pH plus excessive micronutrients may cause lower-leaf tip bronzing, chlorosis, and spreading necrosis in a susceptible cultivar, but absence of those symptoms does not exclude pH stress.
New root tips, canopy expansion, and new-leaf quality should be followed over time; existing necrosis will not reverse and response alone does not prove the original diagnosis.

confirmation: Do not diagnose pH stress from leaf color, tip burn, stunting, one photograph, one video, or a generic nutrient-availability chart.

Measure the actual substrate or root-zone pH repeatedly with a calibrated meter and a method appropriate to the medium; record sampling location, depth, irrigation timing, extraction method, meter calibration, temperature, and replicate values.

Measure root-zone and input EC alongside pH, and document source-water pH and alkalinity, fertilizer formulation, acid or base additions, lime charge, substrate batch, irrigation volume, leaching fraction, and drainage.

Capture serial whole-plant top and side views, root-zone and cleaned-root views, upper- and lower-canopy views, and close-ups of both leaf surfaces under repeatable lighting with scale and a matched same-cultivar control.

Record cultivar, plant age, stage, days of exposure, container volume, substrate composition, water content, root-zone temperature, dissolved oxygen where relevant, and root-tip quantity or standardized root coverage.

Use representative leaf-tissue and root-zone or substrate analysis to separate a pH-associated exposure from a specific nutrient disorder; use a plant diagnostic laboratory when discolored or decaying roots, lesions, or pests remain plausible.
Retain a measured-exposure or suspected label unless the pH history, root or growth response, competing exposures, and analytical evidence are linked to the photographed plant.
immediateActions: Preserve pre-correction pH, EC, alkalinity, solution, substrate, tissue, root, and image records before changing the system.
Verify the measuring method and calibration with repeat samples; avoid large unmeasured acid, base, lime, fertilizer, or flush corrections.
Quarantine uncertain images and videos from diagnostic ground truth until exposure and confounder evidence is linked.
correctivePlan: Correct the verified cause gradually using substrate- and water-appropriate guidance, considering alkalinity and buffering rather than input pH alone.
Restore a balanced fertilizer and irrigation program while monitoring substrate pH, EC, water content, drainage, and new root growth.
Reassess root pathogens, salinity, water status, temperature, and nutrient-specific differentials if new root tips and growth do not improve after the measured pH returns to the intended range.
prevention: Establish a production-system-specific substrate pH and EC monitoring protocol with calibrated meters, consistent extraction methods, replicate sampling, and trend alerts.
Test source-water alkalinity and account for substrate lime and fertilizer acidity before making recurring pH adjustments.
Keep same-cultivar controls and serial root and canopy images so gradual growth restriction is not mistaken for a specific leaf disorder.
warnings: The study supports a measured substrate-pH stress record, not a universal image phenotype or a universal nutrient-lockout chart.
The 5.5 to 6.5 recommendation came from peat-based greenhouse experiments and must not be copied unchanged to soil, field, coco, rockwool, aeroponic, or deep-water systems.
At normal micronutrient supply, low pH increased tissue accumulation without a universal visible toxicity; absence of bronzing does not establish that the root zone is acceptable.
The lower-leaf bronzing sequence occurred in Sweetened under pH 3.8 plus fourfold micronutrients and was absent in Cherry Wine; it is not low-pH-specific ground truth.
A single runoff or reservoir pH value does not prove the pH experienced throughout the root system.
No image or video is admitted for this record because no stable original asset URL was independently verified during this review.
All symptom-only or uncalibrated-pH samples remain low confidence and require human review.

sources.title: Impact of substrate pH and micronutrient fertility rates on Cannabis sativa
sources.publisher: Wiley Periodicals LLC on behalf of the Crop Science Society of America and the American Society of Agronomy
supportedClaims: In a controlled peat-perlite experiment, industrial hemp shoot dry weight was lower at substrate pH 3.0 and 4.0 than at pH 5.0 through 7.0; plant diameter was smaller at pH 3.0, while mean plant height did not differ across that pH range.
Visible root-tip counts in Cannabis sativa Baox mini-rhizotrons were lowest at both measured extremes, pH 3.1 and 7.1, by 21 days after planting, while counts at pH 3.7 through 5.9 were similar.
Termination EC was higher at pH 3.0 and 7.0 than at intermediate pH values in the first experiment, so pH response cannot be interpreted without the accompanying salt and fertility context.

Lower pH increased several leaf-tissue micronutrient concentrations, but normal micronutrient supply did not produce a universal toxicity phenotype; the authors concluded that Cannabis growth was inhibited below pH 5.0 and recommended a greenhouse substrate range of 5.5 to 6.5 for the systems evaluated.

With fourfold micronutrients at target pH 3.8, Sweetened developed lower-foliage tip bronzing that advanced to necrosis, inward spread, and chlorosis, whereas Cherry Wine did not show the same response, demonstrating cultivar- and fertility-dependent appearance.

The experiments evaluated peat-based greenhouse substrates and three cultivars; their pH values, timing, tissue concentrations, and symptom expression are treatment-specific and do not establish universal soil, coco, rockwool, or hydroponic thresholds.

name: Pythium root and crown rot complex
summary: A laboratory-resolved oomycete disease complex that can cause damping-off, feeder-root loss, root or crown decay, stunting, wilt, and death. Canopy appearance, wet conditions, and brown roots are not diagnostic on their own.
affectedParts: whole plant as a secondary response
indicators: Plant-linked washed roots show expanding brown lesions, decay, and loss of normally pale active root tissue.
Decayed roots may shed or slough the outer cortex and leave a thinner central vascular core; record texture and a scale rather than inferring slime from color alone.
Fine-root mass, feeder roots, and root-hair density decline relative to an age-, cultivar-, substrate-, and irrigation-matched healthy plant.
Crown disease can produce brown or water-soaked lesions, girdling, and internal pith browning or blackening; root rot and crown rot should be recorded separately when they do not co-occur.
Propagation evidence can include failed emergence, damping-off, or collapse of a rooted cutting when the affected base and roots remain linked to the same plant.
Stunting, chlorosis, wilt despite a moist root zone, necrosis, defoliation, or collapse can follow root or crown damage but are nonspecific secondary canopy signs.
A useful image or video sequence links the same plant across whole-canopy, lower-stem or crown, washed-root overview, and close root-lesion views over time.
A confirmed label requires compatible plant-linked disease plus selective isolation or a validated oomycete assay; species labels require appropriately resolved molecular evidence.
exclusions: Do not label firm tan roots as rot when color follows substrate or nutrient staining and matched roots retain an intact cortex and active tips.
Do not convert saturated media, low dissolved oxygen, warm solution, or irrigation history into a pathogen label without organism evidence; abiotic hypoxia can produce the same decline.
Exclude measured drought when the root zone is dry and turgor recovers after irrigation without progressive root or crown lesions.
Check for Rhizoctonia-compatible basal lesions, characteristic mycelium, or right-angle hyphal branching and resolve the organism in the laboratory.
Check cut crown and stem tissue for a Fusarium-compatible vascular or internal discoloration pattern and use culture or molecular testing to resolve mixed root disease.
Exclude southern blight or Sclerotinia when diagnostic mycelium and sclerotia are linked to the crown or substrate surface.
Inspect intact washed roots for galls and obtain nematode evidence before assigning root-knot disease.
Exclude root aphid colonies, fungus-gnat larvae, root binding, high EC, and out-of-range pH; canopy-only or detached-root observations remain unconfirmed.

progression.description: Seeds or rooted cuttings may fail, damp off, or collapse; preserve the affected base and roots because the canopy alone cannot identify Pythium.
Pale active tips and feeder-root density decline while small brown root lesions appear; matched healthy plants are important because media staining can mimic color change.
Brown lesions enlarge, root mass falls, and the cortex may soften or slough from the central core; capture intact texture before washing destroys the pattern.
Some plants develop a separate brown or water-soaked crown lesion, girdling, or dark internal pith; crown and root findings must not be assumed to occur together.
Stunting, chlorosis, wilt, necrosis, defoliation, and collapse can develop at isolate-, cultivar-, and environment-dependent rates; no universal image timeline is supported.

lookAlikes: Salinity / high EC or pH-related root stress
confirmation: Capture the same plant in a whole-canopy view, lower-stem and crown views, an intact root-ball view, a gently washed root overview, and lesion close-ups; retain plant, date, cultivar, substrate, and irrigation identifiers.
Record root color, firmness, cortex integrity or sloughing, active tips, feeder-root density, lesion boundaries, crown circumference, and internal pith with a scale and matched healthy comparator.
Sample the active margin of plant-linked root and crown lesions before secondary decay dominates; keep roots, crown, substrate or water, and healthy controls traceable to their plant IDs.
Use an appropriate selective isolation method and microscopy to recover an oomycete while checking for Fusarium, Rhizoctonia, Phytophthora, and mixed infections.

Use a validated molecular test for the Pythium or Globisporangium complex; species-level labels require adequately discriminating loci such as ITS plus mitochondrial COI or COII, or an equivalent validated method.

Measure root-zone moisture or saturation, dissolved oxygen where relevant, temperature, pH, and EC, and inspect for insects, nematodes, root binding, and abiotic injury before attributing the syndrome to a pathogen.

Do not confirm from canopy-only, detached-root, single-timepoint, morphology-only, ITS-only when resolution is inadequate, mixed-pathogen, laboratory-unlinked, generated, or anecdotal media; route those samples to human review.
immediateActions: Isolate affected root-zone water, runoff, tools, and plant material while preserving diagnostic samples.
Correct damaging saturation or oxygen conditions without treating that response as proof of the causal organism.
correctivePlan: Remove irrecoverable plants where appropriate and sanitize wetted equipment using the production system’s documented biosecurity procedure.
Use only legal, crop-appropriate treatments after diagnosis and preserve pre-treatment samples for confirmation.
prevention: Manage irrigation duration, drainage, sanitation, propagation hygiene, and recirculated water risk; verify rather than assume universal temperature or moisture thresholds.
warnings: Photo- or video-only confidence is capped at 0.20 because canopy decline and brown roots overlap abiotic stress and several root pathogens.
Wet or saturated conditions and wounded roots can increase disease risk but do not prove that Pythium or Globisporangium caused an observed syndrome.
Pythium and Globisporangium species differ in temperature and production-system ecology; do not transfer one study threshold to the entire complex.
The controlled hemp 'Wife' study timings and severities are study-specific and must not become universal onset or mortality thresholds.

The existing Figure 7 reference is a multi-organism whole-plant composite without root or crown views; it is reference-only and training-ineligible until panel-resolved labels and human review are available.
Human review is mandatory for canopy-only, detached-root, single-surface, morphology-only, ITS-only, mixed-pathogen, laboratory-unlinked, low-resolution, or rights-unclear samples.
Pythium species differ in temperature and production-system ecology; do not treat one environmental threshold as universal for the entire complex.

sources.title: Several Pythium species cause crown and root rot on cannabis plants grown under commercial greenhouse conditions
sources.organization: Canadian Journal of Plant Pathology (Punja et al.)
supportedClaims: Across 140 diseased plants sampled from seven licensed commercial greenhouses in British Columbia during 2018 and 2019, the authors associated several Pythium or Globisporangium species with crown rot, root decay, wilting, and plant death; mother, vegetative, and flowering plants across 15 strains were affected.

Recovered isolates caused root browning, decay, and stunting in Cannabis grown in coco coir–perlite, but symptom rate and severity varied among isolates; visual appearance therefore cannot resolve the causal species.
Root wounding and prolonged saturation increased disease in the reported experiments, but these are risk modifiers rather than image-level proof of Pythium disease.
The study documented damping-off in rooted cuttings and secondary canopy yellowing, necrosis, defoliation, wilting, and death, alongside crown rot and internal pith browning or blackening.

sources.title: First Report of Pythium ultimum Crown and Root Rot of Industrial Hemp in the United States
supportedClaims: Pythium ultimum was pathogenic to industrial hemp in replicated inoculation work; symptoms began within about one week and the organism was reisolated and PCR-confirmed.
Cool early planting, low-lying/flood-prone conditions, and soil crusting after intense rainfall were risk context in the report, not species-level visual identifiers.

sources.title: First Report of Pythium aphanidermatum Crown and Root Rot of Industrial Hemp in the United States
supportedClaims: Industrial hemp with Pythium aphanidermatum crown/root rot showed chlorosis, stunting, wilt, brown root lesions, feeder-root loss, and sometimes brown water-soaked stem lesions.
The above-ground syndrome overlaps other root diseases and water stress, reinforcing the need for cleaned-root and laboratory evidence.

sources.title: First Report of Pythium myriotylum Causing Root Rot in Cannabis sativa in California
supportedClaims: Greenhouse medical Cannabis with Pythium myriotylum root rot showed stunting, chlorosis, senescence, reduced root mass and root-hair density, and necrotic root lesions.
The Cannabis-specific phenotype does not make canopy appearance species-specific.

sources.title: First Report of Pythium aphanidermatum Causing Crown and Root Rot in Cannabis sativa in Florida
supportedClaims: Pythium aphanidermatum crown/root rot has been confirmed in indoor Cannabis grown in rockwool across multiple cultivars in Florida.
Species occurrence across production systems supports retaining a Pythium complex label unless laboratory evidence resolves species.

sources.title: First Report of Pythium myriotylum Causing Damping off and Root Rot in Cannabis sativa in Florida
supportedClaims: Pythium myriotylum was confirmed causing damping-off and root rot in indoor Cannabis cuttings from five cultivars in Florida.
The expanded cultivar evidence supports propagation-stage scouting and reinforces that Pythium disease can occur before a mature-plant canopy syndrome is available.

sources.title: Pathogenicity and Mefenoxam Sensitivity of Pythium, Globisporangium, and Fusarium Isolates From Coconut Coir and Rockwool in Marijuana (Cannabis sativa L.) Production
supportedClaims: Controlled pathogenicity experiments on hemp cultivar 'Wife' confirmed that selected Pythium myriotylum and Globisporangium irregulare isolates from production substrates could reduce growth and cause chlorosis or wilt; inoculated organisms were recovered from root fragments.

The source facility sampling involved coconut coir and rockwool rather than original diseased marijuana plant tissue, and Koch-style pathogenicity testing used one hemp cultivar, so the host, facility, timing, and severity cannot be generalized.

Figure 7 is a whole-plant, multi-treatment composite at 14 days after inoculation that includes Pythium, Globisporangium, Fusarium, and an uninoculated control; it does not show roots or crown tissue and cannot confirm an unknown plant from appearance.

sources.title: Pythium Root and Crown Rot of Hemp
sources.organization: Utah State University Extension, Utah Plant Pest Diagnostic Laboratory
supportedClaims: The institutional diagnostic note describes stunting and wilt with root rot, including loss of the root outer layer that leaves the central core, and separately describes crown infection that can girdle the stem.
The note states that either root rot or crown rot can progress to rapid wilt and death and cautions that the two syndromes need not occur together, supporting separate root and crown observations.

media.alt: Hemp plants from a controlled pathogenicity trial comparing Pythium, Globisporangium, Fusarium, and uninoculated treatments.
media.caption: Hemp 'Wife' plants 14 days after inoculation with pathogenic Pythium myriotylum, Globisporangium irregulare, or Fusarium oxysporum isolates, plus the uninoculated control (McGehee and Raudales 2021, Figure 7).
media.creator: Cora S. McGehee and Rosa E. Raudales
media.requiredAttribution: McGehee CS, Raudales RE. 2021. Pathogenicity and Mefenoxam Sensitivity of Pythium, Globisporangium, and Fusarium Isolates From Coconut Coir and Rockwool in Marijuana (Cannabis sativa L.) Production. Frontiers in Agronomy 3:706138. CC BY 4.0.
media.diagnosticLabel: pythium-root-rot — controlled hemp root-pathogen pathogenicity comparison including Pythium myriotylum
useLimitations: Multi-treatment composite containing Pythium, Globisporangium, Fusarium, and uninoculated plants; reference-only until panel boundaries and labels are independently reviewed.
One hemp cultivar and one 14-day whole-plant timepoint are shown; there is no root, crown, lesion-detail, or longitudinal view.
Whole-plant chlorosis, wilt, and growth reduction are not Pythium-specific, and the source study sampled production substrates rather than original marijuana plant tissue.
Do not use the composite to visually confirm Pythium in an unknown plant; plant-linked root or crown evidence and laboratory identification remain required.

name: Rhizoctonia sore shin / root and crown rot
summary: A soilborne Cannabis root, crown, and lower-stem disease in which dry brown root rot or reddish-brown lower-stem rot can accompany wilt. The canopy response and lesion color overlap multiple root-zone problems, so image or video evidence alone supports only a low-confidence Rhizoctonia-compatible label.
affectedParts: lower main stem at and just above the soil line
leaves and buds when directly infected
indicators: Dry brown rot is visible on plant-linked Cannabis roots
Reddish-brown rot develops on the lower main stem at or near the soil line
A necrotic lesion just above the soil line accompanies wilt on the same plant
Root and crown necrosis is documented with intact root-to-stem continuity rather than an unlinked close-up
Dry brown leaf tissue or bud infection can occur, but these above-ground lesions are not sufficient for a Rhizoctonia label
Pigmented septate hyphae recovered from an active lesion branch at roughly 90 degrees with basal constriction
Validated sequence or other qualified laboratory evidence supports Rhizoctonia solani from the same plant and lesion
A whole-plant view, soil-line view, and washed-root view show the spatial relationship and progression of compatible disease
exclusions: White cottony basal mycelium with numerous round tan-to-brown sclerotia supports southern blight instead
Soft, water-soaked or sloughed roots plus oomycete evidence support Pythium or another water mold
Vascular discoloration and plant-linked Fusarium isolation or molecular evidence support Fusarium crown/root disease
Black root or crown tissue with microsclerotia and Macrophomina evidence supports charcoal rot
Firm integrated root galls plus nematode recovery support root-knot nematodes
Circling or matted roots follow the container wall and no active necrotic lesion or pathogen evidence is present, supporting root binding
No basal or root lesion is found and measured moisture, oxygen, EC, pH, or water-status data explain the canopy response
A detached root, stem lesion, or canopy image cannot be linked to the sampled plant and laboratory result

progression.description: The disease is historically documented in Cannabis seedlings, but a symptom-free image cannot establish infection and seedling onset is not universal.
Dry brown rot becomes visible on roots; record lesion margins and distribution across the intact washed root system.
Reddish-brown rot or a necrotic lesion develops on the lower main stem at or just above the soil line.
Compatible necrosis extends through plant-linked roots, crown, or lower stem while root function declines.
Wilt, reduced vigor, or collapse may become evident, but no source establishes a diagnostic leaf-age, canopy-position, or temporal pattern.

confirmation: Capture the same plant at whole-canopy, soil-line, crown, and washed-root scales with a ruler or other scale and preserve intact root-to-stem continuity.
Sample several fresh active lesion margins from the lower stem, crown, and roots under one plant identifier; retain paired apparently healthy tissue and substrate history.

Examine lesion-derived fungal growth microscopically for pigmented septate hyphae, approximately right-angle branching, and basal constriction; morphology supports a differential but is not sufficient ground truth by itself.
Use a qualified plant-diagnostic laboratory and validated molecular identification from the plant-linked lesion when assigning Rhizoctonia solani.
Investigate Pythium or other oomycetes, Fusarium, southern blight, charcoal rot, and nematodes when signs are mixed or the first assay is negative.
Measure root-zone moisture, oxygen or drainage, EC, pH, temperature, container geometry, and irrigation history so abiotic stress and disease-conducive context are separated from organism identity.

Keep canopy-only, root-only, detached, morphology-only, ITS-only, mixed-pathogen, unlinked-laboratory, low-resolution, stock, forum, vendor, or generated samples out of the confirmed class and route them to human review.
immediateActions: Separate suspect root-zone material and prevent movement of potentially contaminated soil, roots, debris, containers, runoff, or tools into clean areas.
Preserve fresh plant-linked lesion margins for diagnostic testing before destructive treatment or disposal.
Check drainage, irrigation, EC, pH, oxygenation, and container restriction concurrently without treating any one condition as proof of Rhizoctonia.
correctivePlan: Base disease-specific action on a qualified diagnosis and locally appropriate crop rules; this profile does not convert symptom appearance or warm-soil context into a treatment decision.
Correct measured root-zone stressors and track response with repeated linked canopy, soil-line, and root observations; visual improvement does not prove pathogen elimination.
prevention: Use clean propagation material, media, containers, and tools and avoid moving infected plant debris or soil between production areas.
Inspect transplants at the soil line and roots before placement while retaining plant and source-lot identifiers.
Record irrigation and soil-temperature history because early over-irrigation and cooler emergence conditions can increase risk without proving disease.
warnings: Wilt, reduced vigor, brown roots, and reddish-brown stem lesions are not organism-specific.
The Cannabis-specific compendium statement is historical seedling-disease evidence from Ukraine; it does not establish current prevalence or a universal stage of onset.
The Pacific Northwest environment and symptom descriptions are crop-specific but do not establish a universal cultivar response, severity scale, or image-only label.
Rhizoctonia can coexist with other root pathogens, nematodes, container restriction, or abiotic stress, and a single assay or image may not resolve a mixed case.
Photo/video-only confidence is capped at 0.20; confirmed labels require plant-linked diagnostic evidence and human review.
No Rhizoctonia-specific Cannabis image or video with clear item-level reuse rights and linked organism confirmation was verified for this batch.

sources.title: Surveying for Potential Diseases and Abiotic Disorders of Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa) Production
supportedClaims: A North Carolina 2017–2018 hemp diagnostic survey identified 16 diseases caused by fungi, bacteria, oomycetes, and nematodes; the study used clinic diagnostics, morphology, sequence data for representative organisms, and pathogenicity testing for its confirmed disease set.

Fusarium foliar and flower blight was common in submitted samples and involved F. equiseti and F. graminearum; flowers developed surface hyphae and light-brown necrotic tips while leaves developed circular light-brown lesions about 1 cm wide with dark margins and gray-brown aging centers.
Exserohilum rostratum leaf spot occurred on leaves and stems as round brown-to-black lesions with darkened margins and abundant conidia, with ITS1/RPB2 evidence supporting the identification.

Rhizoctonia solani was found on roots and crowns with plant wilting and necrotic lesions just above the soil line; pigmented septate hyphae showed characteristic right-angle branching and sequence evidence supported R. solani.

Southern blight caused whole-plant wilt in reproductive hemp during hot midseason conditions, with abundant hyphae and russet-brown sclerotia on roots/lower stems and sequence/phylogenetic evidence supporting Athelia rolfsii/Sclerotium rolfsii.
Meloidogyne incognita was identified from galled hemp roots with females and egg masses; affected plants had some associated stunting.

The survey documented Serratia-associated, vein-limited angular hemp lesions and red bacterial ooze emerging from punctured lesions, while emphasizing that hemp leaf diseases overlap visually and require diagnostic separation.

sources.title: Rhizoctonia Sore Shin and Root Rot
supportedClaims: The Cannabis-specific compendium identifies sore shin and root rot as a disease caused by the soil fungus Rhizoctonia solani.

The chapter describes Rhizoctonia sore shin and root rot as the first recorded seedling disease of Cannabis in Ukraine; this is historical crop evidence and does not establish current prevalence, cultivar response, or a universal seedling-onset rule.

The chapter is Cannabis-specific and peer reviewed, but the abstract alone does not support assigning Rhizoctonia from canopy wilt, lesion color, production environment, or an image without organism-linked evidence.

sources.title: Hemp (Cannabis sativa)-Rhizoctonia Soreshin and Root Rot
sources.organization: Pacific Northwest Plant Disease Management Handbook
authors: Pacific Northwest Plant Disease Management Handbook
sources.publisher: Oregon State University, Washington State University, and University of Idaho
supportedClaims: The March 2026 institutional revision identifies Rhizoctonia solani as the cause, states that it can persist in soil for at least several years, has a broad host range, and can spread with infected plant debris.
The hemp description records dry brown root rot and reddish-brown rot on the lower main stem; it also reports dry brown leaf tissue and bud infection in Oregon medical Cannabis.

Warmer soil favors disease, while early over-irrigation and irrigation-related soil cooling can slow emergence and favor the fungus; these conditions are epidemiologic context and are not diagnostic proof.

The handbook recommends rotation away from susceptible hosts and avoiding early over-irrigation, supporting soil/debris movement and irrigation-history checks without establishing a universal treatment interval for every production system.

name: White root rot
summary: A pathogenicity-confirmed hemp root disease reported from one commercial field in southern Italy. The useful visual pattern combines plant-linked canopy decline with white root-surface mycelium and fan-like sub-bark growth, but neither wilt nor white fungal material identifies the pathogen without laboratory confirmation.
affectedParts: root crown and soil immediately over infected roots
field distribution and neighboring root zones
indicators: The same intact hemp plant shows canopy yellowing or apical wilt together with compatible root rot and white mycelium; canopy-only and detached-root observations remain unlinked evidence.
Conspicuous white mycelium covers affected hemp roots in the primary report, while cross-crop institutional guidance describes scattered cobwebby webs or strands on roots and nearby soil.
Carefully lifting the cortex or bark at an active root lesion reveals white, fluffy, fan-like mycelial growth rather than relying only on growth on the exposed outer surface.
White-to-greyish mycelial mats and progressively rotten tissue are useful cross-crop capture cues, but color and texture must not be treated as Cannabis-specific or species-diagnostic.

Older Rosellinia mycelium can darken to tan, brown, or blackish and become crustlike on dead roots, so capture both the living lesion margin and dead center rather than requiring bright white growth at every stage.

In the single Campania outbreak, visible yellowing and apical wilt preceded death by about two to three weeks and about 10% of plants were affected; neither value is a universal progression clock, prevalence estimate, or severity threshold.

A high-value image set links the whole plant and field position to crown, unwashed root system, white surface growth, lifted-cortex interface, lesion margin, and a healthy comparison under neutral light with a metric scale.
A confirmed label requires compatible isolation and morphology plus validated molecular identification from plant-linked root tissue; visual agreement alone is at most a low-confidence suspect label.
exclusions: White growth is present only on dead debris, the container surface, or detached roots without an intact plant and active lesion margin, supporting saprophytic colonization or contamination rather than confirmed disease.
Cottony growth at the soil line with round white, tan, or brown sclerotia supports southern blight and requires its own laboratory workup.
White stem or crown growth with hard black sclerotia within or on affected tissue supports the Sclerotinia white-mold/crown-rot complex.
Water-soaked, brown, sloughing roots in a saturated root zone without white sub-bark mycelium support Pythium or Phytophthora investigation, which must be resolved by oomycete-directed testing.
Brown cortical lesions or damping-off without compatible white sub-bark growth support Rhizoctonia, Fusarium, or another root/crown pathogen and require culture or molecular differential testing.
Large coherent sub-bark fans, mushroomlike odor, rhizomorphs, or basidiocarps support an Armillaria differential; the cited distinction is cross-crop and still requires expert confirmation.

White granules, salt crust, perlite, root hairs, mycorrhizae, insect wax, or a beneficial inoculant remain material or organism confounders unless microscopy and plant-linked sampling demonstrate invasive Rosellinia.
Measured drought, hypoxia, salinity/high EC, pH injury, root restriction, or nematodes adequately explain decline and representative living lesion margins are negative for the pathogen.

progression.description: Contaminated roots, root debris, soil, runoff, or planting material may precede visible disease; history alone is risk context and never a positive label.
White cobwebby strands, webs, or a mat may become visible on infected roots or adjacent soil; record its exact attachment before cleaning or incubation.
Root tissue rots and lifting cortex at the active margin can reveal a white fluffy or fan-like layer; older growth may darken and become crustlike.
