Yellowing and apical wilt develop while compatible root signs remain on the same plant; canopy morphology is nonspecific and must stay linked to the root sequence.

Plants in the one reported hemp outbreak could die about two to three weeks after symptoms appeared, but cultivar, site, inoculum, and environment prevent transfer of that timing as a universal threshold.

lookAlikes: Sclerotinia white mold / crown rot complex
Saprophytic white mold on dead roots or substrate
Trichoderma or another introduced beneficial fungus
Perlite, mineral residue, or salt crust
Root aphid wax or mealybug residue
confirmation: Do not confirm white root rot from a canopy image, white material alone, or a detached root. Cap image/video-only confidence at 0.20 and route every organism-level proposal to human review.

Capture an uninterrupted plant-linked sequence before cleaning: field or bench position, whole canopy, crown, entire unwashed root system, white growth attachment, both sides of a lifted-cortex interface, and active lesion margin with scale and neutral color reference.

Sample multiple fresh living-to-necrotic root margins and sub-bark interfaces, plus a comparable healthy plant; avoid relying on decomposed centers or material incubated without documenting its original attachment.

Record plant age and cultivar, onset and repeat dates, neighboring-plant pattern, prior crop or perennial-root history, planting-stock source, root-debris and soil movement, irrigation/runoff, substrate, root-zone temperature, moisture, pH, and EC.

Submit plant-linked tissue to a qualified plant-diagnostic laboratory for isolation and morphology plus a validated molecular assay; preserve the chain between sample, image, culture, sequence result, and plant identifier.

Request a differential workup for southern blight, Sclerotinia, Pythium/Phytophthora, Fusarium, Rhizoctonia, Armillaria where plausible, and pair pathogen testing with root-zone measurements and nematode assessment.

Use serial imaging to document change but not to prove identity. Keep canopy-only, detached-root, white-growth-only, incubation-only, culture-unlinked, single-locus-ambiguous, mixed-pathogen, low-resolution, cross-crop, stock, generated, vendor, forum, anecdotal, or rights-unclear samples out of confirmed ground truth.
immediateActions: Isolate affected root-zone soil, tools, footwear, water runoff, and root debris from clean production areas while preserving representative plant-linked samples.
Photograph and sample before uprooting or washing; mark neighboring plants and inspect their root zones without spreading soil.
Contact a qualified plant-diagnostic laboratory and follow local plant-health reporting or containment requirements before moving suspect plants or substrate.
correctivePlan: Base culling, sanitation, soil/root-zone handling, and any crop-protection decision on confirmed disease and options currently legal for hemp in the jurisdiction.
Remove or contain infected roots and debris only under locally appropriate biosecurity guidance, and prevent contaminated soil or runoff from reaching clean production zones.
Track marked neighboring plants and reopen the differential if laboratory results, progression, or root-zone measurements conflict with the proposed diagnosis.
prevention: Use documented pathogen-free planting material and inspect roots before introduction where lawful and practical.
Avoid moving soil, water, tools, containers, or persistent root debris from confirmed areas into clean production zones.
Maintain drainage and irrigation records and inspect sites with susceptible perennial-crop history or unexplained root-rot mortality without assuming that history proves current infection.
warnings: The direct Cannabis evidence is one pathogenicity-confirmed commercial-field report from Campania; its approximately 10% incidence and two-to-three-week decline are site-specific observations.

UC IPM and Agriculture Victoria provide non-Cannabis morphology and biosecurity context. Their woody-host symptoms, timing, climate associations, host outcomes, and management claims are not Cannabis thresholds.

Rosellinia/Dematophora taxonomy, white mycelium, and fan-like sub-bark growth do not make images species-resolving; mixed infections and multiple white-growth look-alikes require laboratory exclusion.

The Agriculture Victoria figures are credited to the State of Queensland and lack verified item-level automated-training rights. No media file was copied or indexed, and this profile intentionally remains an explicit licensed-image and video gap.

Human review is mandatory for canopy-only, detached-root, white-growth-only, incubation-only, morphology-only, culture-unlinked, molecularly ambiguous, mixed-pathogen, cross-crop, low-resolution, generated, vendor, forum, anecdotal, or rights-unclear samples.

sources.title: First Report of White Root Rot of Hemp (Cannabis sativa) Caused by Dematophora necatrix in Campania Region (Southern Italy)
supportedClaims: Affected hemp developed yellowing, apical wilt, root rot, white mycelium covering roots, and fan-like mycelium beneath root bark before death.

In the single reported commercial field in Campania, death generally occurred within two to three weeks after first symptoms and about 10% of plants were affected; these are outbreak observations, not universal Cannabis timing or prevalence.
Inoculated hemp reproduced chlorosis, apical wilt, and death while controls remained healthy; the fungus was reisolated and confirmed by morphology and molecular analysis.
Root signs and laboratory confirmation are required because canopy yellowing and wilt overlap many Cannabis root-zone disorders.

sources.title: Dematophora Root Rot, or Rosellinia Root Rot
sources.organization: University of California Statewide Integrated Pest Management Program
sources.publisher: Regents of the University of California, Agriculture and Natural Resources
supportedClaims: In the reviewed woody-host guidance, Rosellinia can produce scattered cobwebby whitish mycelia on lower trunks, soil over infected roots, root surfaces, and beneath root-crown or major-root bark.

Removing infected root cortex can expose a whitish fluffy mycelial layer; older mycelium may darken to blackish, brown, or tan and become crustlike, so absence of bright white growth in a late sample does not exclude the organism.

The guidance distinguishes Rosellinia from larger fanlike Armillaria mycelia and from Phytophthora root rot, which does not produce whitish mycelia; these are non-Cannabis differential cues and do not replace crop-linked laboratory confirmation.

Rosellinia can persist in infected root or woody debris and spread through moist soil, supporting conservative soil, water-runoff, tool, and root-debris biosecurity after a confirmed diagnosis; this source does not establish Cannabis treatment efficacy.

sources.title: White root rot
supportedClaims: The institutional cross-crop profile describes mycelial webs and strands near roots, bark invasion with fan-like growth, and white-to-greyish mats beneath bark that accompany progressive root-tissue rot.

The source identifies a broad host range that includes herbaceous plants, but its apple-tree timing, canopy morphology, climate, and control statements must not be transferred as Cannabis thresholds or expected progression.

Its three credited photographs are copyrighted to the State of Queensland and lack item-level automated-training permission; their landing-page metadata may inform capture planning, but no image is copied, displayed, or indexed as Cannabis ground truth.

name: Drought / water-deficit stress
summary: Water deficit is a measured exposure-response diagnosis, not a synonym for drooping leaves. Cannabis studies document leaf-angle change, chlorosis, reduced expansion, cultivar-specific wilting or shedding, and growth or yield effects, but the label requires plant-linked root-zone moisture and irrigation history plus exclusion of salinity, hypoxia, heat/VPD, root restriction, vascular injury, and root disease.
indicators: Substrate or soil moisture is measurably below the established irrigation target while the plant shows water-deficit stress
Canopy wilt or reduced expansion coincides with a documented dry root zone and improves after appropriate rehydration
Leaf area or biomass growth declines during a sustained measured water deficit without root rot evidence
A time-linked root-zone measurement shows water content below that plant and production system's established irrigated baseline while leaf posture or growth changes develop.

Repeated side-view images show fan-leaf blades and petioles moving downward relative to their own turgid baseline and a matched irrigated control; absolute leaf angle from one frame is not diagnostic.
The temporal pattern begins after a documented missed, blocked, insufficient, or intentionally withheld irrigation event and is strongest in the zone supplied by that event or emitter.

In one controlled flowering experiment, visible wilt followed sustained drying and was accompanied by veinal chlorosis that began on older leaves and occurred less strongly on newer leaves across the plant; this is study-specific, not a universal color signature.
Sustained measured deficit can reduce leaf area, shoot expansion, total biomass, or seed/flower yield even when acute wilt is weak or delayed.
Cultivars can differ in stomatal closure, midday relative water content, wilting score, leaf retention, and recovery, so matched-plant context carries more weight than a generic droop class.

After careful rehydration, water status and posture may improve while photosynthesis or growth remains depressed; different recovery rates support a temporal water-response link but do not exclude coexisting injury.
exclusions: Do not label drought from one wilted, chlorotic, curled, or drooping image without a plant-linked moisture measurement and irrigation timeline.
If the root zone is adequately moist at representative center, edge, and depth locations while wilt persists, investigate other causes rather than assuming hidden drought.
Measure root-zone EC and source-water/fertilizer history because elevated salts can create osmotic stress even when volumetric water content appears adequate.
Exclude overwatering or hypoxia using moisture history, drainage, aeration, odor, and root color and firmness; drought and hypoxia can produce overlapping canopy wilt.

Inspect roots and crown for brown, slimy, sloughed, necrotic, sunken, or internally discolored tissue and obtain laboratory confirmation when Pythium, Fusarium, Rhizoctonia, or vascular disease remains plausible.

Record air temperature, leaf temperature, relative humidity, VPD, PPFD, and airflow because high atmospheric demand or heat/light injury can change midday leaf posture without a primary soil-water deficit.

Inspect intact root-ball geometry and irrigation wetting because root binding, hydrophobic substrate, preferential flow, blocked emitters, and small root volume can create localized water shortage with distinct corrective needs.
Exclude broken stems, girdling, transplant damage, pest injury, and normal cultivar or circadian leaf posture using crown inspection, organism scouting, matched controls, and time-of-day replication.

progression.description: Measured root-zone water content declines; stomatal regulation and transpiration can change before a reliable visible symptom appears.
Leaf angle or turgor changes relative to the same plant's baseline and matched controls, often varying with time of day, VPD, cultivar, and acclimation.
Photosynthesis, expansion, leaf area, or leaf retention may decline; chlorosis was observed in one controlled flowering protocol but is not specific.
Prolonged or stronger deficit can reduce biomass or yield, with magnitude depending on genotype, stage, environment, root volume, and protocol.
Water status and visible posture may recover sooner than photosynthesis or growth; incomplete or absent recovery triggers root, crown, EC, and vascular investigation.

lookAlikes: Normal cultivar-specific or circadian leaf posture
Hydrophobic substrate, preferential flow, or blocked emitter
Transplant shock or mechanical root loss
Potassium or nitrogen deficiency with marginal/older-leaf symptoms
Camera angle, lens perspective, or time-of-day mismatch
confirmation: Assign a plant identifier and capture the whole canopy from fixed front and side positions plus representative fan leaves, substrate surface, container, emitter, drainage, and root-zone context with a metric scale and neutral color reference.

Measure volumetric water content or a validated medium-appropriate moisture proxy at multiple center, perimeter, and depth positions; log calibrated method, timestamp, last irrigation, applied volume, runoff, and the crop-specific baseline.

Repeat leaf-angle or posture images at the same time of day and camera geometry before deficit, during the suspected event, immediately before rehydration, and after rehydration; compare a matched same-cultivar irrigated plant.
Record air and leaf temperature, relative humidity, VPD, PPFD, and airflow at each capture so atmospheric demand can be separated from root-zone water availability.
Measure root-zone EC and pH, inspect emitter output and wetting uniformity, and document intact root-ball volume and boundary condition before disturbing roots.

Inspect roots, crown, and stem cross-sections for decay, lesions, odor, sloughing, galls, insects, girdling, and internal discoloration; send plant-linked samples for pathogen or nematode testing when indicated.

Keep symptom-only, detached-leaf-only, single-timepoint, unmatched, sensor-unlinked, generated, vendor, anecdotal, unverified, and rights-unclear captures out of the confirmed class and every automated training split.
immediateActions: Verify root-zone moisture, emitter function, wetting uniformity, EC, and drainage before applying water solely because the canopy appears wilted.

Preserve pre-correction images and measurements, then rehydrate conservatively according to medium and root condition while monitoring runoff and avoiding abrupt saturation of a compromised root zone.
Segregate or flag plants with root/crown decay, vascular discoloration, galls, or insects for diagnostic review rather than treating them as simple drought.
correctivePlan: Correct the documented delivery failure, insufficient volume/frequency, hydrophobicity, root-volume mismatch, or excessive atmospheric demand using production-system-specific measurements rather than a universal schedule.

Trend moisture, leaf posture, water status where available, EC, new growth, and root health after correction; persistent decline requires reassessment for salinity, hypoxia, structural injury, and disease.
Do not intentionally reproduce a published drought endpoint as a corrective or production recipe; controlled experimental stress thresholds are not validated as universal safe practices.
prevention: Build cultivar-, stage-, container-, substrate-, and environment-specific irrigation baselines from calibrated measurements and plant-linked observations.
Audit emitter output, pressure, wetting footprint, drainage, root volume, substrate rewetting behavior, and sensor placement before high-demand periods.
Use fixed-view, fixed-time healthy reference captures so normal circadian and cultivar posture can be distinguished from a developing water deficit.
warnings: Do not use one wilted photograph as proof of drought; retain it only as an unconfirmed visual lead until plant-linked water evidence and exclusions are available.
Wilting, leaf-angle change, chlorosis, slow growth, and rehydration response are supportive but not specific; drought remains an exposure-linked diagnosis.

The approximately 11-day drying period, -1.5 MPa plant-water-potential endpoint, and roughly 52% leaf-angle change came from one controlled flowering chemovar and must not be used as universal thresholds.

Hemp cultivars differ substantially in soil-drying and VPD responses, and observation time changes apparent wilting; a model must not learn one canopy posture as genotype-independent drought ground truth.
Published effects on cannabinoid concentration, biomass, and yield vary by genotype, severity, stage, and protocol; this diagnostic profile does not recommend intentional drought stress.

No licensed, plant-linked Cannabis drought progression image or verified diagnostic video with reusable item-level rights was located for this batch; publisher figures remain citations only and media stays empty.

sources.title: Genotypic Variation in Photosynthesis and Biomass Partitioning Underlies Agronomic Performance and Cannabinoid Profile in Cannabis sativa Under Drought
supportedClaims: Water deficit imposed at early flowering reduced leaf area and affected plant water status, photosynthesis, biomass partitioning, and cannabinoid response in a genotype-dependent way.
Different Cannabis genotypes used different physiological drought responses, so visual canopy appearance or one moisture reading is not a universal drought-severity scale.

sources.title: Variation in Hydric Response of Two Industrial Hemp Varieties (Cannabis sativa) to Induced Water Stress
supportedClaims: Two hemp varieties showed notably different water-stress strategies, including partial stomatal closure in one and rapid leaf shedding in another.
The genotype-dependent responses support using substrate moisture and plant water-status context rather than a single visual symptom to identify water deficit.

sources.title: Increasing Inflorescence Dry Weight and Cannabinoid Content in Medical Cannabis Using Controlled Drought Stress
supportedClaims: In one controlled container-grown drug-type Cannabis experiment, fertigation was withheld during flowering week 7 until midday plant water potential reached approximately -1.5 MPa after 11 days; substrate volumetric moisture, plant water potential, photosynthesis, and leaf angle were measured against irrigated controls.

At the treatment endpoint, plants were visibly wilted and the measured indicator-leaf angle was approximately 52% greater than its initial angle; veinal chlorosis had appeared after about nine days, first on older leaves and to a lesser extent on newly formed leaves across the plant.

The day after re-fertigation, mean midday plant water potential recovered to the control level while net photosynthesis had only partially recovered, showing that response variables and recovery timing need not move together.

The timing, -1.5 MPa endpoint, leaf-angle change, chlorosis, and cannabinoid results come from one chemovar and one controlled flowering protocol; none is a universal Cannabis drought threshold, visual signature, or production recommendation.
The article figures are publisher-hosted copyrighted scientific content without a verified item-level reusable asset license, so they are citation evidence only and are not indexed as dataset media.

sources.title: Physiological screening for drought-tolerance traits among hemp (Cannabis sativa L.) cultivars in controlled environments and in field
sources.organization: Journal of Crop Improvement (Sheldon et al.)
supportedClaims: Progressive soil-drying trials found substantial cultivar differences in the fraction-of-transpirable-soil-water point at which hemp transpiration declined; five of thirteen cultivars closed stomata comparatively early.
A separate high-VPD screen found cultivar-specific limited-transpiration responses, with fitted VPD breakpoints ranging from 1.2 to 2.6 kPa among four responsive cultivars.

In a rainfed field comparison of six cultivars, wilting scores and relative water content differed among cultivars; Ha3ze, Carolina, and topped T1 had the lowest wilting scores during the reported midday observation period.
Wilting posture therefore depends on genotype, soil drying, atmospheric demand, observation time, and acclimation; the study does not establish one image-only drought threshold for Cannabis.
The publisher PDF and its plots do not provide verified reusable item-level media rights for this dataset, so no figure or frame is indexed as training or display media.

sources.title: Physiological and morphological responses of industrial hemp (Cannabis sativa L.) to water deficit
sources.organization: Industrial Crops and Products (Gill et al.)
supportedClaims: An 85-day greenhouse experiment on industrial hemp cultivar Black Label compared moderate and extreme water deficit with a control and measured morphological, physiological, and biochemical responses.

Water deficit reduced total biomass and total seed yield, reduced stomatal opening and transpiration, increased water-use efficiency and proline accumulation, and still allowed plants to survive and produce filled seed under the tested conditions.

These single-cultivar endpoint responses support drought as a growth and yield stress but do not validate a universal visible severity scale, mortality expectation, or cannabinoid-production response for other Cannabis genotypes and stages.
The article is marked in copyright by its institutional repository; no image, figure, or video is indexed or copied as reusable media.

name: Salinity / elevated root-zone EC stress
summary: Salinity/high-EC stress is an exposure-response diagnosis in which measured dissolved salts coincide with impaired Cannabis growth, physiology, or yield. EC reports total ionic conductivity but not which ions caused it: direct Cannabis experiments produced different responses when EC was raised with NaCl, concentrated nutrients, hydroponic solution, or aquaponic solution. Brown tips, chlorosis, wilt, and necrosis are therefore nonspecific and require plant-linked EC trends, solution composition, pH, moisture, roots, and matched controls.
affectedParts: irrigation water, nutrient solution, substrate, or root zone
sampled leaves of documented age and canopy position
stems, leaves, inflorescences, biomass, and yield secondarily
stages: all production stages with a measured saline or concentrated-nutrient exposure
indicators: Measured irrigation or root-zone EC is elevated relative to the established crop baseline while growth declines
Growth suppression occurs together with a documented saline or high-salt root-zone exposure
Leaf nutrient imbalance appears after a measured salinity increase rather than an isolated single-element withholding pattern
Repeated plant-linked measurements show EC rising before or with reduced canopy expansion, leaf chlorophyll index, biomass accumulation, or yield relative to a matched same-cultivar control.
The affected distribution follows a documented solution, tank, irrigation zone, emitter, recirculation loop, container, or substrate-extraction pattern rather than a random lesion pattern.

Water, nutrient-solution, substrate-extract, or tissue chemistry identifies the ions or fertilizer concentration that produced the conductivity; EC alone does not identify sodium, chloride, or any single nutrient.

Visible leaf necrosis may appear under severe NaCl exposure, but one Early Haze rockwool trial observed it only at its two highest NaCl EC treatments while growth or yield effects occurred without that sign.

Direct studies show that production system and salt composition alter the response: hydroponic and aquaponic solutions differed under the same NaCl treatments, and nutrient-raised EC differed from NaCl-raised EC.
exclusions: Do not label salinity or “nutrient burn” from brown tips, marginal necrosis, chlorosis, curl, wilt, dark foliage, or stunting without a plant-linked EC measurement and exposure history.
If EC is stable within the established crop baseline and no saline, concentrated-fertilizer, source-water, recirculation, or accumulation pathway is documented, investigate another cause.
Measure root-zone water content across representative center, edge, and depth positions because simple drought, preferential wetting, or a failed emitter can resemble osmotic stress.
Exclude overwatering and hypoxia with irrigation history, drainage, aeration, odor, and root color and firmness; a wet root zone does not prove salts are causal.
Measure root-zone pH and review tissue or solution chemistry because abnormal pH or a verified single-element deficiency or toxicity can create a similar canopy pattern.
Inspect intact roots and crown for brown, slimy, sloughed, galled, sunken, or internally discolored tissue and obtain organism confirmation when root disease or nematodes remain plausible.
Record air and leaf temperature, relative humidity, VPD, PPFD, airflow, and recent spray history to exclude heat, light, high atmospheric demand, droplet, and contact injury.

Check root-ball geometry, substrate compaction, container temperature, and root restriction because small or uneven root volume can produce localized water and nutrient stress without primary salinity.

progression.description: A source-water, fertilizer, recirculation, evaporation, drainage, or salt-addition event changes the measured input or root-zone EC; no reliable visible sign may yet be present.
Plant water relations, chlorophyll index, gas exchange, nutrient uptake, or canopy expansion may diverge from matched controls before a specific color or morphology appears.
Repeated whole-plant views may show reduced height, width, leaf production, biomass, or inflorescence growth, but the pattern depends on cultivar, stage, medium, solution type, and ion mixture.

Necrosis or broader decline may develop under severe exposure; direct Early Haze evidence limits visible necrosis to extreme NaCl treatments in that study and does not validate brown tips as a general threshold.

After the documented salt source and root-zone conditions are corrected, compare EC and new growth over time; old necrotic tissue does not reverse, and absent recovery triggers pH, moisture, root, vascular, and pathogen investigation.

lookAlikes: Abnormal root-zone pH or mixed nutrient lockout
Boron, manganese, or other nutrient toxicity
Foliar spray, disinfectant, or contact injury
confirmation: Calibrate the EC and pH meters and record input water, mixed solution, and representative root-zone or leachate values with the extraction method, temperature compensation, units, date, and plant or irrigation-zone identity.
Sample multiple center, perimeter, and depth positions or multiple emitters and containers; compare the trend with the established production baseline and a matched same-cultivar unaffected control.

Document fertilizer products, mixing order and concentration, source-water analysis, sodium and chloride inputs, irrigation volume, drainage fraction, recirculation history, evaporation, and any tank or dosing fault.
When the salt source is uncertain, obtain solution, substrate-extract, and tissue analysis for sodium, chloride, and relevant macro- and micronutrients; do not infer ion composition from EC.
Measure root-zone moisture, pH, and temperature and record air and leaf temperature, relative humidity, VPD, PPFD, and airflow at the same time as each visual capture.

Inspect and photograph the intact root ball, crown, drainage pattern, emitter placement, and root color and firmness; use diagnostic testing when disease, nematodes, or vascular injury remains plausible.

Capture fixed whole-plant front and side views plus top, upper-leaf, lower-leaf, margin, underside, root-zone, meter-display, and source-label views at the same time of day before exposure, during the EC rise, before correction, and during recovery.

Keep symptom-only, detached-leaf-only, single-timepoint, unmatched, meter-unlinked, composition-unknown, generated, vendor, anecdotal, forum, unverified, and rights-unclear captures out of the confirmed salinity class and route them to human review.
immediateActions: Verify the reading with a calibrated meter and a medium-appropriate sampling method before changing fertilizer or irrigation.
Record moisture, pH, roots, solution composition, and the affected irrigation zone before corrective actions erase the exposure evidence.
correctivePlan: Correct the documented salt source, dosing fault, source-water problem, recirculation accumulation, or root-zone concentration with a crop- and medium-specific plan; this record does not prescribe a universal flush volume or target EC.
Trend input and root-zone EC, moisture, pH, new growth, and matched controls after correction; investigate coexisting root or environmental injury if recovery does not follow.
prevention: Trend calibrated input and root-zone EC with consistent sampling methods, units, temperature handling, crop stage, and irrigation-zone identity.
Account separately for source-water ions, fertilizer formulation, drainage, recirculation, evaporation, substrate, container size, cultivar, and crop stage when establishing baselines and alerts.
warnings: EC is a conductivity measurement, not an ion identity: the same EC can be produced by NaCl or by different nutrient mixtures with different Cannabis responses.
The published 1.8 to 12 mS/cm, 1 to 40 mM NaCl, and 0.4 to 6 dS/m treatments are study-specific exposures, not universal safe, toxic, correction, or training-label thresholds.
Do not diagnose “nutrient burn” or salinity from brown tips, marginal necrosis, chlorosis, curl, wilt, dark foliage, or stunting alone; photo/video-only confidence is capped at 0.20.

Visible necrosis was restricted to the highest NaCl treatments in one Early Haze rockwool experiment, while other measured effects occurred without that sign; absence or presence of necrosis is not decisive.

The evidence spans one drug-type chemovar, Early Haze, and Felina 32 fiber hemp under distinct hydroponic, aquaponic, rockwool, mesocosm, nutrient, NaCl, and biostimulant conditions; cultivar and system transfer requires human review.

No licensed, plant-linked Cannabis salinity progression image or verified diagnostic video met the acquisition standard, so media remains an explicit gap and automated training eligibility remains false.

sources.title: Effect of saline irrigation and plant-based biostimulant application on fiber hemp (Cannabis sativa L.) growth and phytocannabinoid composition
supportedClaims: Felina 32 fiber hemp in an outdoor mesocosm was irrigated with NaCl solutions at 2, 4, and 6 dS/m and compared with a 0.4 dS/m tap-water control.
The 2, 4, and 6 dS/m irrigation treatments limited crop growth by 7%, 30%, and 48%, respectively; biomass effects followed measured salinity rather than a diagnostic leaf-color class.

The experiment documented altered sodium, chloride, phosphate, nitrate, potassium, and calcium assimilation in leaves, supporting broad mineral imbalance as a measured consequence rather than proof of a single-element deficiency.

Because the study used one fiber cultivar, NaCl-defined irrigation treatments, an outdoor mesocosm, and a biostimulant factor, its EC values are treatment conditions rather than universal Cannabis thresholds.

sources.title: Aquaponic and Hydroponic Solutions Modulate NaCl-Induced Stress in Drug-Type Cannabis sativa L.
supportedClaims: A controlled indoor flowering experiment tested one type-II chemovar at 1 to 40 mM NaCl in hydroponic and aquaponic solutions and measured canopy growth, chlorophyll content index, gas exchange, chlorophyll fluorescence, water-use physiology, solution pH/EC, yield, and cannabinoids.
At 40 mM NaCl, hydroponic plants had reduced growth index and chlorophyll content index over time, while the same measured responses were not significantly affected by NaCl in the aquaponic solution.
The solution-dependent result and single-chemovar flowering design show that production system, genotype, stage, and treatment composition must accompany any image or video label.
The study did not establish a universal visible symptom signature; image appearance alone cannot identify NaCl exposure or elevated root-zone EC as the primary cause.

sources.title: Salinity effects on yield and nutrient uptake in Cannabis sativa L.
supportedClaims: Early Haze Cannabis was grown hydroponically in rockwool at 1.8, 3, 6, 9, or 12 mS/cm, with EC raised either by increasing N, P, K, Ca, Mg, and S together or by adding NaCl to the 1.8 mS/cm nutrient solution.
Shoot and bud weight declined under both EC-raising pathways, but the response boundaries differed, demonstrating that equal EC does not identify the salt composition or a single causal ion.

Visible leaf necrosis occurred only in the 9 and 12 mS/cm NaCl treatments; absence of necrosis did not exclude yield effects, and necrosis at those extreme study treatments is not a universal field threshold.

Low leaf phosphorus in some low-EC treatments was associated with root-zone pH above 7.5, showing why pH and tissue chemistry must be checked rather than treating EC or leaf appearance as a single-nutrient diagnosis.

The trial used one cultivar, rockwool, hydroponic nutrient solutions, and deliberately constructed EC treatments; transfer to other cultivars, media, salt mixtures, and irrigation systems requires human review.

name: Hop latent viroid
summary: A systemic viroid whose Cannabis expression ranges from asymptomatic infection to genotype- and stage-dependent dudding, poor rooting, stunting, abnormal foliage, and reduced inflorescence or trichome development. Appearance is neither necessary nor sufficient for diagnosis: a ground-truth HLVd label requires a validated molecular result linked to the sampled plant.
affectedParts: young and expanded foliage across the canopy
stages: field growth with symptoms potentially clearer from mid-season onward
indicators: Short internodes
Brittle stems or leaves
Stunted growth
No visible abnormality: infected stock plants and young rooted cuttings can be asymptomatic, so a normal-looking frame is not an HLVd-negative label.
Poor or delayed root emergence in cuttings taken from an infected mother, evaluated against same-age clean comparators; weak rooting is nonspecific and requires root-zone and pathogen exclusions.
Whole-plant stunting or reduced vigor relative to genetically matched, same-age plants under the same environment rather than an isolated small plant without context.
Shorter internodes, smaller leaves, or compact architecture distributed across new growth; severity can vary by genotype and must not be confused with stable genetic stature or deliberate training.
Mild leaf curl, mottling, yellow patterning, generalized yellowing, or misshapen leaves; no single color or leaf-shape pattern is consistently present or specific to HLVd.
Brittle stems or branches affecting otherwise intact shoots; a single snapped or trained branch is not evidence of systemic infection.
During flowering, reduced inflorescence-stem growth, smaller or poorly developed flowers, and yellowing or darkening of leaves surrounding flowers can occur in susceptible genotypes.

Reduced glandular-trichome development may appear as lower resin coverage at matched magnification and maturity, but trichome density or head size alone cannot distinguish HLVd from genetics, maturity, lighting, temperature, handling, or imaging differences.
exclusions: Do not assign HLVd from stunting, short internodes, yellowing, leaf curl, brittle growth, poor roots, small flowers, low resin, or any combination of visible signs without a plant-linked validated molecular result.
Measured root-zone pH, EC, moisture, oxygenation, or nutrient correction explains the change and the suspect plant is molecularly negative on appropriately collected and timed samples.

Root and crown examination plus laboratory work identifies Pythium, Fusarium, Rhizoctonia, root aphids, fungus-gnat larvae, root binding, or another cause of poor rooting and decline without HLVd detection.
Magnified inspection confirms broad mites, hemp russet mites, thrips, or spider mites that account for distorted or mottled new growth, with no supporting HLVd assay.

Compact stature, short internodes, or low trichome coverage remains stable in a molecularly negative clonal lineage under healthy measured conditions, supporting a genetic or developmental trait rather than infection.
Yellowing follows the older-to-younger distribution and timing expected for measured nitrogen deficiency or normal late-cycle senescence, and properly sampled tissue is HLVd-negative.
A single branch is brittle, wilted, or undersized after topping, wind, abrasion, constriction, or another documented mechanical event while the rest of the plant and new growth remain normal.

One negative leaf sample is not a universal exclusion when sampling timing, tissue distribution, extraction quality, or inhibition is uncertain; use the laboratory sampling plan and retest roots or multiple positions when advised.

progression.description: Stock plants, mother plants, seedlings, and young cuttings can carry detectable HLVd without reliable above-ground symptoms. Image or video alone cannot establish either positive or negative status.

Cuttings from infected mothers may root slowly or poorly. Capture matched clean and suspect clones from the same lineage, including root emergence and root-zone conditions, but retain a nonspecific weak-rooting label until molecular testing.

Depending on genotype, plants may remain asymptomatic or develop mild curl, mottling, smaller or misshapen leaves, short internodes, brittle growth, and reduced stature. There is no universal visual order.

Susceptible plants can show more obvious stunting, reduced inflorescence-stem and flower development, altered leaves around flowers, and reduced trichome development. Compare the same genotype, age, environment, and flower position.

Institutional Pacific Northwest observations report that foliar symptoms and stunting may become more obvious from mid-season onward, but environment and genotype alter expression; record serial change rather than inferring infection age from one frame.

lookAlikes: Genetic dwarfism, compact architecture, or cultivar-specific low vigor
Normal late-flowering senescence or cultivar-specific fade
Nitrogen, sulfur, iron, magnesium, or other nutrient deficiency
Excess fertilizer, salinity, or root-zone pH stress
Pythium, Fusarium, Rhizoctonia, or other root/crown disease
Root binding, waterlogging, drought, or low root-zone oxygen
Broad mite or hemp russet mite injury
Beet curly top virus, phytoplasma, or another systemic pathogen
Heat, high light, photoperiod, or plant-growth-regulator injury
Mechanical damage, topping, or training response
Normal genetic or maturity-driven differences in flower and trichome development
confirmation: Submit plant-linked samples to a qualified plant diagnostic laboratory for a validated HLVd RT-PCR, RT-qPCR, or equivalent sequence-specific assay; a photo, video, growth pattern, or trichome image cannot confirm infection.

Follow the laboratory’s current sampling instructions. Because HLVd distribution can vary across leaves and roots, record the tissue type and canopy position and consider paired root plus upper, middle, or lower foliage samples when the laboratory recommends them.

For young rooted cuttings, roots may provide a more consistent testing target than leaves; Oregon State reports that roots can test positive about two weeks after cuttings are made, while young plants may remain visually normal above ground.

Retest when an assay is negative but sample timing, tissue choice, extraction quality, inhibition, chain of custody, or symptoms remain concerning; do not reinterpret one poorly contextualized negative leaf as proof that the whole plant is clean.

Pair molecular testing with same-genotype, same-age, same-environment clean controls and serial whole-plant measurements so reductions in height, internode length, root emergence, flower development, or trichome appearance are not attributed across unmatched plants.

Inspect and document roots, crown, leaf undersides, growing tips, root-zone pH/EC/moisture, irrigation history, light/temperature, and recent training or chemical exposure to evaluate common non-HLVd causes and possible mixed problems.

For image/video ground truth, preserve the plant ID, cultivar or genotype, sample date, sampled tissue and position, assay method and result, symptom date, and source group. Keep unlinked, symptom-only, detached-leaf-only, and assay-panel-only captures out of the confirmed class.
immediateActions: Flag and physically segregate suspect propagation material while results are pending; stop taking or distributing cuttings, pollen, seed, or tools from the suspect plant.
Use separate or decontaminated cutting tools and handling equipment according to a validated facility protocol, and avoid moving sap from suspect plants to clean stock.
Capture matched whole-plant, canopy, growing-tip, root, and flower views before destructive sampling, but label the observation “HLVd suspect” rather than confirmed.
correctivePlan: Base removal, retention, retesting, and sanitation decisions on the confirmed laboratory result and a written facility disease protocol.
If HLVd is not detected, continue the differential workup for root pathogens, mites, nutrient and root-zone problems, systemic viruses or phytoplasmas, genetic traits, and maturity.
Do not promise that a visible recovery, treatment, or single cleaning product eradicates HLVd; verify clean status through the testing and sanitation program.
prevention: Use traceable mother stock, incoming clones, pollen, and seed that have been tested under an appropriate sampling program.
Separate untested propagation material from clean stock and maintain plant IDs linking mothers, cuttings, assay results, dates, and work areas.

Clean sap and plant debris from tools, benches, irrigation components, and equipment, then apply a viroid protocol validated for the specific surface, product concentration, contact time, and workflow.
warnings: HLVd cannot be confirmed or excluded from visible symptoms; infected plants may be asymptomatic and visually abnormal plants may have many other causes.
Growth reduction, flower loss, THC or terpene change, and trichome effects are genotype- and experiment-dependent; do not apply study percentages to an individual plant or cultivar.
One tissue or canopy position may test negative while another tests positive, so sampling context and assay quality must remain attached to every laboratory label.

An RT-PCR signal establishes target RNA in the sampled material; sanitation experiments based on loss of an amplifiable band do not automatically prove every treated surface or plant material is noninfectious.

The two Oregon State hemp figures below are metadata-only references. Their creators are credited, but no explicit reuse license is stated; do not display, copy, modify, or use them for automated training without written permission.
Keep every symptom-only, unlinked assay, detached-leaf-only, unmatched-comparator, low-resolution trichome, or uncertain-tissue sample flagged for human review.

sources.title: Hop Latent Viroid: A Hidden Threat to the Cannabis Industry
supportedClaims: Published Cannabis reports associate HLVd with dudding symptoms that can include stunting, shortened internodes, brittle stems, smaller or malformed leaves, weak rooting, and reduced inflorescence quality, while some infected plants remain asymptomatic.
Because symptom expression can vary with genotype, growth stage, environment, and viroid concentration, molecular testing rather than visual appearance is required to establish an HLVd label.
This article is a review and must not be used as a substitute for the plant-linked molecular evidence or study-specific limits in the primary sources attached to this profile.

sources.title: Symptomology, Prevalence, and Impact of Hop Latent Viroid on Greenhouse-Grown Cannabis (Cannabis sativa L.) Plants in Canada
sources.organization: Canadian Journal of Plant Pathology (Punja et al.)
supportedClaims: Across greenhouse production samples, symptom expression varied with growth stage and genotype: stock and vegetative plants ranged from asymptomatic to mild leaf curl and mottling, while flowering plants could show extreme stunting and reduced inflorescence development.

HLVd was detected in upper, middle, and lower canopy leaves and in roots, but its distribution varied among plant tissues and genotypes; one leaf position is therefore not a universal sampling rule or a reliable negative control.

Under the study conditions, infected flowering plants showed genotype-dependent reductions of 12–42% in inflorescence stem length, fresh weight, and plant height compared with noninfected plants, and diseased inflorescences had lower THC and terpene levels.

Glandular trichomes on affected plants had shorter stalks and smaller heads and appeared shrivelled after inflorescences were dried; these group-level measurements do not make sparse trichomes or reduced resin a visually specific HLVd sign.
The article is CC BY 4.0, but its stage, genotype, and tissue comparisons must remain source-grouped and laboratory-bounded if individual figures are later evaluated for training.

sources.title: Transmission, Spread, Longevity and Management of Hop Latent Viroid, a Widespread and Destructive Pathogen Affecting Cannabis (Cannabis sativa L.) Plants in North America
supportedClaims: RT-PCR/RT-qPCR detected HLVd in asymptomatic stock plants and rooted vegetative cuttings; in the stock genotypes tested, roots were the most consistent positive tissue while individual upper or lower leaf samples were not consistently positive.

After stem inoculation with infectious sap, HLVd was detected in roots within 2–3 weeks and foliage within 4–6 weeks, and spread was faster under a flowering-inducing 12:12 photoperiod than under 24-hour lighting in that experiment.

The study detected HLVd in inflorescence tissue, glandular trichomes, dried flowers, pollen, seeds, and other production-system materials, supporting plant-part and propagation context but not image-only confirmation.

Figure 1 combines stock and flowering plant appearance with tissue-specific RT-PCR results and sequence-confirmed bands; it is a molecularly anchored CC BY 4.0 reference but not a single-class visual training sample.

Chemical treatments in the study were evaluated partly by loss of amplifiable HLVd RNA; absence of an RT-PCR band after treatment must not be generalized into a universal facility sanitation guarantee without a validated protocol.

sources.title: Hop Latent Viroid in Hemp
supportedClaims: Visual recognition is unreliable because infected hemp can remain asymptomatic or show subtle, variable symptoms influenced by viroid strain, plant genetics, environment, and viroid concentration.

The institutional hemp field and survey context includes yellow patterning or generalized yellowing, brittle branches, misshapen or smaller leaves, shorter internodes, stunting, and small buds, with foliar symptoms and stunting often more apparent from mid-season onward in the Pacific Northwest.

Cuttings from infected mother plants can root poorly while young plants may show no obvious above-ground symptoms; roots can test positive about two weeks after cuttings are made and may be more reliable than leaves for testing young plants.

The page recommends tested stock, separation and testing of propagation material, removal of confirmed infected plants, and cleaning tools, surfaces, and equipment that contact sap; it also states that no method reliably guarantees complete HLVd inactivation on contaminated tools.

The page credits the detached-leaf survey composite to Cynthia M. Ocamb and the two-stage field composite to K. Frost but states no explicit reusable-media license, so both assets are metadata-only license-review references.

name: Beet curly top virus disease
summary: A beet-leafhopper-vectored viral disease of field-grown hemp that can produce uneven stunting, bushy or shortened shoots, twisted and upward-curled young leaves, and pale-green, yellow, mosaic, or fully chlorotic foliage.
indicators: Stunted or bushy plant architecture
Twisted, puckered, or upward-curled young leaves
Pale-green to yellow new foliage
Yellow mosaic or generalized chlorosis
Shortened stem growth
Symptomatic shoots beside apparently healthy shoots on the same plant
exclusions: Microscopy confirms broad mites or hemp russet mites in protected new growth
Distortion follows a documented herbicide or plant-growth-regulator exposure pattern
Symptoms are uniform only on the hottest or brightest canopy surface and measured environmental stress explains the distribution
Only older leaves follow a mobile-nutrient pattern without twisted new shoots
A validated laboratory assay is negative on properly collected tissue and another cause is confirmed

progression.description: New growth may begin twisting or puckering while shoots slow; pale-green or yellow coloration can develop, but appearance varies by cultivar, growth stage, temperature, and virus strain.
Plants become stunted or bushy with shortened stems and distorted, upward-curled, yellowed, or mosaic foliage; shoots may differ markedly within one plant.
Early infections are generally more severe, yet some plants appear to outgrow visible symptoms or retain a mixture of symptomatic and apparently healthy shoot portions.

confirmation: Do not confirm BCTV from an image or from beet-leafhopper presence; submit representative symptomatic tissue to a plant diagnostic laboratory using a validated BCTV-targeted molecular assay.
Sample newly symptomatic shoots rather than only old damaged leaves, and include an apparently healthy comparison when the laboratory protocol allows.
Ask the laboratory to consider other viruses or mixed infection when symptoms or assay results do not fully agree; BCTV can occur in mixed strain or mixed pathogen infections.
Record field position, onset date, affected growth stage, nearby weed hosts, and beet-leafhopper observations to support epidemiological interpretation without treating them as proof of infection.
immediateActions: Mark and isolate suspect propagation material; stop taking or distributing cuttings until laboratory results are available.
Scout the crop, field edges, leaf undersides, and nearby weeds for beet leafhoppers and additional symptomatic plants.
Prevent unverified symptom images from being assigned a virus ground-truth label.
correctivePlan: Base roguing or retention decisions on laboratory confirmation and the facility or field disease protocol.
Manage beet-leafhopper exposure with locally recommended legal practices; vector control does not cure an infected plant.
Continue monitoring because visible symptoms may vary among shoots or appear to recede.
prevention: Use tested propagation material and maintain source records.
Monitor beet leafhoppers from spring onward with crop inspection and field-edge trapping appropriate to the production system.
Reduce unmanaged weed and volunteer hosts around field borders using legal, agronomically appropriate practices.
warnings: Visual symptoms are not specific enough to confirm a virus.
A beet leafhopper on a plant does not establish that the insect or plant carries BCTV.

The two institutional hemp photographs below are metadata-only license-review candidates: no reuse license is stated, so they are hidden from the public gallery and prohibited from automated training.

sources.title: Curly Top Disease of Hemp (Cannabis sativa) in California Is Caused by Mild-Type Strains of Beet curly top virus Often in Mixed Infection
supportedClaims: California hemp plants with curly-top-like disease were characteristically stunted and bushy with distorted, upward-curled, yellowed leaves.
A multiplex PCR detected Beet curly top virus in 89% of hemp samples with curly-top-like symptoms, while other symptom types had low BCTV incidence and were associated with other factors.
An infectious BCTV-CO clone reproduced curly-top-like symptoms in hemp, fulfilling Koch’s postulates; mixed BCTV strain infections also occurred.

sources.title: Hemp (Cannabis sativa)-Curly Top
sources.publisher: Oregon State University, Washington State University, and University of Idaho Extension
supportedClaims: Hemp curly-top symptoms vary with variety, growth stage, temperature, and virus strain; predominant signs include stunting, twisted or curled leaves, and pale-green-to-yellow foliage.
Leaves may pucker and curl upward, or remain green while new growth twists and stem growth is stunted; earlier infection generally produces more severe symptoms.
Individual plants can contain symptomatic and apparently healthy shoot portions or appear to outgrow visible symptoms.
The four hemp symptom photographs are credited to C. M. Ocamb, Oregon State University, 2021; the landing page states copyright but provides no reuse license.

sources.title: Curly Top Virus
sources.organization: Utah State University Extension, Utah Plant Pest Diagnostic Laboratory
supportedClaims: Infected field-grown hemp can become stunted and develop yellow mosaic or generalized leaf chlorosis.
Beet leafhoppers transmit curly-top viruses during probing and feeding; scouting is especially important while plants are small and should include leaf undersides, field edges, and nearby weeds.
Yellow mosaic hemp samples should be submitted to a plant diagnostic laboratory, and tomato spotted wilt virus is an early-season look-alike.

name: Waterlogging or root-zone hypoxia
summary: A persistently saturated root zone can suppress Cannabis root elongation, leaf expansion, relative chlorophyll, gas exchange, and biomass; the canopy response overlaps drought, nutrient, transplant, and root-disease injury, so exposure measurements are required.
indicators: Root zone remains saturated or stands in water across repeated observations
Whole-plant growth and canopy expansion slow relative to a matched healthy plant
Root system is shorter or has less new growth than a matched control
Canopy greenness declines over time rather than forming discrete lesions
Leaf-area development and biomass accumulation remain depressed after drainage
exclusions: Container weight or substrate-water measurement shows the root zone is dry rather than saturated
The pattern is restricted to one mechanically damaged branch
Discrete leaf lesions, fungal growth, vascular discoloration, root galls, or organisms provide a better causal explanation
Roots are brown, soft, or decayed and a laboratory test identifies Pythium, Phytophthora, Fusarium, or another pathogen
Measured salinity or pH is outside the crop target and explains the distribution better
Only canopy posture is available without irrigation, drainage, root, or time-series context

progression.description: The container or soil zone remains saturated or flooded; canopy appearance can still be nonspecific, so the event should be labeled from measured exposure rather than leaf posture.
Controlled waterlogging reduced root length, leaf area, leaf-area index, relative chlorophyll, stomatal conductance, and plant biomass in Cannabis cv. G1.
In the same experiment, waterlogged plants remained below controls and water-shortage plants after seven days of recovery, especially for root length, leaf area, and biomass.
Longer exposure reduced canopy leaf area, relative chlorophyll, photosynthetic efficiency, root and shoot biomass, and flower biomass; exact timing and magnitude remain genotype- and stage-limited.

lookAlikes: High root-zone EC or pH-related nutrient unavailability
confirmation: Document irrigation volume and timing, drainage duration, runoff, standing water, container weight, or calibrated substrate-water content across time; a canopy photograph alone cannot confirm waterlogging.

Compare the entire plant and cleaned root system with a healthy plant of the same cultivar, age, medium, and stage, recording root length, active root tips, leaf-area expansion, and recovery after drainage is restored.
Measure root-zone pH and EC because salinity and nutrient availability can produce overlapping canopy decline.
If roots or crowns are discolored, soft, necrotic, or decayed, submit representative root and crown tissue to a plant diagnostic laboratory before assigning an abiotic-only label.
immediateActions: Stop adding unnecessary irrigation and remove standing water while preserving a documented sample of the pre-correction root-zone condition.
Separate drainage and runoff from healthy plants when infectious root disease remains possible.
Inspect roots, emitters, drain paths, and neighboring containers before choosing a correction.
correctivePlan: Correct the measured cause of persistent saturation, such as blocked drainage, excessive shot size or frequency, poor container drainage, compacted media, or flooding.
Return irrigation gradually to a measured dryback pattern appropriate to the crop stage and medium, then score only new growth and root recovery.
Use laboratory results and locally legal crop protocols if a root pathogen is confirmed; drainage correction alone does not establish or cure a pathogen diagnosis.
prevention: Record irrigation input, runoff, container weight or substrate water content, and dryback duration instead of relying on a fixed calendar.
Use matched healthy controls and photograph the whole plant, root zone, and cleaned roots across time.
Keep drainage paths functional and prevent shared runoff from moving between containers.
warnings: Reduced growth, pale foliage, or leaf posture is not specific to excess water and must not be used as image-only ground truth.
The controlled waterlogging results come from one Cannabis genotype and defined seven-to-21-day treatments; symptom timing and severity should not be generalized as universal thresholds.
Brown or decayed roots cannot safely be labeled abiotic hypoxia without excluding Pythium, Phytophthora, Fusarium, and other root diseases.
No symptom photograph with adequate Cannabis-specific confirmation and reusable provenance was admitted in this batch.

sources.title: Impact of varying water stress periods (water shortage vs. waterlogging) on Cannabis sativa growth, leaf physiology, and CBD content
sources.publisher: University of Agricultural Sciences and Veterinary Medicine Cluj-Napoca
supportedClaims: In a controlled Cannabis sativa cv. G1 experiment, waterlogging was imposed by standing potted plants in a two-centimetre sheet of water; diagnosis therefore depended on verified root-zone exposure rather than canopy appearance alone.

After seven vegetative-stage days, waterlogged plants had shorter roots, lower leaf area, lower leaf-area index, lower chlorophyll-meter readings, and less biomass than controls; their growth remained lowest after a seven-day recovery period.

During reproductive-stage exposure, waterlogging reduced leaf-area index, root and shoot biomass, stomatal conductance, relative chlorophyll content, and photosystem-II efficiency as duration increased, but responses varied with stage and duration.

Water shortage produced overlapping reductions in several above-ground measurements, so reduced canopy growth or greenness cannot distinguish excess water from insufficient water without root-zone measurements.

sources.title: Surveying for Potential Diseases and Abiotic Disorders of Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa) Production
supportedClaims: A 2017–2018 North Carolina survey based on 572 agronomic and 117 plant-clinic hemp submissions attributed common environmental disorders to excessive rainfall flooding roots and to poor root development in transplanted clones.
The same diagnostic survey found Pythium diseases in greenhouse hemp, supporting explicit separation of abiotic flooding injury from root-pathogen diagnoses.
